headline: HR buyer comparison-shopping assessments for 600 reps
summary: Amy is evaluating assessment vendors to baseline roughly 600 field staff and decide who can actually sell versus who belongs in an operations or service role, and she is openly comparing Gartner and RPG alongside OMG. Aaron disqualified himself on the operations half of her requirement inside the first two minutes of his overview, then answered her reporting and authenticity questions by screen-sharing a team report. She asked for pricing structure, a sample deck and a division of labor, and the call ended with a 45-minute follow-up booked for the 17th.
outcome_note: Amy booked a 45-minute follow-up for the 17th at 1:00 Pacific and asked Aaron to send the team report and an individual evaluation sample first.

moments.title: Hands her the agenda
moments.quote: So is there anything you'd like to talk or walk through so we can actually make a productive use of your time?
moments.why: One sentence that turns a vendor demo into her meeting.

moments.title: Breaks up the vendor list with a jab
moments.quote: How do you keep all this straight?
moments.why: She has just rattled off two competitors; he neither argues nor ignores it, he teases her about the workload.

moments.title: Lowers the stakes before presenting
moments.quote: And knowing we probably won't change the world in the next 15 minutes — and my middle daughter has a band concert — I'm happy to walk through at a very high level. And if we're off track from there, you can just say, all right, I got a better glimpse.
moments.why: Builds the exit ramp and the time box into the same breath, using his own schedule rather than pressure.

moments.title: Disqualifies his own product out loud
moments.quote: So that's where if you were looking for an all encompassing tool that would help from an operations side or an ops manager side — sorry, Amy, OMG is not going to be the way to go.
moments.why: Half her stated requirement is operations. He kills it in the first ninety seconds of the overview and buys credibility for everything after.

moments.title: Chicken and steak
moments.quote: It's kind of like, if you and I don't like to eat chicken, that doesn't mean we automatically like to eat steak.
moments.why: She tries to stretch the tool into an operations screen; he refuses in a way she laughs at instead of resents.

moments.title: Fight up front
moments.quote: And yes, I will be very transparent, because I'm a believer. And if we're going to fight, let's fight up front to make sure we're on the same page. And if it's not, that's okay. But if it is, it just makes everything so much smoother.
moments.why: States the rule of engagement, and she reciprocates with transparency for the rest of the call.

moments.title: Asks how she takes information before answering
moments.quote: I love how you asked that question. So let's take the trust portion. Are you in the weeds type of person or a big picture person, Amy?
moments.why: Then: 'So I'll give you a big picture answer with a sprinkling of in the weeds.' Steal this before any technical explanation.

moments.title: The googling-the-answer story
moments.quote: Objective Management Group actually has cookies built, that if somebody googles how to pass an OMG, it tags it, and it'll literally tell me — Amy Starr's confidence rating dropped because she actually googled how to pass an OMG evaluation at 1:38 Pacific time.
moments.why: Answers 'can people game it' with a specific, memorable mechanism instead of a reassurance.

moments.title: Draws the line on anonymity
moments.quote: That piece rolls up in a big team report, so it'll give 86% of your people do or do not trust. It will not tell us exactly who. Everything else is back to a person, except for the trust finding.
moments.why: She pushes to see individual trust answers; he holds the boundary without apologizing for it.

moments.title: The prospect asks for the next step
moments.quote: So here is what I would really like to do. I would like to continue the conversation, because I think what you've shown me today aligns with, from what I can tell, the needs that we have.
moments.why: The payoff. Listen to how little he had to do to get here after disqualifying himself at minute eight.

moments.title: Asks plainly for the date
moments.quote: When would you like to talk again?
moments.why: No pitch, no summary, no 'does that make sense' — four words.

moments.title: Won't price it in a vacuum
moments.quote: Amy, you've been very transparent, so I love the transparency, I'll be very transparent back. It's really based upon how much time and handholding and effort is required on our end versus what you guys handle.
moments.why: Refuses the pricing question and reframes it as a scoping question, while crediting her openness.

coaching_notes: Aaron disqualified himself on operations inside the first two minutes of his overview and it bought him the rest of the call. Watch how fast she started volunteering competitor intel afterwards.
'Are you in the weeds or a big picture person?' before answering a reporting question is the most portable thing on this recording.

The money never got touched. Six hundred people in the wrong roles has a number attached — revenue per rep, cost of a bad hire, cost of the Gartner contract — and none of it came up. She asked him for price; he never asked her what the problem was costing.
After minute eight this is a product demo driven by her questions. He asks three real questions in the back eighteen minutes. The call advanced anyway, but on her momentum, not his.

File problems: the filename says 'Alro' but the prospect is PeopleReady — Amy and Aaron both say 'people ready', and the 600-person field with recruiters and national/local account managers is staffing, not steel. The header date (March 17, 2024) also disagrees with the filename date.

headline: Consulting CEO buys assessments for two engineer partners

Call ended with three OMG evaluations agreed, an in-person debrief set for late July, and the retainer range on the table.
outcome_note: Austin agreed to all three completing the evaluation, gave Aaron his partners' names and spellings, and they set an in-person 90-minute debrief for the last week of July with Dana coordinating.

Gives the number without being pushed: retainer-based, no contract, 'you can fire us at any time,' and for three people roughly $1,700 to $2,800 a month. The dollar figure is garbled in the transcript as '1000, $702,800 a month.'
How are you going to frame it up?
I'll send that to you three, and then you'll tell me here, before I hang up, when you guys will have it completed by — knowing it's not a rush, because I'm out next week anyway.

And then we'll walk through the roadmap. And then once you get to that, it's either, hey, yes, this was very helpful, we can figure out some of this stuff on our own — or, no, this is very helpful, we want your help, we believe you can help, what's the plan?

moments.title: The weird question
moments.quote: You ready for a weird question? Everything you have said thus far, especially the last three minutes, I go, holy shit, that's pretty spot on. Why are your skills not transferring?
moments.why: Austin just spent four minutes proving he knows how to sell. Instead of agreeing, Aaron turns the competence into the problem.

moments.title: The golf coach answer
moments.quote: I took my son yesterday for golf lessons. He's five years old. I told the golf coach, hey, he's going to listen to you because you're a coach. You watch me go up there and teach him — I got it, dad, I got it.
moments.why: The prospect hands over the entire reason he needs an outsider, unprompted, because of one question.

moments.title: Asks about the competition directly
moments.quote: Have you talked to the other Sandler people in this town, since they're close too?
moments.why: No hedging, no fear of planting the idea. He wants to know who else is in play and asks.

moments.title: Tests the other two before selling to them
moments.quote: You mentioned a little bit earlier, Austin — do you believe your other two partners in crime have the appetite to sharpen their swords as much as you do?
moments.why: The buyer is enthusiastic; the users may not be. He checks before building a plan around them.

moments.title: Light callback that earns permission
moments.quote: I'm not a good read on people, but I think I picked that one up pretty quick, Austin.
moments.why: Austin has just described himself as flow where his partners are process. The joke lands and the questions get harder right after.

moments.title: Plants the assessment conversationally
moments.quote: And do you think it's more guts to go there, or tools and toolbox?
moments.why: Gets the prospect to split skills from will out loud, before the word 'evaluation' is ever used.

moments.title: The future-state question
moments.quote: And if this group is clicking on all cylinders, asking the right questions, able to follow process and still be authentic and not a freaking robot, growing those current clients — what's different from a business perspective?
moments.why: Produces the only number on the call: triple to four times in three years.

moments.title: Compliments a type A on purpose
moments.quote: I know it's uncomfortable right now for a type A person to actually get a compliment, but I have no incentive to kiss your ass. Where's your humility come from?
moments.why: Names the discomfort before causing it, and gets the grandfather story that explains the whole buying decision.

moments.title: Money before product
moments.quote: Is it worth $1,500 to you to get the data from Mehrdad, Dustin and Austin to figure out exactly what needs to happen to help you three x this company in the next three to four years?
moments.why: He has still not described what Lushin does. The commitment comes first, the explanation second, and Austin says yes in one word.

moments.title: Lab work
moments.quote: First thing I'm going to do is send you guys across the hall for some lab work, so to say. We're going to do the lab work first, find out if we need bandaids or Pepto-Bismol or surgeries.
moments.why: The cleanest version of the assessment framing in this batch — one metaphor, no feature list.

moments.title: Sets the floor on frequency before price
moments.quote: So if you're hoping that that conversation ends with, hey, we'll see you twice a year, I'm going to say we can just stop in two minutes, because it won't change anything.
moments.why: Kills the once-a-quarter workshop fantasy while the prospect is still enthusiastic, not after a proposal.

moments.title: Makes him rehearse the internal sell
moments.quote: How are you going to frame it up?
moments.why: Austin is about to explain this to two partners in two hours. Aaron hears the pitch before it happens.

coaching_notes: No up-front contract. Austin monologued for four minutes and Aaron let him, which worked because Austin self-qualified, but there was no stated agenda, no time box and no agreed exit.
He asked for the $1,500 commitment before describing a single feature. Study the order: problem, future state, humility, money, then product.

'Find out if we need bandaids or Pepto-Bismol or surgeries' and 'send you across the hall for some lab work' — the same framing he uses on Standard Electric two months later. It is his standard move and it works.
He set the engagement cadence expectation before giving a number, so the retainer landed against 'ongoing' rather than against 'a workshop.'

Transcript problem: Fireflies mis-assigns speakers through most of the back half. Several of Aaron's questions — 'How did you find us?' (9:14), 'Where do you get your humility from?' (19:47), 'You ready for the million dollar question?' (22:56) — sit inside Austin's blocks. Read by content, not label. The retainer figure at 28:35 is also garbled, and the prospect company is never named aloud.

moments.title: Up-front contract in her language
moments.quote: So to help your fun week remain fun, let's make this conversation productive for you. What would you like to make sure you get hammered out today, Tammy?
moments.why: Picks up 'fun week' from thirty seconds earlier and uses it to open the agenda. Warm and structured at the same time.

moments.title: Reframes the one-day ask without saying no
moments.quote: What drives the structure, Tammy? Is this to bring awareness, or is it more about some repetition to create some change? If you're looking to have more of embedded change, it's about smaller doses over a little bit longer period of time, versus a one day thing and then a one day thing a month later. Same amount of time, it's just spread out different.
moments.why: She asked for something he doesn't sell. He changes the shape of it on the spot and she never notices she was redirected.

moments.title: They don't know what they don't know
moments.quote: Tammy, with this group of ten, how much of it do you think is they don't know what they don't know?
moments.why: Her answer is one word — 'All of them' — and it justifies everything he proposes for the rest of the call.

moments.title: Plants the assessment before naming it
moments.quote: Is there any merit in Tammy's eyes to help them get clarity on what skill sets they're missing to be effective up front, what head trash they have from a sales perspective up front, what some of those guts and hidden weaknesses are — so they know what to correlate content back to?
moments.why: Describes the entire output of an OMG evaluation as a question about her training problem.

moments.title: Finds the hole in their hiring
moments.quote: And is there any data you collect throughout your hiring process from a sales perspective?
moments.why: Answer: no. That 'no' is the reason the assessment lands four minutes later.

moments.title: Keeps a hard question from stinging
moments.quote: You don't sit around all day with your feet propped up, Tammy.
moments.why: She just admitted nobody listens to the recorded calls. Instead of pressing, he gives her an out and the rapport holds.

moments.title: Asks permission to pivot
moments.quote: Can I make a suggestion here, and you can tell me if I'm way off base?
moments.why: Four seconds that convert a recommendation from a pitch into something she invited.

moments.title: The stutter step
moments.quote: There's a stutter step we often take to help find out the data and science behind literally what skill sets are they missing to be good hunters... and we review it with the Tammys of the world and go, here are the items that are going to have the biggest impact in the shortest amount of time, so we're actually addressing those things that are key and relevant and not touching the things that are natural to them.
moments.why: Positions the assessment as something that saves her training capacity, which is the constraint she named.

moments.title: The one-line justification for slowing down
moments.quote: And all we do is slow down up front to ultimately get the results faster.
moments.why: Pre-handles the objection to adding a step before the training she asked for.

moments.title: Prices it flat, unhedged, mid-call
moments.quote: If we send them across the hall for some lab work, and depending upon the number of people, it's $250 a person and $2,500 for the overview.
moments.why: No preamble, no apology, no 'it depends.' Listen to the delivery as much as the number.

moments.title: The differentiator in one sentence
moments.quote: Most quote-unquote sales training companies believe everything's about skills, and unfortunately it's not.
moments.why: Sets up strengths-versus-technique, and she immediately commits to a position — 'I think it's technique' — which is exactly the opening he wanted.

moments.title: Gets the decision process in two questions
moments.quote: Who's all sitting at that table? ... Tammy brings her go-to, Susie brings her go-to, and Bob brings his go-to?
moments.why: Payoff: it's her and the other three directors, and 'if we make that decision, then it's basically done' — the boss and owner are informed, not consulted.

coaching_notes: He converted a request for a one-day onboarding class into an assessment-first conversation without ever telling her no. The reframe at 2:35 is the whole move.
Price came out at minute eleven of a seventeen-minute call, unprompted and unhedged, right after she agreed on the approach — not at the end, not in a follow-up email.

No next meeting was booked. The call ends on 'Could I call you right back?' with nothing on the calendar and a video he owes her. That is the one clear miss, and it is a good example of how a warm call can still stall.
The decision-process questions at 15:18 and 16:27 are worth copying verbatim: who's at the table, does everyone bring their own vendor, and do the others see it the way you do.
Transcript quality is poor on names: Fireflies renders Tammy as Cammy, Timmy and Tim, and Aaron as 'Erin.' The header date (November 21, 2023) also disagrees with the filename date.

moments.why: Rare to hear on tape. Note that Rob doesn't pile on.

moments.title: One line instead of an argument
moments.quote: But it's hard to fix, really, anything in three days.
moments.why: Doug has just handed him the opening. Rob takes exactly one sentence of it.

moments.title: Ends on time
moments.quote: Why don't we do this? Because I have to go here — we were slotted for fifteen minutes.
moments.why: The slot was fifteen minutes and he treats it as real. Doug respects it and books the next one himself.

moments.title: Two options, no calendar ping-pong
moments.quote: Next Tuesday at eight or next Wednesday at nine.
moments.why: No link, no 'send me some times,' and the meeting is on the books ninety seconds later.

coaching_notes: This is not a prospect call. Doug Peterson owns the Crestcom franchise for Indiana, Ohio and Kentucky and is selling Rob on a referral partnership — study it as a call where the Lushin coach is the buyer, and watch how a trained seller behaves on the other side.

'What would I be hearing that should make me think of you?' is the reusable asset here. It converts an abstract partnership into a concrete trigger list, and it works just as well on a client who wants to refer you business.

Rob defines the fence precisely — customer-facing and revenue-impacting is Lushin's, HR/ops/finance leadership is open — which is useful language for any conversation about scope with a partner or a client.

He never asks what Doug wants in return, what volume either side could realistically send, or what a referred Crestcom client actually spends. The partnership stayed abstract, and the second meeting is Doug's thirty-minute overview rather than a working session on referral flow.
No up-front contract at the top; the fifteen-minute slot was pre-agreed but never restated, so Rob had to invoke it mid-sentence at 13:45.

19:00 through 19:38 is the best sequence in this batch: make the prospect guess the disqualifier, then state the single condition under which the relationship fails. It is a deal-killer question asked while the prospect is still enthusiastic.

'How much business is out there that you aren't getting?' produced 'easily double' and he left it there. No dollars, no units, no conversion to revenue — and no money of any kind was discussed on a thirty-minute call with a buyer whose father is already inclined to invest.

He surfaced the real obstacle out loud — two of eight leaders won't engage, and the president is himself a micromanager — and still asked for the next step rather than retreating from it. The homework for Graham and Eddie separately is a smart way to test the alignment he just heard is missing.

And so what that exercise looks like on your end is basically everybody that's in the sales organization spends about 45 minutes answering a bunch of questions. You and I get in the same room together, deliver the results, and then talk about whether the problems are worth fixing, how you'd like to fix them, if you'd want my help fixing them.
So if we wanted to, again, 45 minutes, everybody puts the time in. Your price on that is 97.50.
Asked what it costs to assess only the sales leader, Rob answers with a single word: "400."
Walk me through that. How do you make that decision?
So what do you think his take on all this will be?
So when do you want to talk again?

moments.title: Sorts the questionnaire for weak AND important
moments.quote: It could be weak, but not important. Are they weak and important? What do you think?
moments.why: A one-line filter that turns a survey of low scores into a short list worth money.

moments.title: The prospect takes back his own answer
moments.quote: And that's a good way of putting it because I said generally. Let me take that back. Generally, no. … So they're committed now, they're getting in front of people, but the level of skill isn't very high just because they don't know how.
moments.why: The payoff of a patient, low-pressure question. Rob said almost nothing; Loren corrected himself.

moments.title: Converts 'a lot' into a number
moments.quote: And when you say a lot, do you ever think of that in terms of dollars, percentage of quota? How would you articulate a lot or measure a lot?
moments.why: The single highest-value question on the call — everything priced later rests on the answer.

moments.title: Stress-tests the triple
moments.quote: So some people could quadruple or quintuple? Some people would double, not triple. But at the end of the day, you would triple the revenue?
moments.why: Rob keeps pushing on a number that is in his favor, which is exactly what makes it hold up later.

moments.title: Builds the team math
moments.quote: How many people on the team? How many people are at that $4 million mark?
moments.why: Three old-guard producers and eleven new hires on a draw — the whole shape of the problem comes out of four short questions.

moments.title: Tests whether the people can actually change
moments.quote: You think that they're willing, they would be committed, they would take responsibility, they would accept coaching, that it's within them to achieve what you need to achieve.
moments.why: Qualifies the team before selling a program to train the team.

moments.title: Does the leader know the right questions?
moments.quote: Do you know what the right questions are? Does your sales leader know what the right questions are, or is that a little bit of a mystery?
moments.why: Moves the gap from the reps up to leadership, which is where the engagement would actually live. Loren answers 'it's a mystery.'

moments.title: Names what he just did
moments.quote: So typically, Lauren, what the first step would be — when you say, I really believe that my people could triple, and I fired enough bullets into that, where I really do think that you believe that. And that's real.
moments.why: 'Fired enough bullets into that' is the transition from discovery to prescription, said out loud so the prospect hears the logic.

moments.title: Price with no cushion
moments.quote: So if we wanted to, again, 45 minutes, everybody puts the time in. Your price on that is 97.50.
moments.why: No justification, no apology, no bundling language. He says the number and stops talking.

moments.title: The reduced-risk fork
moments.quote: If you're thinking, hey, this makes sense, I want to do it, then I would just stop you there. If you're thinking, I don't know if this makes sense — then we would start with him. Leave the team out of it, start with him.
moments.why: Offers the $400 single assessment only to a hesitant buyer, and conditions it on the buyer admitting hesitation first.

moments.title: Doesn't accept 'seven to ten days'
moments.quote: Walk me through that. How do you make that decision?
moments.why: Turns a timeline into an actual process, which surfaces that the sales manager is a part-owner and already open to coaching.

moments.title: Books it on the call
moments.quote: So when do you want to talk again?
moments.why: Date, time, channel, phone number and a calendar invite sent while still on the line.

coaching_notes: The spine of this call: get the number from the prospect's own mouth (triple), pressure-test it from four angles, then price against it. The $9,750 lands softly because the prospect has already said the gap is worth millions.
'I fired enough bullets into that' at 18:25 is a transition worth memorizing — it tells the buyer why the recommendation is coming now and ties it to his own words.
The $400 leader-only assessment is a clean downsell, but notice it is offered conditionally, after Rob asks the buyer to self-identify as uncertain. Offered up front it would have killed the $9,750.
Rob worked the decision process hard but never asked decision criteria — what would make this a yes versus a no — so the follow-up call starts without knowing what Loren's partner will judge it on.

Transcript problems: Fireflies invented a phantom 'Speaker 1' that collects short interjections from both parties, so several answers sit under the wrong label (e.g. 'roughly 4 million' at 9:36 and 'Eleven' at 10:51 are Loren's, not Rob's). The header date reads March 24, 2024 but the content is clearly November 2023. The prospect is 'Loren' in the filename and 'Lauren' in the transcript, and the company is never named.
company_note: Brightstar (per the filename; never named in the transcript) — a used-equipment sales business near Middlebury, Indiana, founded 2017, 14 salespeople plus a sales manager

moments.title: The deserted island
moments.quote: I was on a deserted island since the year 1995, and I had my phone and I was making cold calls, but otherwise I was cut off from the world, and someone showed up and tried to sell me HubSpot. It's a great idea, but I just wouldn't get it.
moments.why: A memorable, portable analogy for the difference between no problem and no awareness.

moments.title: Problem aware vs. solution aware
moments.quote: It's not that it doesn't fix a problem, it's that I'm not aware. I'm either not problem aware or solution aware. And that's where having conversations and asking questions is or can be the solution.
moments.why: The cleanest one-sentence case for why a salesperson exists at all.

moments.title: Why demos don't close
moments.quote: Most software teams suck at this. They think that demoing will get it done and it doesn't.
moments.why: Short, unhedged, and the kind of line that earns a second meeting with a technical buyer.

moments.title: The milestone list, delivered conversationally
moments.quote: Do you have an issue? Is it impactful? Would you like to fix it? Is the money available, is the time available, is the change capital available, or do you want to make the investments? Who else is involved in the decision?
moments.why: A full consultative sales process said out loud in fifteen seconds without jargon — directly stealable for explaining what multi-call selling means.

moments.title: Why efficiency is a hard sell
moments.quote: We are way less attracted to efficiency than we should be. Because the problem that you're fixing, the business is profitable and succeeding, and I'm going to get out of bed and have a job tomorrow whether or not I hire Carl.
moments.why: Explains in plain terms why 'we'll save you money' stalls, using himself as the example.

moments.title: The buying signal
moments.quote: I don't know how we would work together, but the sales organization thing is always something that I have no experience building a sales organization.
moments.why: The prospect opens the door himself. What Rob does with it in the next twelve seconds is the lesson of the call.

moments.title: Tests timing instead
moments.quote: What is your timeline? Because it doesn't seem too forthcoming.
moments.why: An honest, efficient disqualifier — but asked instead of exploring the opening, so the call ends on a 'not yet' that was never tested.

moments.title: The non-close
moments.quote: You got my email, my number, and all that, whenever the time ever strikes you.
moments.why: An explicit decision to leave the next move entirely with the prospect — worth debating as a group.

coaching_notes: A good study in deciding early whether a conversation is a sale or a favor. Rob spent twenty-five minutes being a thought leader and roughly ninety seconds qualifying; by the time he asked about timeline there was no runway left.
The up-front contract was one line ('what do you want to make sure we cover') with no time frame and no right to say no, which left Carl driving the agenda the entire call.
25:09 is the single most reusable passage in this transcript — the full consultative milestone sequence delivered as conversation, not framework.

When Carl says at 29:43 that he has never built a sales organization, that is the opening. A follow-up question there ('what worries you about that?') costs nothing and might have produced a future-dated next step instead of an open invitation.

Transcript problems: the header date reads March 24, 2024 but the content is clearly November 2023 (pre-Thanksgiving, the OpenAI board turmoil referenced at 30:41). The prospect's company is never named, and the first ninety seconds are dead air and fumbling.

moments.quote: Okay, but what are your thoughts?

moments.title: All decisions are emotional
moments.quote: When somebody falls in love with something — all human decisions, whether you want to believe it or not, are emotional based. There isn't a logical decision you've ever made in your life. Even if you want to argue that you have, I'll prove you haven't.

moments.why: Directly contradicts the client's instinct, with a reason, inside the first fifteen minutes of a first meeting.

They're selling against change of chemicals.

moments.title: Binary, not good-better-best

coaching_notes: Brian sells by teaching and lets the value accumulate until the prospect asks for pricing unprompted at 41:01. Nothing in the first forty minutes is positioned as a pitch, and the buyer still gets there.
'Okay, but what are your thoughts?' at 1:41 is the move of the call — on a referred meeting, refusing the referrer's framing and making the buyer articulate the problem himself.

The gap was handed to him and never used. Matt says '$3 million today to $30 million' at 3:23 and it is never revisited — no impact question, no cost of staying where they are, no commitment test. A $3k/month price against a $27M gap would have been trivial to justify.

Price and terms were given verbally with no proposal ('we don't tie people to anything'), which is consistent and low-friction, but the call ends with the decision routed back through Michael, a person who was never on the call. The real decision path was left vague.

moments.why: The best question on the call. It turns a plan number into the CEO's actual reasoning about debt, culture, risk and ambition — information no questionnaire would surface.

moments.why: Pre-empts the easy answer. Wes stops, reconsiders, and lands on developing healthy behaviors instead.

moments.title: Asks permission before prescribing
moments.quote: Okay, can I make a suggestion here?

moments.title: Matches the buyer's standard
moments.quote: I don't want us to linger. At the end of that we're going to know — does it make sense to take another step together? And if it doesn't, it's not the right fit, no harm, no foul. I'd rather know that early.

moments.why: Low-effort pre-work that both qualifies commitment and gives him a scored agenda for the next meeting.

coaching_notes: A textbook short FTC: up-front contract inside the first minute, four pain questions, a permission-asked prescription, an up-front contract for the next meeting, and a booked in-person hour — all in 23 minutes.
'Why 400%?' is the move to steal. Two words against a number the prospect volunteered, and it produces his real decision criteria (organic growth, no debt, protect the culture) for free.
Asking 'can I make a suggestion here?' before prescribing is cheap and effective — it converts a pitch into an invited recommendation and the prospect accepted the next step without negotiating.

The weak stretch is 16:35–19:36, where Shad hands back a long four-area framework. It is accurate but it runs nearly three minutes, and it cost him the chance to dig into the brother, the retiring door-opener, or the under-built pipeline — all of which were sitting open.

moments.title: The compact contract
moments.quote: A couple questions lead into that, and then here's what that would look like. And if it makes sense, next steps. If it doesn't, no harm, no foul.
moments.why: Twenty seconds of structure on a call the prospect opened, and it buys him permission to ask questions before presenting.

moments.title: Frames the choice before answering it
moments.quote: Are you looking for something that's like an ongoing, help them really drive behavior change — or are you looking for just kind of a shot in the arm every so often?
moments.why: Puts the two options on the table in the buyer's language, which lets Shad argue for one of them later without it sounding self-serving.

moments.title: The actual pain
moments.quote: We have had cases where they have delivered messages to the customer in a way that jeopardized the deal. So that's what we want to avoid.
moments.why: This is the one sentence worth money on the whole call, and nobody follows it — how many deals, how big, how often.

moments.title: The constraint, stated plainly
moments.quote: We don't expect them to sell anything. We just want to make sure that they don't cause any problem for the sales.
moments.why: A useful reminder that not every training buyer wants salespeople; scoping this wrong would have lost the deal.

moments.title: Behavior, technique, mindset
moments.quote: There's kind of three parts of change that happen. Behavior change. Then there's a technique change. And then there's also usually a mindset shift.
moments.why: A clean two-minute teach done live on a shared screen; it's also how he justifies ongoing work over a workshop.

moments.title: Argues against the one-off
moments.quote: Yes, you can give people a couple of sessions, but anything really in life, if you really want good change that's going to stick, it's going to have to be ongoing. A couple of sessions probably aren't going to hit it, because people go, oh, that's good, I got it — but it's a regular reinforcement of that that gets it to stick.
moments.why: Makes the case for a year of work using the change model he just taught, rather than asserting it.

moments.title: Won't name a session count cold
moments.quote: Well, it depends specifically on what specific things we want to make sure we're working through with them.
moments.why: The right instinct — but he gives a number three minutes later anyway, without ever getting the specifics he said he needed.

moments.title: A year, twelve sessions
moments.quote: I would say we're probably going to need a year to get through it. So it'd be twelve sessions.
moments.why: Worth listening to alongside 7:00 — this is the moment the engagement gets sized on topics rather than on outcomes.

moments.title: The price
moments.quote: For a group this size, it would be hourly. Typically it's a thousand an hour. So if we're working 90 minutes, that would be 1500 a month.
moments.why: Delivered flatly and without hedging, in response to a direct question. Note the prospect's garbled readback immediately after.

moments.title: How does the decision get made
moments.quote: I appreciate you're talking to the team and colleagues — how do you decide if it makes sense for you guys?
moments.why: The strongest question on the call, and it arrives with ninety seconds left. Earlier it would have reshaped everything before it.

moments.title: The honest answer about the CEO
moments.quote: It's usually required, my partner's input, our CEO, and he's not very quick in making decisions. So please give me a couple of weeks, and if I didn't get back to you by then, please feel free to reach out.
moments.why: The prospect hands over the real decision bottleneck — the thing Shad would have wanted to know at minute two.

moments.title: Dates the follow-up out loud
moments.quote: I'm just going to put a reminder — if it's like 15 April and I haven't heard from you, I'll reach out by then. Does that sound good?
moments.why: Converts 'a couple of weeks' into a specific date with the prospect's agreement. Cheap, and it keeps the deal from evaporating.

coaching_notes: This is not a first-time conversation — it's a second call, a scoping-and-pricing follow-up. It sits in the FTC library because of the folder name, and should be labeled as a second meeting for anyone studying it.

The whole call sizes a solution for a problem that was never sized. 'Messages that jeopardized the deal' at 2:56 is a quantifiable pain — how many deals, what were they worth, how often — and nobody asks. With no impact number, price became the only figure in the room.

The buyer ran the agenda: how many sessions, how many people, what about new hires, how do you charge. He left with everything needed to compare Shad against another vendor and nothing that commits him.

The decision-process question at 14:21 was the best move and came thirty seconds from the end. Asked at minute two it would have revealed the slow CEO and the executive-team path before any pricing was given.
Worth stealing: dating the follow-up out loud at 15:37 instead of 'I'll check in sometime.'

Transcript problems: the prospect's name appears as Amin, Armen and Armin; the company is never named; his 'so hundred per month' at 12:17 is a garbled readback of $1,500; the header date reads March 29, 2024 while the filename says March 25.
company_note: per the filename; the company is never named in the transcript

coach_confidence: high — Speaker 1 gives his own name and number while demonstrating a voicemail at 18:53 ('Shad Tidler, 317-512-6969') and references the ASA webinars he ran. headline: Group Q&A on cold-call objections, then he sells them
summary: Four people from Horizon Staffing bring Shad live sales questions from a webinar follow-up: what to say when a prospect already uses five staffing firms, how to get past gatekeepers, and what voicemail actually gets a call back. He answers all three with scripts — a negative reverse on the five-vendor brush-off, the buyer's-process explanation of why people hang up, cadence and twelve-to-fifteen attempts, and the 'I don't even know if you're the right person, can you help me out' callback. At 27:23 he flips to selling, asks what else they're running into, gets soft answers, and uses his own reversal on them — which Paula catches and calls out.
outcome_note: Lisa agrees to Shad emailing to set time for a deeper conversation about where they are and where they want to get to, and he agrees to send the recording for the team.

milestones.text: Are there some particular things that you want to make sure we cover here in the next 26 minutes?
Now I'm going to ask — what are some of the challenges besides what we've talked about here that you're seeing from a selling side? What are things you're running into when you're out there?

I hear some from the prospecting. But what about — are we seeing, is it harder to get decisions from folks, or it's taking longer, or they're pushing back on your rates versus value? Those are some common things I've heard from staffing companies.
Is it making it harder just to reach some of the goals, taking longer?
I didn't know if this is something that made sense for you, if you wanted to talk further and see how I could help or not. So that's why I was asking.
Can I send an email and we'd set some time to talk further about where we're at, where we want to get?
Lisa, I know you and I coordinated originally — best to kind of coordinate with you?

moments.title: Names the clock and asks for the agenda
moments.quote: Are there some particular things that you want to make sure we cover here in the next 26 minutes?
moments.why: Recovers a meeting that lost four minutes to audio trouble by stating the real remaining time and handing the agenda to the group.

moments.title: Decodes the brush-off
moments.quote: A lot of times they're saying that just because they're like, I know if I tell you that — even if I got problems or challenges with my staffing companies, or I do need some help — you'll go away.
moments.why: Reframes 'we already use five' from a fact into a tactic, which is what makes the response that follows possible.

moments.title: The negative reverse, scripted
moments.quote: Laura, I appreciate you sharing, you got five staffing companies. There's probably not any reason that you would need to talk to another one. You're probably not running into any certain challenges — you probably don't run into stuff like people not showing up, do you?
moments.why: The core script of the call, built live out of Laura's own example of what prospects complain about.

moments.title: Makes them be the prospect
moments.quote: How do you react when somebody cold calls you?
moments.why: Turns the lesson into their own experience; the room answers honestly ('I usually hang up') and the teaching lands without argument.

moments.title: Paying the sins
moments.quote: You pay the sins for every other bad salesperson. Even if you're trying to help, you're paying the sins.
moments.why: A phrase a rep will still have in their head a month later, and it defuses the personal sting of rejection.

moments.title: Why 'you probably don't' works
moments.quote: The reason why I say 'you probably don't' is because if they do, human nature is to correct.
moments.why: Explains the mechanism rather than just handing over the line, which is what makes it transferable.

moments.title: Open with their problems, not yours
moments.quote: Here's some of the common challenges we hear — are these things you're seeing or hearing? Where you start to bring up what are some of the common problems they may be facing, instead of talking about here's all the great things we can do.
moments.why: The reusable structure underneath every script he gives on this call.

moments.title: Twelve to fifteen attempts
moments.quote: To get to ideal decision makers it takes anywhere from twelve to fifteen attempts. And so if we're stopping after five, we actually may be getting to people — we're just not putting enough effort into it.
moments.why: Converts 'they never answer' from a prospect problem into a cadence problem the team controls.

moments.title: The voicemail, demonstrated
moments.quote: Hey Paula — Shad Tidler, 317-512-6969. Thought it's important we should talk. Give me a call back. 317-512-6969.
moments.why: Performed, not described: short, number twice, no company name, clear call to action. The reasoning follows at 19:16.

moments.title: The 'can you help me out' version
moments.quote: Hey Paula, here's what I was calling. I don't know if you're the right person to talk to, or if this even makes sense. Can I share with you why I called? … I don't even know if that's something your organization experiences. I don't know if that's something I'd talk with you or someone else. Can you help me out?
moments.why: Deliberate weakness as posture — the second best script in the transcript, and the room immediately names who on their team could run it.

moments.title: The turn
moments.quote: Okay. Can I ask a couple questions?
moments.why: The pivot from free teaching to qualifying, done with permission. Watch the group deflect it: 'I think we just answered that.'

moments.title: Caught running his own play
moments.quote: Wait, wait. He just used his own line that he told us against us people.
moments.why: Paula catches the reversal live, and Shad's answer — 'I never teach clients anything I don't do myself' — turns the catch into credibility. The most instructive thirty seconds in this batch.

coaching_notes: This is a group teaching call that doubles as a live demo of the technique being taught: at 32:03 Shad runs the reversal on his own prospects, gets called on it by Paula, and converts the catch into proof. Play that passage for anyone who thinks the method only works on strangers.

Four strong, stealable scripts in one call: the five-vendor reversal (6:05), the 30-second commercial (22:31), the 'I don't even know if you're the right person, can you help me out' callback (23:49), and the demonstrated voicemail (18:53).

He gave away twenty-seven minutes of value before his first qualifying question. The permission-asked turn at 27:23 was clean, but it was late enough that the group had the answers they came for and could deflect ('I think we just answered that').

He never got an impact answer. He asked twice what the sales climate was costing them and got 'in general, yes' and anecdotes about credit checks and vendor lists. The meeting advances on goodwill, not on a quantified problem — which is exactly the gap he'd coach a rep about.

Transcript problems: the first two minutes are audio-trouble crosstalk; Fireflies has folded a fourth Horizon participant ('Mike') and at least one stray address of Shad ('Chad', at 18:02) into the Speaker 1 block, so Speaker 1 is not purely the coach early on; Speaker 3 is greeted as Paula once and as 'Veronica' once.
company_note: a staffing and temporary-labor firm working the Savannah and Atlanta markets; attendees came out of Shad's ASA webinars

headline: HR referral with no urgency behind it
summary: Alex Perry had delivered a presentation-skills class to GW Berkheimer's management team and handed Shad to Maureen, the HR leader, after the marketing director asked about customer-service and sales training. Shad gathered the background, asked what was driving it now, and proposed a three-way call with the marketing director. Maureen then revealed the real state of play: the marketing director never followed up with Alex, the department is consumed with an April sales meeting and three new locations opening April 30, and the project is nowhere near the top of his list. Shad agreed to send website links and pinned a May 15 phone call to find out whether a meeting is worth setting.
outcome_note: No meeting with the actual buyer; Shad sent literature and booked a May 15 check-in call with an explicit out.

moments.title: Opens on the referral, not on himself
moments.quote: Well, thanks for taking the time here. Alex spoke very highly of you and that we should connect. So I figured we'd just kind of do some intros and then talk about what made you say, yep, let's jump on here.
moments.why: A light agenda plus the referrer's name, in two sentences, before any pitch.

moments.title: Describes Lushin through the prospect's world
moments.quote: Most people in customer service don't want to be salespeople. And I don't blame them. That's not why they got into customer service. So just helping how they more effectively determine, okay, is this a good opportunity to help further the conversation, hand off if it goes to the sales team, or even sometimes themselves.
moments.why: He frames the service of Lushin as removing discomfort rather than adding a sales quota, and Maureen answers with 'that sounds exactly like what we were looking for.'

moments.title: Asks what the teams are actually running into
moments.quote: You said the marketing director requested it. What are some of the things the marketing director and you talked about in terms of what the teams are running into or challenges they're seeing?
moments.why: Turns a vague referral into a description of the problem in the buyer's own words.

moments.title: The prospect makes Lushin's argument for it
moments.quote: You and I know that you can't just train once and magically think that it's going to forevermore be ingrained in their brains. And every time we have a new person, they did not get the benefit of that training, so we don't have any way to perpetuate it.
moments.why: She states the case for ongoing reinforcement before Shad does; he reuses it verbatim seven minutes later.

moments.title: Why now
moments.quote: So what's driving this now? Like you said, you've had some kind of one-off training over the years. What's driving, hey, now we want to take a look at this and see about getting some help?
moments.why: The single best question on the call, and the one that eventually produces the truth about priority.

moments.title: Goes straight at the buyer he hasn't met
moments.quote: It probably would make sense for you, me and the marketing director to have a conversation. Just better understand where you're at, where you're wanting to get to and what you're looking for and why. Does that sound like a good next step from here, or what do you think?
moments.why: He asks for the decision maker early rather than selling the coach-to-HR relationship.

moments.title: The truth about priority
moments.quote: So while this is important, it's not at the top of his list in terms of sense of urgency.
moments.why: Three minutes of honest context from the prospect that would have been invisible if he had just taken the meeting request at face value.

moments.title: She asks for literature to sell internally
moments.quote: If you had some materials about some things that you could do or some potential training opportunities, because I have to convince him that this is worthwhile for him to spend time with us.
moments.why: A classic champion request. Listen for what Shad does not ask: what would make it worth the marketing director's time.

moments.title: Customized versus off-the-shelf programs
moments.quote: One-time shots in the arm every so often, yes, it gets people riled up and going, and maybe they make a couple of changes from it for a little while, but then they slip back into old habits. So we believe in regular touches and small bits over time to not only train, but coach, reinforce and help make the change.
moments.why: A clean, short answer to the most common early question, built on the words the prospect just used.

moments.title: Permission to say no on the next call
moments.quote: When would be best to talk again and just see, hey, is there an interest in setting that meeting? And if not, no harm, no foul.
moments.why: Low-pressure framing that makes it easy for a stalled prospect to agree to a date.

moments.title: Pins an actual date instead of 'reach out in May'
moments.quote: If I could suggest May 15, I've got some time available at either 11:30 or 12 or between one to 2:30. That way you can say, hey, yep, we're at a good place where it makes sense, I've talked to him, it makes sense to schedule that next meeting. Or, hey, we're not, and that would be fine.
moments.why: The one concrete act that keeps a deferred opportunity alive; he offers slots and sends the invite on the call.

moments.title: Rapport after the business is done
moments.quote: So, Maureen, I gotta ask. You've been at GW Berkheimer for about a year. So what made you make the move or the change?
moments.why: He waits until the calendar is handled, then earns the personal story, which is where the real relationship gets built.

coaching_notes: He pinned a date and time rather than accepting 'let's touch base in May,' and gave her an explicit out on the call. That combination is why a low-urgency opportunity still has a pulse.
The literature request went unexamined. No question about what the marketing director would need to see, or what would have to be true for this to reach his top three.

Nothing was quantified on this call: no revenue, no headcount, no growth number, no cost of doing nothing. A single 'what should that number be' would have given the May 15 call something to anchor on.
Asking 'what's driving this now?' is what produced the April sales meeting, the three acquisitions and the honest statement about urgency. Without it he would have walked away thinking this was warm.
Transcript quality: the opening agenda line is ASR-garbled, the company is rendered as both 'Burkhammer' and 'Berkheimer,' and 'Shad' appears as 'Shan.'

headline: Account manager handed a hunting role she's never done
summary: Taralu has spent 27 years in staffing on the account-management side and was just asked to take over business development at Geo Temps, an eight-person mining-niche staffing firm that is not profitable. Her quota is two to three new clients billing per quarter; she has been reactivating lapsed accounts and has sent 19 renewal contracts, but has never cold called and has no plan, no ideal client profile and no goals of her own. Shad asked permission to keep digging, separated the company's goal from hers, surfaced that the previous BD rep did nothing for two years without anyone noticing, then walked through Lushin's strategy-structure-staff-skills model and deferred all cost and time questions to a meeting with her manager. He booked that joint call on the spot.
outcome_note: A one-hour joint meeting with her operations manager Doug Oster was scheduled for the following Friday, with an up-front contract for what that meeting decides.

moments.title: Opens with her agenda, not his
moments.quote: Give me just a little background on yourself, and share with me what would you like to make sure we talk through and cover today.
moments.why: Two requests in one sentence: who you are, and what you need out of this. She answers with her entire situation.

moments.title: The number, stated plainly
moments.quote: What they want me to do is get two to three new businesses billing on our payroll a quarter.
moments.why: The quota lands inside the first five minutes because he asked for the goal of the role rather than the pain of the role.

moments.title: The real obstacle is reputation, not technique
moments.quote: We're in the mining niche, and sadly, some of the individuals that have been my predecessors have really dropped the ball. Some of our past clients have not been touched for a year to two years. And in the arena that we are in, it's upon reputation and people talk. So I'm fighting a battle of, well, you guys disappeared, and now you're coming back and you want my business.
moments.why: The answer reframes the whole opportunity; this is not a cold-calling problem.

moments.title: Makes her say her weak answer out loud
moments.quote: What do you say to that when you hear that?
moments.why: Rather than diagnosing for her, he has her perform her rebuttal, then asks what response she gets. She hears how thin it is herself.

moments.title: A mid-call up-front contract
moments.quote: I'm going to keep asking questions so I can really understand it before I can share on how we can help. Is that okay?
moments.why: Buys explicit permission to keep digging, so continued questioning reads as diligence rather than evasion. The single most stealable line on this call.

moments.title: Separates the company's goal from hers
moments.quote: I know the company's saying, hey, we need two to three new businesses billing on the payroll per quarter, that's the goal. What's your goal for this role?
moments.why: She has none. 'I have not even really stopped to put that into place.' That gap becomes the hook for the next meeting.

moments.title: Asks how she feels about it
moments.quote: When you're stepping back and looking at that, how to set your goals, how to make sure you're getting the contracts out, cold calling, how are you feeling about all that?
moments.why: Answer: 'I'm nervous.' A feelings question after a string of factual ones, and it gets the honest one-word response.

moments.title: Two years of nothing, unnoticed
moments.quote: Our last business development gentleman had been with us for ten years, and it took quite a bit of time for them to actually figure out the lack of business that he was doing. He was released in October of last year, and when they started to go back through, they found out that he had not really done anything for roughly two years.
moments.why: She is handing him the management problem behind the sales problem, and she knows it: 'that'll give you a little bit of a mindset as to what the level of management looks like.'

moments.title: She raises money before he does
moments.quote: I think it's going to really depend on what we're going to be able to get back out of it and truly how much it's going to be, because we are certainly not a profitable company right now. We are not profitable. Even close.
moments.why: A volunteered budget signal that goes completely unexplored. Worth noticing what a coach does when a prospect hands over the constraint unasked.

moments.title: Hands the design back to her
moments.quote: How do you see me helping? What would you like to see me help with then?
moments.why: Her answer names ideal client profile, how to make the first call, and how to turn business away, which is exactly the agenda for the manager meeting.

moments.title: Refuses to price before the manager conversation
moments.quote: Now, in terms of cost, time, that's really what would need to happen: we have to have a next discussion with him, anybody else that would need to be involved. And then I'd be able to say, here's what it would take time-wise, here's what it would take money-wise.
moments.why: Turns the price question into the reason the next meeting has to happen, without sounding cagey.

Four straight minutes of the strategy-structure-staff-skills monologue starting at 15:38. The fifteen minutes of questions before it did more selling than the model did.

headline: Free coaching session that never becomes a sale
summary: Julie and Eric attended Shad's webinars and booked time to ask two questions: how to get contact information for decision makers, and how to unstick proposals that go into limbo. Grant, the outside salesperson the call was partly about, never joined. Shad split the call cleanly in two, recommended ZoomInfo, RocketReach and Lusha, argued for the phone over email, pushed back on their company's goody-bag doctrine, taught the 30-second commercial structure and his voicemail scripts, then reframed every stalled proposal as a priority problem rather than a price problem. He closed with a soft probe about whether the rest of Exact Staff has the same issues, offered to send the recording, and booked nothing.
outcome_note: Thirty minutes of coaching delivered with no up-front contract, no qualification of the account and no next meeting; he offered the recording link and said 'reach back out if I can help.'

milestones.text: Julie states the problem herself: she cannot get an email or a contact when cold calling, so she dials by name hoping to reach anyone who can route her to the hiring manager.
All right, Julie, so being able to find out the contact info is one thing. What else would you like to make sure we cover here?

So let's take the first part, which is getting the contact info, getting in front of them. And then we'll take the back part, which is, hey, now we're in the sales process, how do we get them to actually commit and get a good decision, or if it's a no, get that faster.

First thing: do you know the titles of the ideal decision makers you want to be in front of? I know it can vary, but for 90 percent, is it an operations manager, an HR manager? Who are the titles of the people that you want to get in front of?

So the key, you've got to look back in your sales process and go, in our process, when we're having the conversation before we take the contract or agreement to them, are we determining, is this a priority for them?

If you've got a bunch out there where you sent a proposal or contract and they're giving you the blow-offs, what I would do is call them up, have a conversation, and just go, hey, the question I've got is, is this even a priority for you to fix right now? If it's not, that's fine, let's close this out and maybe we have a conversation down the road.
Is this something, like, throughout Exact Staff, that a lot of people run into similar challenges?

moments.title: The admission underneath the question
moments.quote: I'm not going to lie. I'm not a salesperson, and neither is Eric. And you do get nervous. After the sale is made and we got them as a client, I'm perfectly fine. I'll give them customer service all day long.
moments.why: The real problem on this call is identity, not technique, and she says so nine minutes before Shad addresses it.

moments.title: Splits the call into two problems
moments.quote: So let's take the first part, which is getting the contact info, getting in front of them. And then we'll take the back part, which is, hey, now we're in the sales process, how do we get them to actually commit and get a good decision, or if it's a no, get that faster.
moments.why: Two questions from two people, organized into an agenda in one sentence. Worth copying whenever a group dumps several problems at once.

moments.title: Phone over email, with the math
moments.quote: I would advise picking up the phone and calling because less people are doing that these days. The average decision maker of an organization takes about twelve to fifteen attempts if you're cold calling to get to them. You short-circuit the back and forth emails. Get somebody on the phone, it's harder for them to hide behind an email.
moments.why: He sets the expectation of twelve to fifteen attempts so the first few no-answers don't read as failure.

moments.title: Contradicts the company's own doctrine
moments.quote: No, that's... here's the thing. You gotta differentiate yourself. A lot of people are doing that.
moments.why: Julie says 'our company is like, do it, do it, nobody else is doing it.' He disagrees flatly, then immediately replaces it with a reason, which is how you push back without losing the room.

moments.title: Why people actually take the meeting
moments.quote: Here's why people are going to talk to you: you show up different from the start and you make it about them and bring value from the start, not because you dropped off something.
moments.why: The replacement argument, delivered in one sentence right after the disagreement.

moments.title: Show up and throw up
moments.quote: The typical pitch a lot of times is, I call it the show up and throw up. You finally got in front of them, you're like, I only got fifteen seconds to impress them. Well, and I'm nervous. So what do I do? I tend to just vomit everything I can about what's going on and hope something sticks, which actually has the opposite effect.
moments.why: Names the behavior Julie just confessed to, without making her wrong for it.

moments.title: The three-part opener
moments.quote: Can I take a minute here and tell you why I called? And from there, if you don't want to talk, just let me know, and if you do, we'll keep going. ... Hey, I usually talk to HR managers like yourself, Julie, and here's some of the things that I'm hearing. ... Based on that, is any of that stuff that you're running into? Should we keep talking from here?
moments.why: Small agreement, pattern of people like you, then a yes-or-no exit. The whole cold opener in three moves.

moments.title: The voicemail scripts
moments.quote: Hey Julie, Shad Tidler, 317-512-6969. Thought it was important we should talk. Give me a call back. Or: Julie, Shad Tidler, had a couple quick questions I could use your help on. Give me a call back. Very to the point, very short. They're usually in a managerial, decision-making, leader-type role. They're quick, they're to the point. I'm not going to give a whole ton of info; they're only going to listen to ten or fifteen seconds anyway.
moments.why: Two scripts and the reasoning behind their length. Julie's reaction: 'that's not what I've been doing.'

moments.title: Reframes every stalled proposal
moments.quote: We're still reviewing, we haven't decided, we'll make that decision later. That's the key. It's not a priority. You can give them all the best pricing and rates in the world, it ain't going to matter.
moments.why: The central idea of the call, and the one Julie says nobody had ever simplified for her.

moments.title: The price trap
moments.quote: If they're making it about just getting the lowest price, as soon as someone comes in and undercuts you, they'll do the same thing to you.
moments.why: One line that ends the markup-is-too-high conversation they'd been having since minute three.

moments.title: The family-gathering analogy
moments.quote: I love my family to death, but there's certain family members, every time I show up, they complain about the same crap, and I look at them and go, what are you going to do about it? Next time they show up, still complaining about it. Just because it's a problem doesn't mean they're going to do anything about it.
moments.why: Makes the difference between pain and commitment obvious to two people who do not think of themselves as salespeople.

moments.title: The Richard reframe
moments.quote: Richard comes to you, has a problem and says, hey babe, need to talk to you, need your advice. At the end of it, you give him some advice. What are you gonna ask him about that advice you gave him? ... You're probably gonna go, what are you gonna do with it?
moments.why: He takes selling out of the category of selling entirely. This is the passage that produced 'nobody's ever simplified it like that.'

coaching_notes: The strongest pure coaching on this recording: the priority reframe, the family-gathering analogy and the Richard exchange all transfer word for word to a rep who is afraid of selling.
He contradicted the client's own house strategy on goody bags directly, then replaced it in the next breath. That sequence, disagreement plus immediate substitute, is the part to study.

No up-front contract, no discovery on Exact Staff itself, and no next step. He gave away the full playbook and left with nothing booked. The only qualification attempt comes at 30:34, thirty minutes in.

The teaching is almost entirely tactical answers to the questions as asked. He never asked Julie what the stalled proposals are worth, or what the cost of not fixing this is, which is the question he was teaching them to ask.

headline: CEO who could get better versus has to
summary: Murray runs a 32-person data-collection firm that did $4M last year and is tracking to $5M, but the new Florida office is stuck: roughly $250-300K last year, $150K so far this year, against a target over half a million. The rep there follows up poorly and nobody has been clearly assigned to hold him accountable. Rob diagnosed the rep, the accountability gap and the reactive goal-setting, then stopped and told Murray directly that 'we could get better' people rarely change anything, which pulled out the real stake: they cannot float Florida's cost forever. He proposed OMG assessments on Murray, Nate in Georgia and the Florida rep at $1,200, quoted roughly $3,000 a month for ongoing work, and asked to be in the decision conversation.
outcome_note: Murray took it to his leadership meeting the following week; Rob agreed to send a Vidyard walkthrough instead of being in the room, and left the next call to Murray booking from his calendar link.

moments.title: Three-way diagnostic on the underperforming rep
moments.quote: Is it he gets in front of opportunities and doesn't close opportunities, or doesn't get in front of opportunities to close? What is it?
moments.why: Forces a vague 'he could use some coaching' into one of three specific failure modes, inside the first three minutes.

moments.title: Who owns accountability
moments.quote: So you mentioned accountability. Who should be playing that role of holding this particular rep accountable?
moments.why: Picks up the prospect's own word and turns it into a question. The answer, 'that's probably something we've not clearly defined,' is the real opening.

moments.title: Why does it matter
moments.quote: Why does it matter that you grow in Florida faster than you are?
moments.why: The pivot from facts to stakes. Everything useful on this call comes after this question.

moments.title: Three numbers in one breath
moments.quote: What is it now? Where should it be? And what's the timeline that you wanted to get there?
moments.why: Current state, target state, deadline. Produces $250-300K, $150K year to date, and 'we should hopefully be doing over half a million this year.'

moments.title: Asks permission to be blunt
moments.quote: Can I shoot you straight, Murray? Is that okay?
moments.why: Six words that buy the right to say the next ninety seconds. Study what he does with the permission he just got.

moments.title: Names his own reservation about the deal
moments.quote: The thing that I haven't figured out yet, so I'll just be as transparent as I can be, is that you guys are doing pretty well. You told me the growth happens sort of without intent. It's going to happen anyway. And the number in Florida that you're behind isn't that sizable of a number. When I hear stories from entrepreneurs where it's like, we're doing pretty good, and we'd be doing pretty good if we did nothing different, those usually aren't the same kinds of people that will dig in and do what they have to do to create the change they need.
moments.why: He argues against his own sale out loud. This is the centerpiece of the recording.

moments.title: The distinction that does the work
moments.quote: And I appreciate that, but there's a difference between we could get better and we're dying to get better.
moments.why: Murray's first answer was a polite deflection about being open to feedback. Rob does not accept it, and restates the gap in one sentence.

moments.title: The real stake finally lands
moments.quote: If we don't get better in Florida, then we're gonna have some big decisions to make. We can't float that level of expenditure forever. I'm not just sitting here on a hope and prayer that we're going to get more sales. I'm actively wanting to make improvements and changes.
moments.why: The payoff for the whole challenge sequence. A consequence Murray had not stated in the first eighteen minutes.

moments.title: The commitment test disguised as logistics
moments.quote: I couldn't, no. I don't have five.
moments.why: Rob asks whether he could find four or five hours a week. Murray's flat no is more honest than anything he said about wanting to improve, and Rob uses it rather than retreating from it.

moments.title: Makes the assessment concrete with two outcomes
moments.quote: One outcome would be, Nate has low desire and low commitment around sales management, and we would say, that's great that he's a sales producer, but leading other people probably isn't the right fit for him long term. Another outcome would be Nate is high desire, high commitment, high responsibility, with tactical weaknesses. He's never been taught how to be great at coaching, how to hold people accountable, how to be great at motivating.
moments.why: Sells the assessment by describing what the findings would say about a specific named person, not by describing the product.

moments.title: Positions the data as a conversation, not a verdict
moments.quote: All of this I'm testing against your real-life experience with these guys. Here's what the assessment tells me, Murray. Do you buy that? And nineteen times out of twenty, when I bounce a finding off of the founder, they say, yep, that's spot on. And so then the plan comes from that.
moments.why: Pre-empts the 'can a test really tell you that' objection by making the CEO the validator.

moments.title: Asks to be in the decision conversation
moments.quote: Could you bring me in, not to that meeting, but can we just have a conversation with the people involved in making the decision? I think that's usually easiest.
moments.why: He tries to avoid being sold on his behalf by a document. Worth listening to how the ask lands, and what he settles for.

coaching_notes: The 16:14 to 18:19 sequence is the reason to open this recording. Rob stated his reservation about the prospect's commitment out loud, refused the polite deflection, and got the real consequence in return.
He priced in the same breath as the proposal, with no hedging or justification: twelve hundred for three assessments, roughly three thousand a month after. No apology, no build-up.
'Could you find five hours?' works as a commitment test because the answer is unarguable. Murray said no, and that no is better data than any stated intention.

Weakest stretch is the close. He asked to be in the decision conversation, was refused, agreed to send a Vidyard anyway, and did not trade that document for a date. The next meeting was left to a calendar link.
The prospect's company is never named on the recording, so the library entry has to carry the industry description instead.

headline: Coach disqualifies a staffing deal as an ops problem
summary: This is the joint meeting Taralu booked at the end of her March 27 first conversation, with her operations manager Doug Oster in the room. Doug laid out the picture: roughly 130 customer agreements and only 17 active, direct hire underperforming, the temp side needing to go from about 100 people to 160 just to cover overhead, and a reputation damaged by predecessors who stopped calling clients. Shad dug into why the clients left, asked what the customers themselves would need to see, and exposed that Doug's ideal customer profile and Taralu's hunting were not aligned. Then he asked permission to be candid and told them the problem was operations and fulfillment rather than sales, coached them for free on reopening the lapsed accounts by phone, and left without proposing anything.
outcome_note: Shad told them he was not sure where he could help, gave them a reopening script and a farm-your-17-clients plan, and closed with an open invitation rather than a next meeting.

moments.title: Full up-front contract with both outcomes named

moments.why: A bare 'why' after a long answer. Doug's response finally gets to overhead, closed offices and 160 people against roughly 100.

moments.title: Permission, then the disqualification
moments.quote: Can I be pretty candid here? Honest? It sounds like more of the challenge here for both of you is it's more of an operations fulfillment than it is a sales piece.
moments.why: The model for telling a prospect they do not have the problem you sell. He asks first, states it flatly, and offers 'unless I'm missing something' as the only hedge.

moments.title: Says it out loud

moments.why: No pivot to a smaller package, no discount, no let's-set-up-a-follow-up-anyway. Worth hearing how little drama there is in it.

moments.quote: Pick up the phone, go, hey, here's who I am. I know we've dropped the ball in the past. Let's acknowledge it. Let's get the elephant in the room out there. moments.why: Free, specific, immediately usable. He gives away the exact language after deciding there's no deal here.

moments.title: The throat to choke
moments.quote: I had a former client of mine when I was in the logistics world tell me, go, Shad, I know personally you didn't miss on scheduling this load, but you're the local throat to choke, and I need a throat to choke right now. Okay, hey, I'm here. Choke.
moments.why: The story that gives Taralu permission to own damage she did not cause, which is the hardest part of the call she now has to make.

moments.title: Start with the 17 you still have
moments.quote: Start with your current clients, the 17 you've got that are doing work with you. Talk to them. Go, how else can we help you? What are some other challenges you run into with staffing that we could be helping with? Are there other groups within your company, other divisions, that need staffing help?
moments.why: The cheapest growth available to them, named explicitly, in place of the cold-calling training they came asking for.

coaching_notes: A model disqualification. He asked permission to be candid, named the real problem as operations rather than sales, and said out loud that he was not sure he could help, then kept coaching anyway. No pitch, no discount, no face-saving follow-up meeting.
'What do the customers want to see to help repair it?' is the single best question in this batch. Both people answered 'that's a good question,' which is the diagnosis.
Asking the owner to define the ideal customer and then immediately asking the rep whether she sees the same thing is a reusable two-step for exposing misalignment without accusing anyone.
He asked for the revenue behind the headcount goal at 22:10 and never got it; Doug answered in people, weeks and worker-comp codes, and Shad let it go. The one place he stopped pressing.

headline: Client call: metrics first, then a $9,500 upsell
summary: A recurring coaching call two days after Rob ran an in-person session for the Brightstar team.
