moments.title: The one-thing theory of training value
moments.quote: The thing about Eugene is that it's not about how much stuff he gets. It's how much the one little trick gets him. It's like the one little investment that pays off a hundredfold. The people that aren't really any good can get fifteen things, but there's not as much leverage because they're just not as good. But for him, it's that one little thing.
moments.why: The answer to 'my best rep didn't get much out of your session,' and it reframes the objection into an argument for working with top performers.

moments.title: Does the new manager hold them to behavior
moments.quote: What about, does he hold them accountable for their prospecting behavior, for the amount of calls that they make, the results of that?
moments.why: Jonathon had just praised Bud for accountability generally. Rob immediately narrows it to the one kind that matters.

moments.title: Why don't you have the number yet
moments.quote: Why can't we get to the number about how many stops?
moments.why: A blunt question to an existing client about an open loop they've been circling for a week.

moments.title: The four things to track
moments.quote: Well, it's different for everybody, but here's what you track. Stops, conversations. And a conversation is basically me getting through my thirty-second commercial with you paying attention. ... Then it's appointments booked.
moments.why: The whole prospecting scorecard defined in under a minute, including a usable definition of 'conversation.'

moments.title: The ratios tell you what's broken
moments.quote: Those proportions will tell us what the problem is. So we had twenty stops, we talked to eighteen people, and only two conversations. Well, you must not be doing the pattern interrupt. We had twenty stops, talked to eighteen people, had twelve conversations, and didn't book the appointment. Well, the thirty-second commercial might be wrong, or the questions afterwards might be wrong.
moments.why: Turns activity tracking into diagnosis. This is the passage to send a sales manager who asks what their numbers should be.

moments.title: Suspect to closable in one conversation
moments.quote: People that call in and people that we cold call are suspects. And then people who have an issue become prospects. And then somewhere around here they become a qualified prospect, they have pain, they've got an issue, and then around here they become closable. For you guys, this is interesting because someone could go from suspect to closed in one conversation, but they go through all these stages.
moments.why: Adapts a standard pipeline to a business where the whole sale can happen at the door, without abandoning the stages.

moments.title: Why numbers reviews happen one-on-one
moments.quote: You can, it's just way easier to do it individually, especially right out of the gate. What you end up with is people wanting to tell stories and make some excuses, which then becomes a little difficult to navigate. I want to be able to say, whoa, let me stop you there, just give me the numbers, comfortably.
moments.why: Answers the manager's real question, which is how to avoid a group meeting turning into a round of justifications.

moments.title: Pick the tool you'll actually use
moments.quote: Stick with the technology that you're going to use. The most important thing about what tools you use is that they actually, you're going to use them. So if you have something that you're kind of using, or that kind of works, just keep with that.
moments.why: Refuses to let a tooling decision become a reason to delay the behavior change.

moments.title: Names the price and the client's own hesitation
moments.quote: I think the number that we got to with the team assessment was like $9,500. So part of it was like, man, do we want to put that much?
moments.why: He voices the objection before Jonathon can, which is what keeps a previously declined proposal from feeling like a re-pitch.

moments.title: Why assess the top performers
moments.quote: The reason that I like it for your top performers is because we know we're not going to triple their performance. That's not what we're trying to do. But you have to probably feel that there are gaps there that we will probably put our finger on and learn about eventually. It would be nice to go, here are the three things going on with Eugene that would make a difference for him.
moments.why: Sets a realistic expectation and still justifies the spend. The opposite of promising a transformation.

moments.title: How one rep's result becomes culture
moments.quote: If I can get Eugene saying, oh yeah, I did just this one thing and here's what happened, now it starts to become cultural. The change starts to...
moments.why: Connects the assessment back to the one-thing idea from minute four, so the upsell has a through-line to the session they just ran.

moments.title: Do it now, with clear expectations
moments.quote: I would do it now and just set really clear expectations with them about, when you're being asked about your manager, you're being asked about Bud. And then we have the included checkpoint, the reevaluation, in nine or twelve months, and get a clearer picture about Bud's impact on the team. Because three months from now nothing would be better than now, and then we're just delaying when we would do the checkpoint.
moments.why: Handles the 'should we wait until the new manager settles in' objection with a reason to go now rather than a reassurance.

coaching_notes: Not a first time conversation despite the FTC in the filename. This is a twice-monthly coaching call inside an active Brightstar engagement, and the sale inside it is an upsell of the OMG team assessment that the owner had already declined once.
Rob priced by naming the client's own past objection first, then offered a $500-600 individual assessment as a smaller on-ramp. Clean way to reopen something that was turned down on price.

The stops / people seen / conversations / appointments model at 9:47 and the ratio diagnosis at 11:21 are the most transferable minutes on the recording, and they answer the 'what should the numbers be' question without inventing a benchmark.
No decision date was requested. The call ends on 'you just let me know,' which is exactly why this is still open; compare with how he handles timing in the Milosi and Murray calls.
Speaker numbering is inverted relative to most files in the library: Rob is Speaker 2, the client is Speaker 1.

headline: Kickoff expectations and a sales-process teardown
summary: Taylor runs Milosi, a Nashville-area landscape design-build and maintenance company restructuring into separate commercial and residential lines under John and Austin, with roughly six or seven salespeople on each side. Rob spent the first half setting expectations for the engagement: the four-S model, why structure carries the leverage, the learning sequence that precedes behavior change, learn-know-live-own, the change curve, the new toy phase, thirty-day truth-telling check-ins, and a pre-planted referral ask. He then had Taylor screen-share the Milosi process and interrogated it, pressing for milestones, prospect decisions and expectations, and noting that a process this good should not produce their sales-cycle problem. They closed on the May 14 in-person leadership kickoff with the scope set as shortening the sales cycle.
outcome_note: May 14 in-person kickoff confirmed for 7 to 11 a.m. at the Hendersonville office with Austin and John added, scope agreed as shortening the sales cycle, and Taylor to bring his process documents.

milestones.text: Can we do some high level expectations?

Rob confirms the May 14 date, the 7 to 11 a.m. window, the Hendersonville office, and who needs to be in the room, which surfaces the whole commercial/residential restructure and gets John added alongside Austin.

Taylor sets his own criterion for the engagement: is the program fluid and responsive to their week-to-week needs, or a regimented sequence they get plugged into, and what happens each time a new salesperson is onboarded.

Not that I want to evade responsibility for how successful we are together, but truly, the thing that is predictive of how successful we will be together is you and your leaders. You probably already know that, right? But there it is.

Where we want to be is we want a sales process with all the right milestones that's adequately sequenced, that's predictive of results. The reason that I started with this is a lot is because one of the things that EOS does really well is they make it simple enough to use. We need a sales process that's simple enough to use.
So a lot of what you just told me is actually pretty good, but they can't be doing all that super well, or else you wouldn't have the sales cycle issue, right?

Taylor explains where the cycle actually stalls: a $5,000 design chasing a $500,000 project, with 40 to 80 to 100 hours sunk into design and estimating before anyone knows whether the budget was ever real.
What's that number now?

We're gonna look at the four S, strategy, structure, staff, skills, through the lens of shortening the sales cycle. And we'll start kind of where we were at just now, with me interrogating what already exists. Here's what is good about it, what can we get rid of, and then what's missing.

moments.title: What success actually looks like
moments.quote: If you can look at your team and go, everybody on the team, or most people on the team, are incrementally turning into better versions of themselves, then the rest of everything else kind of will take care of itself. Revenue is kind of a lagging indicator for that piece of work.
moments.why: Sets the measure of the engagement before any numbers are discussed, which is what protects month three.

moments.title: Why structure carries the leverage
moments.quote: The leverage that we have, and how well we take advantage of that leverage, is going to be based off mostly structure, because all the reinforcement mechanisms... I get in front of the room for four hours, and then it's up to the leaders to reinforce that for the next three months.
moments.why: The clearest one-sentence case for doing infrastructure before training.

moments.title: Why leaders go first, even when the client wants speed
moments.quote: People go, well, can we get the team started right away? And it's like, God, believe me, I would love to do that. But the team at some point is going to be looking at the leaders, asking questions, looking at the leaders if they're skeptical, looking at the leaders for reinforcement. We just need them five or ten steps ahead of their team.
moments.why: Acknowledges the client's impatience as reasonable, then gives the mechanical reason it doesn't work.

moments.title: The four stages of evidence before behavior changes
moments.quote: We'll change the way that they see the world from a sales standpoint. We'll get them increased awareness. Then we'll get them talking a little differently with a common language, whether it's pain or compelling reason or up-front contracts. And then finally we'll get some behavioral change. Leading up to that, it's not that nothing's happening.
moments.why: Pre-empts the week-six 'is this working?' conversation by naming what progress looks like before results appear.

moments.title: Learn, know, live, own
moments.quote: You learn an idea and you could start to apply it, but it still requires time, energy, effort, conscious thought. Then you know it, where it becomes habitual. Then you live it, when you've changed your behavior patterns. And then owning is when everything that we teach is innate to you, you use it in your personal life, you use it to get a table at a restaurant.
moments.why: Explains a four-year average client relationship as a function of depth rather than dependency.

moments.title: Structure the hell out of three months
moments.quote: We tend to structure the hell out of like three months at a time. But the problem, especially with a new client, is that you might not be able to see ninety-one days into the future. So you don't want to be so structured that you have no fluidity for when you're thirty-one days in and it's like, we need to do more of this and less of this.
moments.why: The direct answer to Taylor's structured-versus-fluid question, and it concedes the real limit instead of promising a system.

moments.title: The change curve, and the dip people misread
moments.quote: If we're sixteen days in and someone blows something up that used to be pretty easy, their instinct is going to be, I shouldn't have done that, this doesn't work. When the reality is, you didn't do the thing that we asked you to do very well, therefore we got a negative outcome.
moments.why: Inoculates the owner against the first bad result, which is usually when training programs get quietly abandoned.

moments.title: New toy phase and telling each other the truth
moments.quote: There's this moment where it's new stuff, fun, new toy, and that wears off, and it'll get difficult, and we'll get into the dog days of application of technique. Sometimes that's day thirty-one, sometimes it's day sixty-one. You and I will get together and tell each other the truth every thirty days.
moments.why: Names the predictable slump and attaches a standing meeting to it in the same breath.

moments.title: Plants the referral ask before any work is done
moments.quote: People that are happy with the work that we're doing together, that they're seeing the results they expect to see from us, make introductions and referrals for me. So I just, if you're cool with that, I'm going to ask you for that in the future.
moments.why: Asks for permission to ask, at the one moment when there is nothing to be awkward about.

moments.title: Three questions that turn a flowchart into a sales process
moments.quote: So what are the milestones associated with each? To advance an opportunity. And then also, what decision does the prospect need to make to advance? And then, what expectations are we setting with them? Do we have any of that?
moments.why: The most portable moment on the recording. Works on any client's process document.

moments.title: Interrogating the process out loud
moments.quote: I'm interrogating the process here. A lot of what you just told me is actually pretty good, but they can't be doing all that super well, or else you wouldn't have the sales cycle issue, right?
moments.why: Cuts into a guided tour with a contradiction, and it gets Taylor to locate the real bottleneck in design and estimating rather than in selling.

moments.title: The $50,000 end table
moments.quote: People ask about price early for two reasons: because they want to disqualify you, or because they don't want to be embarrassed when you give them the number. I went into a furniture store, and there was an end table, and the guy told me fifty. And I was like, there's no way it's fifty dollars. And he was like, sir, it's fifty thousand. And I felt like a stupid hick. You have to protect people's okayness.
moments.why: A story Taylor can hand straight to his designers, aimed at exactly the moment he had just described as their weakness.

coaching_notes: Despite FTC in the filename, this is a kickoff and program-design call with a client who has already agreed to work together; Kyle referred them and the first conversation happened earlier.

The block from 7:17 to 29:36 is the most complete version of Rob's onboarding script in this batch: four-S, learning model, learn/know/live/own, change curve, new toy phase, thirty-day truth-telling, and the referral ask planted before any work has been done. Worth listening to end to end before a kickoff.
'What are the milestones? What decision does the prospect need to make to advance? What expectations are we setting?' is a three-question teardown that works on any client's process document.
Rob let Taylor hold the floor for long stretches of the process tour. The sharpest minute came when he broke in with the contradiction at 42:26 rather than continuing to take notes.

Transcript quality: Speaker 3 is a diarization artifact carrying backchannel from both men, and roughly ninety seconds starting around 24:18 is Taylor off-mic dressing his son for a school ball. Milosi is also transcribed as 'Melosi.'

headline: COO inherits a sales team with no system

The call ended with a scheduled follow-up and two industry referrals to be sent by Tuesday.
outcome_note: Renee asked for staffing-industry referrals and a written overview; they booked a decision conversation for the 24th at 5:30 Eastern / 2:30 Pacific before hanging up.

moments.title: Two paths, stated up front
moments.quote: Usually at the end of the conversation we take one or two paths. Either — appreciate it, not a fit for us, not right now, that's fine, no harm no foul. Or — yes, we want to take the next step.
moments.why: A clean, 20-second up-front contract that gives the prospect an explicit right to say no before any questions start.

moments.title: Refuses to answer the diagnostic question
moments.quote: Well, why do you think they're stuck?
moments.why: She asked him whether it's normal to have that many deals parked in negotiation; he hands the question straight back and gets a far better answer than he could have given.

moments.title: Second why on the same story
moments.quote: So why do you think that that person didn't pick that up right away?
moments.why: She has already blamed the rep; the second why moves her from blame to a real cause — they got excited and believed what the office manager told them.

moments.title: Hands her the BAT triangle and makes her use it
moments.quote: If you look at your team, if they're struggling to get in front of decision makers, what do you think is missing of those three things?
moments.why: He teaches behavior / technique / attitude in 90 seconds and then immediately makes her self-diagnose against it rather than lecturing.

moments.title: The alignment test
moments.quote: So if I was to ask your salespeople what makes a qualified deal or opportunity, would they tell me the same thing you just told me?
moments.why: One question that exposes whether a leader's standard actually exists anywhere but in her own head.

moments.title: Who plays the bad cop
moments.quote: So if he's not that person, then who's going to play that role?
moments.why: The answer is the whole deal: 'Well, fortunately, I have been, but it's not going very well because I'm the bad guy.'

moments.title: Pushes past the business reason to the personal one
moments.quote: Why that for you?
moments.why: She answers with the company line twice; he asks a third time until she says growing it is how she proves she can be a CEO.

moments.title: Find out, or wonder
moments.quote: Find out if they can do it, or wonder if they can.
moments.why: The line that reframes the evaluation from a product into the obvious next move — worth stealing verbatim.

moments.title: Why the sales manager hire she wants will fail
moments.quote: Before you were to even go out and hire a sales manager, you've got to have the right pieces in place for that sales manager to be effective. Ten years of doing this — it's a rare bird you find that wants to come in and build that for you.
moments.why: He disagrees with the prospect's own proposed solution without losing the room, then uses it to make the evaluation the logical first step.

moments.title: Why the leaders go first
moments.quote: If you remember back when they were kiddos, they might have said, mom, I want to swim. If you didn't know how to swim, they get out there and they're drowning — you're not going to be able to help, because you're just keeping your own head above water.
moments.why: Justifies a three-month leaders-first sequence with an analogy instead of a methodology argument.

moments.title: Asks about money without flinching
moments.quote: So budget wise, are those scary numbers, doable?
moments.why: He names the discomfort himself right after quoting roughly $40K year one, and she answers honestly instead of going dark.

moments.title: Two belief questions before scheduling
moments.quote: Do you believe I can help at this point?
moments.why: Checks understanding and capability separately before asking for the next meeting — the answer tells him exactly what the referrals have to do.

coaching_notes: Watch the question discipline: across the first 25 minutes he asks 'why do you think' five separate times and never once supplies the answer. Every useful fact in this call came out of her mouth.

Money is handled flatly and in sequence — $300 per person, $1,500, $3,000 overview, $4,500 total, then $600 per person per month — with no softening and an immediate 'are those scary numbers doable.' No discount, no flinch.
He never pinned down who actually signs. She says 'we're fine financially' and talks about the CEO as a separate voice, but he never asks whether the CEO has to approve a $40K-plus commitment.

Minutes 45-56 drift into answering her questions about HubSpot, cold calling vs marketing, and his ASA history — good credibility, but it is presenting, and it pushed the close into the last five minutes of a 63-minute call.

headline: Founder scaling past founder-led sales, no next step
summary: Evan runs a 17-person product design and engineering agency where his partner is the only salesperson, and deal flow is the bottleneck. Rob spent 20 straight minutes qualifying — a thermometer question on how much help they need, how hard the thing is to sell, what the average deal is worth, what the rep would have to close, and what they would pay someone that rare — before asking permission to say anything about himself. He talked Evan out of part-time or split-role selling, explained that he only starts with hiring if it is part of a longer build, and framed money as something a CEO accepts easily when the problem work was done first. The call ended with someone knocking on Evan's door and no next step agreed.
outcome_note: Evan said it was 'mostly exploratory' and that he needed to sync with his leadership team; Rob's 'what do you want to do next' never got answered because Evan was interrupted and left it at 'we can follow up on email.'

milestones.text: Evan names the bottleneck himself: 17 full-time staff, one salesperson who is also his partner, and deal flow capped as a result.

Let me ask you this thermometer type question. I get in front of a lot of entrepreneurs that are like, we just literally don't know what to do at all. That's one end of the spectrum. The other end is, Rob, we would probably find a way to be pretty successful without you — we just have a couple gaps. Where are you guys out there, do you think?
It's important to have an honest conversation about what you sell and how hard it is to sell. What do you guys do, and how challenging do you think it'll be for a non-founder to do it?
And this person needs to close six of those twelve, or all twelve of those twelve?
If somebody's selling three to $6 million, what's their comp to do that?

If you met me today and I said, I have all these family contacts that need you, and I dumped $3 million of business into your lap — what would you pay me for a referral fee? What's the max you would pay me?
If this is your guys' idea of, we're going to assess people on the team for role fit of salesperson — just be real open minded for when the assessment tells you this person cannot do it.
I normally can help people be more successful than they would be without me, but I don't do just like hiring and then we cut loose. Does that make sense?
Evan says it is mostly exploratory for him and that he needs to sync with the rest of the leadership team to see where this might plug in.

moments.title: The thermometer question
moments.quote: I get in front of a lot of entrepreneurs that are like, we just literally don't know what to do at all. The other end of the spectrum is, Rob, we would probably find a way to be pretty successful without you. Where are you guys out there, do you think?
moments.why: A reusable opener that gets a self-rating instead of a feature list, and gives both ends of the spectrum so neither answer is embarrassing.

moments.title: How hard is this to sell without you in the room
moments.quote: It's important to have an honest conversation about what you sell and how hard it is to sell. What do you guys do, and how challenging do you think it'll be for a non-founder to do it?
moments.why: Goes straight at the thing most founders never examine — whether the sale is transferable at all.

moments.title: Turns eight-to-twelve clients into a quota
moments.quote: And this person needs to close six of those twelve, or all twelve of those twelve?
moments.why: Converts a vague ambition into a number the rest of the qualification hangs on.

moments.title: Gun to your head
moments.quote: If there's a gun to your head right now, what would you say? It's an unfair question. If you said 150 to 600,000 — you can give me a crazy unfair range, that's fine. I just want to know.
moments.why: How to get a number out of someone who genuinely has not thought about it, by making the unfairness of the question explicit.

moments.title: The referral-fee reframe
moments.quote: If I dumped $3 million of business into your lap, what would you pay me for a referral fee? What's the max?
moments.why: When the direct comp question stalls, he reframes it as something Evan can actually price, and gets 5-10% in fifteen seconds.

moments.title: Why he distrusts big guarantees
moments.quote: I'm not a believer in guarantees. I'm really skeptical of people who want large guarantees, because large guarantees oftentimes lower the glass ceiling.
moments.why: Rob takes a position that costs him nothing and buys credibility — and it is the opposite of what a founder expects a sales consultant to say.

moments.title: Are your people becoming better versions of themselves
moments.quote: Do you get results from your people? Is everybody on your team becoming a slightly better version of themselves because of their interaction with you guys?
moments.why: His general leadership question lands flat, so he reissues it as something concrete and gets a real answer.

moments.title: It's almost always the founder's fault
moments.quote: I ask that question because when companies fail to scale outside of the founder-led sales model, it's almost always the founder's fault.
moments.why: Says the uncomfortable thing early, while it's still abstract, so it is already on the table if the engagement ever happens.

moments.title: Asks permission to present, 20 minutes in
moments.quote: I've been asking you questions for 20 minutes. What would you want me to share about me or what I do?
moments.why: A whole first call's worth of discovery before a single word about himself, and even then the prospect chooses the topic.

moments.title: The case against part-time sales
moments.quote: Part-time sales I'm a lot less bullish on, because selling is harder than all the other roles in the organization. You have to face social rejection, and human beings aren't really wired to do very well with social rejection.
moments.why: Talks the prospect out of the cheap option on the merits, which is more persuasive than any pitch would have been.

moments.title: Nobody admits to being too wimpy
moments.quote: At the end of the month I don't come to you and say, hey boss, I'm just a little too wimpy to do prospecting. I come to you and say, I had all this other stuff to do.
moments.why: The single most quotable line in the call, and it makes the split-role failure mode impossible to unsee.

moments.title: Why money is easy with a CEO
moments.quote: CEOs are great because they care about the problem. Money becomes really easy if we have the right conversation up front. At the end of my sales process the CEO is saying, we've got big problems that have big impacts that we're dying to fix, and we believe you could fix them. And then when I give them the number, they're like, oh yeah, easy.
moments.why: He describes his own close while answering Evan's pricing-model question — teaching the method by narrating it.

coaching_notes: The qualification sequence is the lesson here: readiness, difficulty of the sale, deal size, required quota, comp, locality, who manages, and how good they are at developing people — all before he says one word about Lushin.
He disqualifies two of the prospect's own ideas (part-time selling, hire-only projects) and gains ground doing it. Disagreeing well is the whole move.

The close is the weak point. He asks 'what do you want to do next' once, Evan gets interrupted by someone at his door, and Rob accepts 'we can follow up on email' without proposing a date or a reason to meet again. A 34-minute call this good deserved a booked next step.

No budget was ever discussed for Lushin itself — only what a salesperson would cost. Evan left without knowing what working with Rob costs, which makes the internal leadership conversation harder to win.

Diarization is briefly scrambled between 1:37 and 1:52: 'Is this your first foray into sales training?' and 'No, no, no — just growing the sales team outside of founder-led sales' are both Rob, attributed to the wrong labels. Lushin is transcribed as 'Lucian.'

coach_confidence: high — Anthony thanks 'Chad' at 28:30, which is the transcription of Shad

headline: Onboarding kickoff with two new reps, not a prospect
summary: This is not a first-time prospect conversation — it is a program kickoff with two brand-new salespeople at an existing client, A Plus Staffing, whose leaders Brittany and Allison had already set it up. Shad opened with a full agenda, walked them through the Sales Essentials weekly classes, the twice-monthly A Plus-only coaching sessions, the newsletter, and Sandler Online, then spent the back third asking what each of them wanted worked on. Anthony named adult-to-adult positioning and reversing on the phone; Kelsey named setting role expectations and converting referral promises into actual names. He mapped each request to a specific tool and closed by recapping who would send what.
outcome_note: Already-sold engagement; the call ends with Shad listing the setup steps — Brian Daniels sends class access and Sandler Online logins, Shweta sends the recurring coaching invites.

milestones.text: I know we've got an hour, but I think we're going to need maybe 30 minutes. Here's what I plan to cover with you: introductions, a background on both of you, background on myself. Then we'll talk about the Lushin sales training program, how it works, the things you'll be getting involved in — the weekly foundation classes, the couple-times-a-month sales training sessions, some of the other tools. Then how I'll go about getting those set up for you. And then what are some of the things from a selling side you want to make sure we work on.
Anything else either of you want to cover or talk through?

What are some things that you're hoping that we work on in the training and coaching — whether it's past challenges selling that you ran into, or working with clients, or if it's 'I want to figure this out'?

Shad recaps the setup: Kelsey gets class access so she can join Anthony on Thursdays, both go on the newsletter, both get added to the twice-monthly A Plus coaching sessions, and both get Sandler Online logins — Brian Daniels and Shweta own the sends.

moments.title: A full agenda before anyone speaks
moments.quote: I know we've got an hour, but I think we're going to need maybe 30 minutes. So here's what I plan to cover with you.
moments.why: Gives back half the booked time before asking for anything — a small move that sets the tone for every session after it.

moments.title: Why a rep leaves after a $300K year
moments.quote: Ended up billing around 300k in my first year. But this wasn't really the type of company feel I was looking for, and I felt the leadership was just very young, to be transparent. I didn't really feel like I was getting the mentoring that would foster long-term success.
moments.why: The prospect's own words on why coaching and mentorship beat comp for a strong young rep — useful language for any hiring conversation.

moments.title: Not a script, your voice
moments.quote: How do I make this natural to me, that I can use day to day, that sounds like me and not like a robot and not like 'here's how Shad said I've got to say it.' We don't believe in a lot of scripts. We believe in giving you processes, tools, guidelines, rules, and then you putting it into your own voice.
moments.why: Pre-empts the single biggest objection new reps have to sales methodology, in the first session.

moments.title: Training wheels
moments.quote: When you took the training wheels off, what happened the first time? You wiped out. You skinned up your knees and elbows, you had to adjust and make tweaks for the next time.
moments.why: Sets the expectation that the tools will fail on first use, which is the thing that otherwise makes new reps quietly stop using them.

moments.title: Pre-authorizes the mid-cycle call for help
moments.quote: I want you to know that when you hit those things and it's not working perfect, that frustration — that's normal. In between sessions, if you're like, I tried that, it didn't work, I need some help — reach out. Do not be bashful about reaching out in between.
moments.why: Names the exact feeling and the exact behavior he wants, so the ask later feels like compliance rather than weakness.

moments.title: Lets them set the curriculum
moments.quote: What are some things that you're hoping that we work on — whether it's past challenges selling that you ran into, or if it's 'I want to figure this out'?
moments.why: Ten minutes of the kickoff spent collecting their agenda, which he writes down and references in the recap.

moments.title: Maps a vague want onto two named tools
moments.quote: There'll be that establishing expectations — that tool we call an up-front contract. Part of it also is we'll work through something called transactional analysis, which is how do we stay in that adult-to-adult, especially when they're in conflict or putting pressure on us.
moments.why: Anthony says 'adult to adult' and gets two concrete tools back in fifteen seconds — proof the program already has an answer.

moments.title: Why referrals stall, and what to do instead
moments.quote: They're not giving referrals every day, and they don't necessarily know what makes a good referral for you. I went through his LinkedIn and sent him a specific list of folks and said, here's some that I think may fit. Out of that he sent me four good referrals last week.
moments.why: Answers Kelsey's 'they just say we'll think about it' with a mechanic that is immediately usable, plus his own live example.

moments.title: The new-car analogy for referral awareness
moments.quote: If you bought a new car and suddenly you see those cars all over the road — well, they were always there. You're just training your brain to look for them. When you're asking for referrals, people have connections. We've got to help turn that part of their brain on.
moments.why: Explains why specificity works, so the tactic survives the first time it does not produce names.

coaching_notes: Filename problem: this is labeled Prospect / FTC but it is a kickoff with two new hires at an existing A Plus Staffing engagement. Anyone studying it for first-conversation technique will be studying the wrong thing — it is a model onboarding session instead.
The one transferable first-conversation element is the opening: a full agenda, time given back, and 'anything else either of you want to cover' before anyone has spoken.

Roughly six minutes (3:42 to 10:05) are consumed by Anthony's microphone failing and a dial-in workaround. Shad keeps the session moving by giving Kelsey the class overview while Anthony reconnects — a good recovery, but it leaves Anthony with no program overview of his own.
The back half is the strongest coaching: he collects what each rep wants, names the specific tool for each request, and recaps both the logistics and their requests at the close.
Lushin appears as 'Lucian'/'Lucien' and Shad as 'Chad'/'Shad' throughout the transcript.

coach_confidence: high — Speaker 1 addresses the prospect as Emily repeatedly and describes Lushin's evaluation and coaching model; the prospect Emily is the Atria contact, not Emily Shaw

other_speakers.label: Speaker 2
other_speakers.who: Emily, recruitment team manager and operations lead at Atria Consulting, seven years with the firm

headline: Four full-desk recruiters, 100 calls, two meetings
summary: Emily runs the recruiting team at Atria Consulting, an 18-year-old staffing firm, and was asked last October to pivot herself and then the whole team onto sales. Since April four people have been making roughly 100 cold calls a day and have booked two meetings in three months, revenue is dipping, and she is openly saying she feels like she is failing at training, managing and selling at once. Shad diagnosed it as technique and mindset rather than effort, warned her against scripts, laid out his strategy-structure-staff-skills sequence, and eventually gave a number — roughly $3,000 a month for a team of four plus the evaluation. She said she is comparing three vendors for her CEO and is leaning toward hiring a dedicated senior salesperson instead; he countered with the bird-cage-for-the-bird caution and left it in her court.
outcome_note: No meeting booked — Emily will forward Lushin's website to the CEO as one of three options in a comparison, and promised to let him know either way.

Emily's seven years, the October pivot to sales, the March team training
The number: ~100 calls a day, two meetings in three months
Why else can't you get through to decision makers

Impact: revenue dipping, one-off placements, no longevity
Emily: I feel like I'm failing at all three jobs
The approach: evaluate, fix management first, then the team
She presses for process, timeline and cost — and reveals who actually decides
Bird cage for the bird, and the soft exit

milestones.text: I went on your website, but I want to hear a little bit more about Atria and you and your background. Then, where are some of those areas you'd get help? And I'll share here's how from a high level we help. And then the goal — does it make sense to talk further or not? Does that sound good?
Emily lays out the number: four people making about 100 calls a day since April, two meetings booked in three months, four clients brought in and all of them one-offs.
I know you said you're having a hard time getting to decision makers and you're getting some bad info — but why else do you think you're having a hard time getting through to them?

There's kind of three areas, Emily, to look at when we're doing a lot of behavior and action and work and it's not paying off. One of them is, are we doing enough behavior? And it sounds like you are. So the next piece is technique — what are we saying in our voicemails, our emails, our LinkedIn messages? And then the last piece is mindset.
I know you said since you started on this you brought in a few accounts, but how else is this impacting the company right now?
So, that being said, what's the owner's take on all this?
What I've got to make sure is that anything you and I do, the owner's aligned with it. Because if not, it's a problem — she's going to come back to you and go, what are we doing here?
Really quick — how are you going to make the decision between the various companies you're talking to?
Two things. Can't tell you without us talking further, because I don't know exactly what all we would help you on. And same thing for the cost, until we talk further and I get a better picture.

Dollar-wise, typically a team of four people, it's going to be running in the neighborhood of about $3,000 a month. But that's again depending on what we need, and that's the coaching piece. Then there's the evaluation, which is based on number of people also.

Typically where we take the conversation first is a further conversation with yourself and whoever this is important to, if it's the owner. I'd send you some homework to help pick out some things in those areas. And if we get to the end of it, Emily, it's — based on what you're offering, it just doesn't work for us, no harm no foul, part friends. Or if it does, then here's the next step we would take.

moments.title: The number that defines the call
moments.quote: Between the four of us we make about 100 calls a day and are not booking any meetings. In the last three months I think we've had two meetings booked.
moments.why: The prospect's own arithmetic is the whole diagnosis — effort is not the problem, and both of them know it from minute four.

moments.title: Why else
moments.quote: I know you said you're having a hard time getting to decision makers and you're getting some bad info — but why else do you think you're having a hard time getting through to them?
moments.why: He acknowledges the answer she already gave and asks for the next layer, which is where 'I don't know, I really wish I knew' comes out.

moments.title: Behavior, technique, mindset — then hands it back
moments.quote: It sounds like you're doing a lot and you're targeting. It sounds like this may be some technique and mindset pieces. I don't know — what do you think?
moments.why: He lays the framework over her situation, reaches a conclusion, and then asks her to confirm or reject it rather than declaring it.

moments.title: Finds the real buyer in one question
moments.quote: So, that being said, what's the owner's take on all this?
moments.why: Thirteen minutes in he establishes that Emily is not the decision maker, which should have shaped everything after it.

moments.title: The admission
moments.quote: I'm almost feeling like I'm failing at sales training, the sales managing, and bringing in sales for the company. It kills me because I love working here.
moments.why: The payoff of fifteen minutes of patient questions — and it comes without him asking for it.

moments.title: Takes the blame off her, and she refuses it
moments.quote: Well, Emily, don't beat yourself up. You're not a salesperson by nature.
moments.why: She pushes back — 'I also have to recognize there's something I'm not doing right' — which is a stronger buying signal than agreement would have been.

moments.title: The caution on scripts
moments.quote: Scripts are good to give an outline. But we've got to be careful being too scripted, because it's like the cold calls you probably get — this isn't a person talking to me. And also, if things don't go to plan of the script.
moments.why: Corrects the exact thing she has been doing with her team, without telling her she was wrong to do it.

moments.title: Up-front contract for a meeting that never got booked
moments.quote: If we get to the end of it, Emily, it's — based on what you're offering, it just doesn't work for us, no harm no foul, part friends. Or if it does, then here's the next step we would take.
moments.why: Textbook framing of the next conversation, including the homework and the right to say no. Worth hearing alongside the fact that he never asked for a date.

moments.title: Holds the price back, then gives it anyway
moments.quote: Can't tell you without us talking further, because I don't know exactly what all we would help you on. Same thing for the cost.
moments.why: Listen to this next to 34:34 — she presses three times and he eventually prices the engagement from the podium, before the owner conversation he just said he needed.

moments.title: How will you decide between us
moments.quote: Really quick — how are you going to make the decision between the various companies you're talking to?
moments.why: Gets her to reveal the whole competitive picture, including that other firms declined the work because there is no existing sales process to fix.

moments.title: The bird cage
moments.quote: Do I have the bird cage ready for the bird?
moments.why: His last and best shot: if you hire a senior salesperson with no strategy, structure or tools, you either won't get the good bird or the good bird will fly the coop.

coaching_notes: The discovery in the first twenty minutes is excellent and gets to a genuine emotional admission at 18:01. The last ten minutes give it all back — he prices the engagement, hands over a website link, and leaves without a date.

He identified at 15:13 that the owner decides and said at 35:17 that the owner has to be aligned, then still let Emily leave as the messenger carrying his website into a three-vendor comparison he will never be in the room for.
He answered 'how long and what's the cost' after resisting twice. Watch the sequence: the resistance was correct, the capitulation under a third ask is the teachable error.

Strong individual mechanics worth stealing: the behavior/technique/mindset triage, the script caution, the decision-criteria question at 36:06, and the bird-cage reframe against hiring a senior rep into a vacuum.

Transcript issues: the opening line is rendered 'Hi, I'm Linda' (garbled greeting), Lushin appears as 'Lucien'/'Lucian', and at 39:32 the coach appears to call her 'Dave' — ASR noise, not a third participant.

other_speakers.label: Speaker 2
other_speakers.who: Scott, co-owner of Mattison (rendered 'Madison' by the transcriber), an association management company

headline: Referral call disqualified in fourteen minutes
summary: Andy Chapman connected Shad to Scott, who co-owns an association management company that staffs and runs about fifteen larger nonprofits and has been around since the eighties. Scott took the call out of respect for Andy, not out of need: the firm grows through client growth, new programs and acquisitions, passes on 90% of inbound opportunity, and has never really sold itself. Shad offered his three common problem areas, asked why Scott would want the team more sales-minded, and got an answer about process and membership churn rather than a problem. He named it — this does not sound like a priority — and ended the call at fourteen minutes with the door open.
outcome_note: Shad disqualified it himself: 'focusing on sales doesn't sound like it's a top priority right now,' Scott agreed they are 'more passive on it,' and they parted with contact details and nothing scheduled.

milestones.text: Sets a light agenda off the Andy Chapman referral — background on his connection, what Lushin does, and then a decision about whether to talk further — and gets a yes before continuing.
Scott names the only thing resembling a gap: a majority of his people are not sales-minded, and the culture change has been slow going.
Well, Scott, why look to try and get them more sales minded?
It sounds like the team's doing pretty well already, and focusing on sales doesn't sound like it's a top priority right now.

moments.title: Uses the referrer as a joke and an opener
moments.quote: Well, in true Andy Chapman fashion, he didn't tell me a whole lot on you. I still looked you up online, but give me a little background on yourself.
moments.why: Admits he was given nothing, signals he did the homework anyway, and hands the floor over — all in one sentence.

moments.title: Asks what's good before asking what's wrong
moments.quote: What's some of the best things about it?
moments.why: Opens with the positive and gets the company's core values and mission in Scott's own words, which is where rapport actually comes from.

moments.title: Why did you take this call
moments.quote: So, Andy connected us. So what made you say, yeah, I'll jump on this conversation here?
moments.why: The answer — 'I hadn't heard from Andy in quite some time, but if he's recommending we meet, it's worthwhile' — is the first clear signal there is no driving problem behind the meeting.

moments.title: Three areas, offered as a menu with permission
moments.quote: Kind of three big areas we help. I'll just share those and you tell me if any of those are things you guys are running into. Does that sound good?
moments.why: A compact way to present capability without pitching: he asks permission, lists three problems, and makes the prospect do the matching.

moments.title: The one question that settles it
moments.quote: Well, Scott, why look to try and get them more sales minded?
moments.why: The answer is about EOS process and membership attrition that already replaces itself — a reason to tidy, not a reason to buy. The call effectively ends here.

moments.title: Says it out loud instead of pitching into it
moments.quote: It sounds like the team's doing pretty well already, and focusing on sales doesn't sound like it's a top priority right now.
moments.why: The whole reason to listen to this call. He takes it away, Scott half-defends and then concedes 'we're more passive on it,' and nobody wastes another month.

moments.title: The exit that keeps the referral intact
moments.quote: You got my contact information, so if things do change where you go, hey, it's something we want to be a little more proactive on — then absolutely, happy to talk and see how we can help again.
moments.why: Disqualifies the opportunity without disqualifying the relationship or embarrassing the person who made the introduction.

coaching_notes: The shortest call in the set and arguably the most instructive: a referral with no pain gets fourteen minutes, one 'why,' and a clean no. Nobody gets sent a proposal.
Pattern to copy — best things about it, why did you take the call, three areas with permission, then one 'why do you want that.' Four moves and the qualification is finished.

Fair criticism: he took the first 'it's slow going but it's improved what we do' at face value. There may have been a membership-retention problem underneath, and a second why at 12:50 could have tested whether chasing renewals every year actually costs them anything.

He also never asked about money, timing or who else would be involved — correct here, because there was nothing to qualify, but worth noticing that he stopped the moment the pain failed rather than pushing through the rest of a checklist.

headline: Owner hires a coach before the problems start
summary: Carlos owns an investment fund and a two-and-a-half-year-old exterior services company, PG Service Group, that sells valet trash into Central Florida resorts and short-term rental communities on two-to-five-year contracts. He has just moved Jennifer — likable, industry-experienced, no formal sales training — into business development three weeks ago, and he wants the coaching in place before she struggles rather than after. Alejandra, who will manage her, admitted she has no framework for setting goals or holding anyone accountable. Shad walked them through strategy, structure, staff and skills, declined to price anything, and sent a four-S survey as homework ahead of a deeper conversation booked on the call for the following Thursday.
outcome_note: Next Thursday at 2:00 p.m. Eastern booked and the invite sent before they hung up, with a ten-minute four-S survey to be completed separately by Carlos and Alejandra beforehand.

milestones.text: Thank you both for jumping on. I figure we'll just do a little intros and backgrounds. Angela had connected us and didn't share too much on background. She mentioned you had some interest in sales training, coaching, potentially getting some help, so we'll talk about that. And usually at the end of this we figure out, does it make sense to talk further or not.
Tell me a little bit more — you said tactical aspects in prospecting. What's some of the things she's running into?
You mentioned long sales cycle. I know you said most contracts are two to five with an average of three. What does the sales cycle itself look like right now?

Carlos, you said there's a lot of opportunity in the market, got to work fast ahead of the competition. If you look over the next couple of years, what does the opportunity in the market look like in terms of sales?
Carlos gave me his take on things and his focus. How about for you, acting in that sales manager role?

Now, to answer your question in terms of what that takes — I don't know, until we get into a deeper conversation. There's a little piece of homework I'd have you do just to better understand those areas.

I work with most of my clients in one year buckets. I've been with a lot of my clients four to five years now. The first year or so is a lot of putting pieces in place, getting people to change behaviors and techniques and mindsets and getting that consistent.
Is that something typical for both of you when you make a decision — just having a couple references around it?
Carlos takes 2:00 p.m. Eastern the following Thursday; Shad sends the calendar invite and the four-S survey before the call ends so he does not forget.

I'm going to send a separate email with that homework ahead. Then when we get in the meeting we're going to dive in, ask some questions off that, get a better, deeper picture of where we're at, talk a little bit more about wanting to get to that $5 million. And from there I'll be able to share, here's what it would take, what that looks like in terms of time, effort, dollars. And then we usually figure out, do we want to take a next step from there or not.

moments.title: Agenda plus the exit ramp, in twenty seconds
moments.quote: Usually at the end of this we figure out, does it make sense to talk further or not.
moments.why: Short, unceremonious up-front contract on a three-person call where one participant has just fought her way through bad internet.

moments.title: The prospect states his own gap
moments.quote: It's a great business, and we have a tremendous amount of connectivity in this space, but we also need to start selling — and that's not what I do, or what Alejandra does.
moments.why: Rare clarity from an owner about what he is not. Everything after this is about who will do it and how.

moments.title: Answers 'how does it work' with process, not product
moments.quote: Generally from here we set a longer conversation, 45 minutes to an hour, and that's where we really get into: here's where we're at, here's where I want to get to, here's where some of the gaps are.
moments.why: Describes the sales process itself as the answer to a pricing-adjacent question, which both buys time and models the behavior he teaches.

moments.title: The question whose answer reframes the call
moments.quote: What's some of the things she's running into?
moments.why: Carlos says there aren't any yet — she started three weeks ago and they deliberately hired the coach first. That is a different sale from a rescue, and Shad adjusts.

moments.title: Converts enthusiasm into a number
moments.quote: If you look over the next couple of years, what does the opportunity in the market look like in terms of sales?
moments.why: Gets $5M in three to three-and-a-half years, $300-500K average contracts, and current run rate around $1.6-1.7M — the sizing that makes the engagement defensible.

moments.title: Brings the quiet third participant in
moments.quote: Carlos gave me his take on things and his focus. How about for you, acting in that sales manager role?
moments.why: Alejandra, silent for twelve minutes, says she wouldn't know what goals to set or how to ask for results — the most important disclosure on the call.

moments.title: Crawl, walk, run
moments.quote: We have very much a belief of crawl, then walk, then run. So you've got to have the right pieces in place to support that.
moments.why: Justifies starting with management and structure rather than training Jennifer, which is what they came in asking for.

moments.title: Why you record the calls
moments.quote: You're coaching one of your people and you say, did you do what you should have? And they're going to say, well, yes. Maybe they don't have awareness of what they missed. Maybe they don't want to look bad. When we actually record calls and review those, we can see here's reality. It's like a sports coach.
moments.why: Makes call review feel like film study instead of surveillance — useful language for introducing it to a nervous new manager.

moments.title: Sniffles or sickness — and the best line of the call
moments.quote: Sometimes my clients have a sales sneeze or the sniffles — a few little things we can adjust. Sometimes it's a full-blown sickness we've got to work on.
moments.why: He uses it to refuse to price; Carlos answers 'the good thing for us is we don't even have a patient. There's nothing to cure.' Listen to the whole exchange.

moments.title: No quick punch in the arm
moments.quote: We don't believe in a quick punch in the arm. We believe in repetition changed over time, because that's how most humans change anyway.
moments.why: Sets the expectation of a year-long engagement before anyone has asked how long, and Carlos immediately says he likes the approach.

moments.title: Normalizes the reference request
moments.quote: Is that something typical for both of you when you make a decision — just having a couple references around it?
moments.why: Instead of just agreeing to send references, he turns the ask into information about how they buy.

coaching_notes: A pre-emptive engagement rather than a rescue: the buyer has installed a brand-new rep and wants the coaching in place before she fails. Notice that Shad still runs the same sequence — problem, why, impact, structure — and finds the real gap in Alejandra, not Jennifer.
He refuses to price twice (16:15 and 22:41) and holds it, unlike the Atria call the same month. The homework survey is what lets him hold it: he has a concrete reason the number does not exist yet.

Best practice on the close: he opens the calendar on the call, offers a window, books it, and sends both the invite and the homework before hanging up, with the agenda and the no-harm-no-foul exit stated for the next meeting.

What's thin: he never asked who signs or what Carlos would allocate, and he did not probe the two-year sales cycle against the three-year market window — a one-rep plan may not reach $5M in that time, which is the strategic question underneath the whole engagement.

Was there something in particular? Is it just like how to do it? Is it kind of a mindset? What in particular did you want to talk through?

You've got the mindset first, right? If you think of anything that you want to improve, there's three components — behavior, attitude, technique. Behavior sounds like you've got. Attitude sounds like you've got. So the last piece here is technique.

Ellie names the second problem: she can convert the merely okay candidates easily but cannot get the genuinely strong ones to engage, and two good clients are already annoyed at the quality of submissions.
So, first off, do you know what really good looks like?
You've got my email address. Can you send me some examples? I'd be happy to look through and give you some feedback.

moments.title: Narrows a vague ask before answering it
moments.quote: Was there something in particular? Is it just like how to do it? Is it kind of a mindset? What in particular did you want to talk through?
moments.why: She came in with 'I want to be more confident and close faster'; he turns that into one specific, workable problem before saying anything useful.

moments.title: Goes to the whiteboard
moments.quote: I'm going to use the whiteboard here, because sometimes it's easier to grasp if you just kind of write it out or draw it out. And I'm going to pre-apologize, because I'm not a very good artist — that's obviously why I'm in sales.
moments.why: Drawing the BAT triangle live turns a webinar follow-up into a coaching session, and she ends up photographing the board.

moments.title: Curiously skeptical
moments.quote: Attitude for me would be: I'm curiously skeptical. Curious — where did that number come from, is that real, because that's not my experience. Skeptical — I know people like to inflate things so they look better.
moments.why: A two-word posture she can carry into any conversation, and he tells her she already has it rather than selling her a fix she doesn't need.

moments.title: The two-number question
moments.quote: Thanks for sharing. Is that what you're wanting and hoping to go for, or is that what you're actually making right now? Because both are helpful for me to know.
moments.why: Replaces the confrontation she was using ('that's not what I've heard in the industry') with a question that makes both answers safe to give.

moments.title: Defusing the bomb
moments.quote: I call it beating them to the punch, or defusing a bomb. The best way to defuse a bomb is before it goes off.
moments.why: The core technique of the call: raise the predictable objection yourself, with context for why you need both numbers, before the candidate has a chance to inflate.

moments.title: One-off versus trend
moments.quote: If it's a one-off, okay, we deal with the one-off. But if it's a trend — I'm seeing this 30, 50, 75% of the time — the best thing you can do is go, how do I get ahead of that trend? How do I put out the fire before it starts?
moments.why: Generalizes the fix beyond comp inflation into a rule for handling any recurring objection.

moments.title: Cards on the table
moments.quote: It's like playing a game of cards. You're just going, here's my cards all on the table. Most people will go, okay, you're being open and honest with me ahead, now I can be open and honest with you. You're interrupting the pattern of what I expected here.
moments.why: Explains why transparency works mechanically rather than morally — it breaks the pattern the other person came in braced for.

moments.quote: 70% of the time they should be talking, 30% of the time you should be talking. The only way to do that is to ask questions and listen. And please don't go measure it out.
moments.why: She had just confessed to over-explaining; he gives her a ratio and then immediately takes the pressure off applying it literally.

moments.title: The best-friend exercise
moments.quote: What's the name of your best friend? If Carrie came to you and said, Ellie, I'm looking for a job, I need some help talking through a new position — what questions would you ask her?
moments.why: She produces three good questions in ten seconds, which proves his point before he makes it.

moments.title: The payoff of the exercise
moments.quote: That's the conversation you'd have with Carrie. Have that conversation with candidates.
moments.why: Nine words that dismantle the phone-screen script she had been rebuilding — and he then describes running his own next sales call exactly that way.

moments.title: Go back and define 'great' with the client
moments.quote: Clarify that with the client. What does good, great for this position look like? I want to make sure I'm on the same page with you and looking for the right stuff.
moments.why: Her instinct was to search harder; he redirects her to the client conversation that is actually causing the bad search.

moments.title: Years versus capability
moments.quote: Somebody can have 20 years of experience, but if they only learned a certain skill set in year one, they've just done it 20 years over. Versus — no, we need four years of this really good skill set experience.
moments.why: Gives her the exact argument to make when a client's requirement list is what's shrinking the candidate pool.

coaching_notes: This is a give-first call, not a sales call: no qualification, no budget, no decision process, no pitch. The prospect is a three-month recruiter at a franchise office with no authority to buy anything, and Shad spends 28 minutes coaching her for free off a webinar.

The teaching mechanics are the reason to listen — whiteboard the framework, tell the person which legs they already have, hand them one technique, then generalize it into a rule (one-off vs trend) they can apply elsewhere.
The best-friend exercise at 18:34 is the most portable move in the whole batch: let the person demonstrate the natural version of the behavior, then tell them that was it.

What's missing from a business standpoint: he never asked who runs her office, whether the team buys training, or whether there is a conversation to be had with her managing partner. The one next step is an unpaid InMail review with no date attached.
Filename says 'MRN Network' — it is MRINetwork, and specifically their Boston office. The prospect goes by Ellie; Shad is transcribed as Chad; her former employer Cotiviti appears as 'Cotivity.'

moments.title: Too busy is code
moments.quote: As you probably know, Sandra, too busy is code for it's not a priority.
moments.why: One sentence that reframes a prospect's whole excuse, delivered without argument.

moments.title: Behavior, attitude, technique
moments.quote: Anything you want to improve, there's three components. There's a behavior component, attitude component, technique.
moments.why: Shad pulls up a whiteboard mid-call and teaches the diagnostic frame before prescribing anything.

moments.title: Two choices
moments.quote: So you have two choices. One, get back to me or we set up a time to talk, we can clear this up. Two, you don't, and here's what's going to happen. Choice is yours.

moments.title: Clarity is caring

moments.title: This fire versus that fire

moments.title: The prospect's own verdict

moments.title: I know that question, and I've not been asking it

moments.title: Three rocks, three outcomes
moments.quote: What would be the three most important outcomes? Any kind of training or development is, all right, what's not happening that should? What can some people do that not everybody can do?

moments.title: Closing warm leads is the easy part

moments.title: Why would we hunt?
moments.quote: If you have a thing that's working but you've only got the dial turned to five out of 100, then it's like, cool, why would we hunt?

moments.title: Passive referrals as a signal
moments.quote: If we are getting referrals passively, just by being good at delivering, oftentimes that is an indicator that there's a pretty massive opportunity if we were a little more proactive.

moments.title: Calling in the previous commitment
moments.quote: Now, in the future, I'm not asking for a favor. I'm calling in the previous commitment.
moments.why: The whole mechanic of setting a referral expectation at close so the later ask is not an imposition.

moments.title: Experience dial versus job ad
moments.quote: The more specific of a fit that you want, both from education and experience, the less likely it is for us to succeed to post a job ad. You can care a lot about competencies, which we should, and less about experience, and have a lot of success posting a job ad.

moments.quote: Normally what they're doing is between 25 and 70 percent of what I would teach somebody who doesn't know how to do it. They've self-discovered how to do a thing that we've studied how to do well, and we just have to help them name that and then template that.
moments.why: Positions training as extraction and codification rather than replacement, which is what founders can hear.

moments.title: Mine the departing partner's calls with AI
moments.quote: Hey, ChatGPT, how is he uncovering pain? How does he talk about budget? What are some consistencies that happen? What does he do well?
moments.why: Practical answer to capturing a leaving founder's sales process from existing call recordings.

moments.title: Do you have a passion for selling?
moments.quote: Do you have a passion for selling? Do you want to be on sales calls? Do you see sales calls on your calendar and go, man, I'm excited for this conversation?
moments.why: The question that reframes whether Evan needs a hire at all, and Rob refuses to accept his stereotype-based answer.

moments.title: Get the stereotype out of your head
moments.quote: Get the stereotype of what a good salesperson is out of your head. And since you guys have succeeded, you went from zero to 4 million, and you say, I like to have sales conversations. That is evidence that you might not need this person.

moments.title: No long-term agreement, long-term clients

moments.why: How to answer 'how long do I budget you for' without asking for a commitment.

If you happen to want to do this on Friday, I've got a chunk of time on Friday afternoon that just happens to be open.

moments.title: Is that sustainable?
moments.quote: So is that what you want long term? Is that sustainable?
moments.why: Six words that open the real subject of the call, asked right after she describes the handoff to Brett.

moments.title: I hate it when my clients split the sales role
moments.quote: The thing that you haven't said out loud yet that you might want to think about is that I hate it when my clients split the sales role, because sales is just more challenging. There's all this rejection, all this social rejection.
moments.why: Rob names the structural problem the prospect was circling and takes the blame off her.

moments.title: The subconscious picks the easier job
moments.quote: I can predict this person will neglect their sales role to go do other stuff, because on the subconscious level the subconscious goes, well, what can I do that's a little easier? And it's not their fault that they do that. It's just human nature.
moments.why: Explains the failure mode without making the prospect defensive about her own behavior.

moments.title: A walkable path
moments.quote: For now, if we could fix a couple of these issues, get the structure in place, get some good things happening, and then we could make a hire to get Meghan out of the role. That's a walkable path.
moments.why: Converts his criticism into a sequence the prospect can take to her CEO.

moments.title: Nobody's favorite part
moments.quote: People won't engage in good faith. People will be jerks. People will ghost you. You have to ask people that you don't get along with really challenging questions, and people will get pissed off at you. And no one ever says, this is my favorite part about sales. But that's a big part of the role.
moments.why: The commitment test, delivered as description rather than challenge. The best passage on the call.

moments.title: The prospect's real evidence
moments.quote: When I sent my first round of outreach emails and got one cold contact to respond, it felt like the most exciting thing in the world.
moments.why: Her answer to the commitment test, and the reason Rob moves to an assessment rather than a disqualification.

moments.title: Introducing the assessment
moments.quote: There is a sales assessment that you could do that will give us pertinent information about your ability to hunt, your ability to ask questions, and your ability to sell value.
moments.why: He frames it as clarity for her, not qualification for him.

moments.title: What the assessment actually measures
moments.quote: More important information about the level of desire that you have to succeed in sales, the level of commitment, the level of motivation, and then some of the hidden mindset weaknesses. Do you have a fear of rejection? Do you have a need for approval? Do you get emotionally involved in sales calls?
moments.why: The clearest short explanation of the OMG assessment in this batch.

moments.title: Far from your ceiling
moments.quote: If you're really far from your ceiling, any success that you've had is despite the fact that we have all this room to grow.
moments.why: Pre-frames a bad result as good news, which is how you get an honest assessment taken.

moments.title: Referrals you create versus referrals that arrive
moments.quote: You get referrals because you create them through a quality experience. But do you proactively create referrals that don't come to you?
moments.why: A distinction most agencies have never drawn, and she answers in two words: they just come to us.

moments.title: A quarter of what's available
moments.quote: Typically the pool of people that will proactively refer you maybe represents only about a quarter of the referrals that you could be receiving. If you're already getting referrals, chances are there's way more people out there that would give you referrals if you just shook their tree a little bit.
moments.why: Reframes cold prospecting as the harder, later option and gives her a counter to Brett's resistance.

moments.title: We'll talk them into it
moments.quote: Well, we'll talk them into it. So here's what you'd be saying yes to.
moments.why: Handles a CEO's objection by assuming it away and moving straight to the close in the same breath.

coaching_notes: A textbook first conversation ending in an assessment: pain named, impact quantified, commitment tested, next step scheduled on the call with a clear agenda for it.
Budget and decision process never came up. Brett controls the money and resists the referral strategy, and Rob neither asked who signs nor what they would spend.
Four minutes of unstructured New York and hockey small talk sit between the close and the scheduling; the deal survives it, but it is a long detour after a yes.
Steal the pairing at 23:41 and 24:21: explain what the assessment reads, then pre-frame a weak score as upside before the prospect can get defensive.
company_note: SEO and PPC agency

other_speakers.label: Speaker 2
other_speakers.who: Sam Collins, MRI Network's international leader; runs offices outside the US and the weekly coffee break calls

headline: Referral call that books a stage, not a deal
summary: This is a referral out of Shad's MRI webinar and his follow-up with Sandra Hill, not a cold first conversation, and Sam opens by saying Shad has wowed Sandra. Sam then spends nearly six minutes touring MRI's offices from Kuala Lumpur to Lagos to Costa Rica before Shad cuts in to say currency devaluation in Nigeria is outside his expertise. Shad narrows to the selling impact of all that instability, Sam names the real issue as his recruiters' fear of controlling the process, and the call lands on Shad speaking to the international coffee break call on September 5. Sam also volunteers to introduce him to APSCo as a preferred vendor.
outcome_note: Booked to speak at the MRI international coffee break call on September 5 at 2:00 pm UK, with Shad sending a bio and Sam sending the link and an APSCo introduction.

arc.label: Zoom trouble and warm-up
Sandra Hill's referral opens the call
Sam tours the international network, office by office
Shad interrupts: that's out of my area of expertise
What all that instability does to selling
How can I help, and the coffee break call invitation
Shad shapes the content toward mindset and scarcity
The old MRI-Sandler relationship surfaces
