milestones.text: From a selling standpoint, what's been the impact?
Sam quantifies the slowdown: a process that used to take two months now takes three or more, and one office waited two months just for candidate feedback.
Sam names the root cause himself: his recruiters have a fear of controlling the process, because clients and jobs are both hard to find and they are frightened to use a takeaway.

Let's talk about some of the challenges we're facing. Why are we facing these? The psychology, some of those hidden weaknesses, and then some pieces from a process. But let's get more into the psychology of how do we keep a strong mindset in these challenging times.
Sam proposes September 5 at 2:00 pm UK for the coffee break call; Shad agrees and says he will move his one conflict.

moments.title: Interrupting the tour
moments.quote: That's out of my area of expertise, Sam.
moments.why: After six minutes of monologue, Shad declines to pretend he can help with currency devaluation in Nigeria. Honest, and it resets the call.

moments.title: The one question that narrows everything
moments.quote: All these things, the political changes, recession, the manufacturing industry challenges. From a selling standpoint, what's been the impact?
moments.why: Takes a world tour of macro conditions and converts it into one answerable sales question.

moments.title: Two months for candidate feedback
moments.quote: We had one office the other day who said he's waited two months for feedback on a candidate. Apart from the fact I wanted to leap into the screen and shake him by the shoulder.
moments.why: The prospect delivers his own impact number, with the emotion attached.

moments.title: Fear of controlling the process
moments.quote: The problem is they have fear of controlling the process. They're frightened that if they do that, they'll lose the client.
moments.why: Sam diagnoses his own people more precisely than most coaches would in a first call.

moments.title: If they don't come back, they don't respect you
moments.quote: As you rightly said at one point in your recording, if the client hasn't come back to you, they haven't got any respect for you.
moments.why: The prospect quoting the coach's own webinar back at him. Evidence of how content-led prospecting pays off.

moments.title: How can I help here?
moments.quote: Got it. Okay, well, how can I help here?
moments.why: Five words that stop the exposition and make Sam state the ask. Everything concrete follows this.

moments.title: The brief, in the prospect's words
moments.quote: I'd love to have you come in and tell them it's okay to say no and walk away if the client's not playing ball with you. I'd love them to hear that there has to be mutual respect on both sides.
moments.why: Sam hands Shad the content outline and the emotional need behind it, unprompted.

moments.title: Adding the layer Sam didn't ask for
moments.quote: Going a little deeper into the psychology of being on that same level and being okay if you say no. A lot of times people have that fear because they don't like rejecting others, but also it's a scarcity mindset.
moments.why: Shad expands the brief into his own strongest material instead of just taking the order.

moments.title: Qualifying the audience
moments.quote: How big is the group usually?
moments.why: He asks about reach before committing, and learns one recording gets replayed to 27 recruiters across two countries.

moments.title: The unprompted referral
moments.quote: So maybe we can, if you like, repay a little bit by introducing you to APSCo. They have approved vendors which could be appropriate for you.
moments.why: What a generous webinar buys you: an introduction to an international trade body with a training budget.

moments.title: Declining both dates offered
moments.quote: So here's the challenge. You pick two days when I'm traveling. Can we look in October, if possible?
moments.why: He does not contort his calendar to be accommodating, and Sam immediately finds an earlier date instead.

moments.title: The prospect takes the work
moments.quote: I will put you in for that date and I will start knocking heads to get them signed up for you.
moments.why: Confirmation that the host now owns promotion, attendance and the recording distribution.

coaching_notes: The opening six minutes are the prospect's, not the coach's. Shad sets no up-front contract and lets Sam monologue; the recovery move, 'how can I help here?', is the one to steal.
No commercial qualification of any kind: no budget, no decision path, no discussion of what paid work with MRI internationally would look like. The call optimizes for reach, not revenue.
Note the compounding referral chain across this batch: one webinar produced Sandra, Sandra produced Sam, Sam offers APSCo. Worth studying as a prospecting pattern rather than as a single call.
Fireflies renders 'Shad' as 'Chad' and 'shadow', and 'Sandra' as 'Alessandra' at 1:14.

headline: Candidate interview filed as a prospect call
summary: This is not a sales call. Rob is screening Austin Reese as a sales-hire candidate on behalf of his client Wagon Wheel, whose owner Angie he met through EO Nashville. Rob runs a tight competency interview: why Austin would leave Hilti, what he likes about selling, his numbers (163 percent of forecast in his best year), a deal he lost and why, and how he moves a stranger to a qualified prospect. Austin's answer on the lost Bateman deal, that he backed the wrong influencer and took him at face value, is the strongest moment. The call then runs seven minutes of personal small talk before Rob commits to debriefing Angie.
outcome_note: Rob said he would debrief Angie before the weekend and that she or Catherine would come back to Austin directly.

milestones.text: This tends to be a pretty straightforward conversation. I do jump around just a little bit, not to be tricky or gamey, I just follow my curiosities. We have 30 minutes. I'll try to leave a couple minutes at the end for any questions you might have for me, although most of your questions are probably better for Angie.
Rob explains the internal path: he will debrief Angie before the weekend, then Angie or Catherine will come back to Austin directly.
But I'll let them know that we spoke. I'll give them the debrief, and then they'll get back to you, if that works.

moments.title: Setting expectations, including what he cannot answer
moments.quote: I'll ask you if you have any questions, then I won't be able to answer any of them is probably what's going to happen.
moments.why: Disarms the candidate and pre-handles his own limits in one joke. Works equally well in a sales context.

moments.title: Why would you do something so different?
moments.quote: Why would you be doing something so different from that? Why would you be interested in that?
moments.why: Opens with the motive question rather than the resume, which is where the real answer lives.

moments.title: Why not just stay?
moments.quote: Why wouldn't you just play it out at Hilti? There's opportunities for advancement and all that stuff there.
moments.why: A negative-reverse applied to a candidate. Austin has to argue for leaving instead of being sold on the job.

moments.title: What do you like most about selling?
moments.quote: What do you like most about selling?
moments.why: The baseline competency question; everything after this is Austin revealing his orientation unprompted.

moments.title: What else?
moments.quote: Okay. All right, what else?
moments.why: Three words that produce the second and third answers, which are always more honest than the first.

moments.title: Quantify it
moments.quote: Can you quantify the growth that you've brought to it, either by revenue or number of people or orders or something like that?
moments.why: Refuses to let 'I grew the territory' stand without a number. Austin produces three.

moments.title: What do you attribute that to?
moments.quote: What do you attribute that to? 163 is a pretty good number.
moments.why: Tests whether the result was luck, timing or repeatable behavior, and Austin separates the two himself.

moments.title: You don't miss by miles, you miss by inches
moments.quote: You probably got the experience where you don't miss by miles, you miss by inches, right? And when you miss by inches, what normally happens?
moments.why: The best-framed question on the call. It makes a loss safe to describe and gets a specific, named deal.

moments.title: Pushing past the comfortable explanation
moments.quote: Do you think you missed anything? You might not know what you don't know, but do you think there's some other universe where they could have done it now?
moments.why: Austin's first answer was 'they don't spend money mid-year'. This question gets the real one.

moments.title: The candidate diagnoses himself
moments.quote: What I really missed was I thought the son, Taylor, had more decision making power than he does. I chose the wrong influencer in that account and latched on and took them at face value for what they were saying they could decide on.
moments.why: A coachable self-assessment with no prompting. This is the answer an interviewer is hunting for.

moments.title: Stranger to qualified prospect
moments.quote: How do you go from a stranger, in a cold call situation, what do you have to accomplish to go from nothing to interested prospect, qualified prospect?
moments.why: Tests whether the candidate has a process or just instincts. Austin answers 'ask questions' and then proves it.

moments.title: Is there anything I should have asked?
moments.quote: Do you have any questions for me, or is there any questions I should have asked you that I haven't asked you yet?
moments.why: The catch-all close that gives the candidate one last door. Useful verbatim in sales calls too.

coaching_notes: Mislabeled file. The filename says 'FirstTimeConversations_Prospect', but this is a candidate screening interview Rob is running for his client Wagon Wheel. The milestone taxonomy mostly does not apply, which is why only three milestones are tagged.
The interview questions themselves are worth studying as sales questions: 'what else', 'you miss by inches', 'what do you attribute that to', 'quantify it'. All transfer directly.
Roughly seven minutes (19:00 to 26:00) are personal small talk about woodworking, flooring, cabinets and sports. It builds rapport but it is a third of the call.

Confidentiality flag: at 24:02 Rob discusses an active prospect by name (Evan at OYVL, the 2024_08_09 call), including that he is mid-partnership-split, and only then learns Austin is Evan's brother. Worth discussing as a cautionary moment, not as a technique.
Rob's up-front contract here is the cleanest in the batch: time, how he will behave, what he will not be able to answer, and who to take questions to instead.

moments.title: Opening with their outcome, not his
moments.quote: What are you both hoping that we figure out in today's conversation here?
moments.why: He asks both people separately and gets two different agendas: fit and money from Carlos, how it works from Alejandra.

moments.title: Besides money, what makes it a good fit?
moments.quote: You said, is it a good fit? Besides budget, financial, what else in your head makes it a good fit?
moments.why: Strips money out of the fit question so the real criteria surface early. Carlos names track record and chemistry with Jennifer.

moments.title: What's different for you personally?
moments.quote: And if you get there, personally for you, what's different when you get there to 5 million with this company?
moments.why: Moves from the company's number to the owner's reason. The answer is about influencing the people around him.

moments.title: A mirror that misses
moments.quote: This is about your legacy and leaving that behind for those folks.
moments.why: Carlos pushes back: 'I wouldn't necessarily call it a legacy thing.' A useful example of labeling too fast.

moments.title: No pain, by their own admission
moments.quote: And right now, without that being there, how's that impacting selling for the company?
moments.why: Carlos answers 'not really, we are on track to accomplish our goal.' The honest discovery of a want, not a need.

moments.title: Do you want help on this?
moments.quote: Well, I guess my question is from here. Do you want help on this? And if so, talk through what that looks like.
moments.why: Direct, unhedged, asked before any structure or price is presented. Carlos answers yes in one word.

moments.title: The prospect pushing the coach to go faster
moments.quote: How do we accelerate that timeline?
moments.why: Carlos objects to Jennifer waiting 60 days. Listen to who is creating urgency in this call.

moments.title: Holding the sequence
moments.quote: If we don't have the right pieces in place from a strategy and structure standpoint to support, and we don't help you get one step ahead from a management leadership standpoint, we're not going to have the right tools to help support her, and it's going to make it a lot harder for you to reinforce when she's not with me.
moments.why: Defends the methodology under pressure, then concedes the calendar without conceding the order of work.

moments.title: How would you know it's being applied?
moments.quote: How would you know whether or not she is, in fact, applying what she's being coached?
moments.why: Carlos's sharpest question. Shad's answer, awareness then behavior then recorded calls then results, is the best explanation of the model in this batch.

moments.title: Three other coaches
moments.quote: I'm not going to lie. We just have to line it up against the other three coaches that we're interviewing to see how it all stacks up.
moments.why: The bake-off lands immediately after the price. Shad's response, 'how are you going to line it up?', is the right next move.

moments.title: Asking for the damaging feedback
moments.quote: Based off initial, we've only had a couple of conversations here. Do you feel like I click with Jennifer, or is it way off at this point?
moments.why: He asks for the bad news directly and gets it: the level of conversation is pitched above where Jennifer is.

moments.title: The no-harm-no-foul contract
moments.quote: Here's my one ask. Can we have a time on the calendar where you tell me, here's where we're at. And if you guys went another direction, no harm no foul, and I ask questions. And if you didn't, then we figure out next steps. Does that sound fair?
moments.why: The single best close in this batch: a scheduled yes-or-no with permission to debrief a loss. Carlos: 'I wouldn't have it any other way.'

coaching_notes: The pain question at 17:20 got an honest 'not really', and Shad accepted it and moved on to presenting. Worth debating: should he have kept digging for a compelling reason before pricing a 2,500 a month engagement?
The up-front contract was asked of both people, which surfaced two different buying agendas. Replicate that on any multi-stakeholder first call.
Price was delivered flat, with no pause and no check on reaction, and the bake-off objection arrived 90 seconds later. The recovery, asking how they will compare, is better than the delivery.
The 42:08 close is the thing to steal: a dated decision meeting framed so that a no is welcome and debriefable.

Transcript issues: Carlos calls the coach 'Zach' at 0:57 and 'Chad' later (both are Shad); the transcript alternates 'Alejandro' and 'Alejandra' for Speaker 3; Alejandra drops off the call around 39:54 and rejoins; a garbled number string '721 81' appears at 45:21. The filename 'Real Fund PG Service Group' conflates Carlos's investment fund with the operating company.

headline: Marketing head wants cold-call muscle for merged energy division
summary: Amy runs marketing and sales across Keystone Cooperative's four divisions and came in via a referral from Rodney. Her agronomy sellers have plenty of development resources; her energy division — liquid fuels, propane, lubricants sold into construction firms, fleets, municipalities and schools — is six months into a merger and has become order-takers who do not knock on doors. He proposed a three-way working session with a pre-work survey and an explicit right to say no.

moments.title: A loose agenda in one breath
moments.quote: I figured we just hop on here, introduce ourselves, and then talk about whatever you'd like to discuss from us connecting from Rodney. Does that sound good?
moments.why: Low-ceremony up-front contract that still gets a yes before the prospect starts talking.

moments.title: Thanks her for the dump, then asks permission
moments.quote: Thank you first for, as you said, puking it out. I appreciate you being transparent. One of the things that you mentioned — I'm going to ask a few questions around this, if that's okay with you.
moments.why: He converts a five-minute monologue into a license to interrogate, instead of responding to it.

moments.title: Plays her own word back at her
moments.quote: So what you said, folks are more order takers. What do you think that is right now?
moments.why: Uses the prospect's loaded word verbatim rather than softening it, and gets the two-legacy-cultures answer.

moments.title: Will before skill
moments.quote: Do you believe they got the — are they motivated to go out there and be the hunters that you guys are looking for?
moments.why: Moves the conversation off training and onto motivation, which is where the real problem turned out to be.

moments.title: Says out loud why he asked about the manager
moments.quote: The reason why I asked — A, I want to hear what his take is, and B, is he open? Let's say the three of us meet, is he open to hearing alternative ways and getting help in some of these areas?
moments.why: Transparent questioning: naming the intent behind the question makes the openness check feel collaborative rather than like qualifying.

moments.title: Asks for the meeting before pitching
moments.quote: Well, do you think it makes sense for you, me and him to meet and talk further and just better understand here's where you're at, where you want to get to, and I would be able to better tell you here's what we could help and what that looks like?
moments.why: He tries to close for the next step at the 18-minute mark; Amy's counter-question is what pulls the overview out of him.

moments.title: Why assigning training first fails
moments.quote: A lot of times what an organization in my space might do is they go, okay, great, let's just assign some training to go after those things. Problem is, we don't know what's causing folks not to be able to do those things.
moments.why: The cleanest version of the diagnose-before-prescribe argument in this batch.

moments.title: The belief that kills the skill
moments.quote: If they believe in their head that picking up that phone and cold calling somebody out of the blue is rude — we've got to work past that, because you can give them all the tools and training and all the skills, but if in their mind they're going I can't even imagine doing that because that's so rude, they're never going to apply the skills and tools.
moments.why: A concrete, non-jargon way to explain why a self-limiting belief has to be dealt with before any skills work.

moments.title: Honest about the industry gap
moments.quote: Yes, I have a lot of experience through various clients. Have I worked a ton in the energy sector? No. But have I worked with clients with similar challenges, in similar fashion, and helped them work through those? Yes.
moments.why: Answers the vertical-experience objection by splitting it into two questions and conceding the one he loses.

moments.title: Reframes the 30-year-veteran question
moments.quote: And Amy, the piece I'm going to add there is — can you get them to? Depends on if you understand what would motivate them to.
moments.why: One sentence that turns her can-you-teach-an-old-dog worry into a motivation question, and she immediately concedes the point.

moments.title: No harm, no foul
moments.quote: And if you say, hey, appreciate it, just not a fit for us, don't think it's right — that's no harm, no foul.
moments.why: Gives the right to say no as part of describing the next meeting, which lowers the cost of agreeing to it.

moments.title: Buys permission to chase
moments.quote: Is there a time next week or whenever you'll talk to him? If I haven't heard from you, that you and I can talk and you just tell me — either nope, we're not, or yep, makes sense, let's schedule some time.
moments.why: Converts a soft I'll-get-back-to-you into a dated follow-up with an explicit no as an acceptable answer.

coaching_notes: Shad never asked for a number. Growth is the stated driver, the energy division is the profitable one, and no revenue target, gap, or cost of inaction ever enters the call — so there is no pain-impact to point back to in the next meeting.
The best sequence is 9:51 to 11:22: he repeats her own phrase, then goes straight at motivation rather than skill. That ordering is what sets up the diagnosis-first pitch later.

At 18:37 Amy deflects his close with 'what are your thoughts, how would you approach an organization with this?' and he gives a four-minute overview. It works, but a coach could watch this as a decision point — he could have answered in thirty seconds and gone back to closing.
He got a decision-maker (Mike Bradley) named, confirmed as open, and a dated callback with permission to chase. That is a strong finish for a call with no scheduled meeting on the books.
Transcription: 'Shad' renders as 'shad' and 'Chad'; the header date (Aug 24) disagrees with the filename date (Aug 21).

other_speakers.label: Speaker 1
other_speakers.who: DJ — fractional COO newly installed at Clayton's company; previously built and sold membership-management company WebLink for $118M. Rob greets him as 'DJ' at 5:15 but signs off with 'thanks, Steve' at 23:28

headline: Fractional COO re-engages Rob to support a new sales manager
summary: Rob had previously coached this sales team and ran into an obstructive sales leader, Jeff. DJ has since come in as fractional COO, Jeff is being moved to an advisory role, and Shelley is arriving as the new sales manager ahead of a Series A raise. DJ ran almost the entire call: he briefed Rob on Shelley, the $1-2k deal size, the 20% close rate on heavy inbound, the CRM mess and the new KPIs he is installing. Rob contributed his read from the prior engagement — facilitate decisions faster, stop reading demo enthusiasm as probability to close — asked three questions, and let DJ route the commercial decision back through Clayton.
outcome_note: DJ said he would take it back to Clayton to formalize and that they would touch base monthly, but nothing was scheduled and Rob never proposed a date.

milestones.text: The classic principle of selling consultatively, especially when we have a volume play, is to facilitate decisions faster. The ones we're not going to win, or not going to win right now — let's facilitate that decision on the first conversation, not the ninth follow-up. And the ones we are going to win, how can we facilitate that decision faster?
DJ names the gap: heavy inbound volume with only a 20% close rate, and a win rate he believes should be far higher.
DJ places himself as the champion and Clayton as the decision maker: he will take it back and let Clayton formalize the engagement with Rob.
DJ raises his one concern about fit — he knows Sandler from six-figure enterprise deals and wants to be sure the approach suits a one-touch, $1-2k, close-and-move-on product.

moments.title: Names the problem without piling on
moments.quote: I was doing what I can to work with the team, with Jeff being an obstructive force and all that.
moments.why: States the real obstacle plainly, then immediately protects Jeff's character when DJ invites him to go further — 'he's not a bad guy, he just didn't get it.'

moments.title: Facilitate decisions faster
moments.quote: The classic principle of selling consultatively, especially when we have a volume play, is to facilitate decisions faster. The ones we're not going to win, let's facilitate that decision on the first conversation, not the ninth follow-up.
moments.why: The single most portable idea in this call, and the thing that made DJ say 'yeah, that's where I was at.'

moments.title: Selling to an indecisive board
moments.quote: It's almost like a B2C, and this isn't the main thing that they pursue every day. And then they have a board and they're kind of indecisive and they don't know how they should do it. There was always this opportunity to help the board figure out how they can make the decision, or help the person who's in front of us figure out how to aggregate the board.
moments.why: Reframes a committee as something you help the buyer navigate rather than something you wait on.

moments.title: Buying back time even when you lose
moments.quote: I always felt that there was a lot of opportunity to facilitate decisions faster, even if we weren't changing outcomes. There was an opportunity to buy back a lot of time in our day to do other valuable things if we could get the decisions faster.
moments.why: Makes the business case for killing deals early without claiming it raises the win rate — a more credible argument.

moments.title: Checks his read against the buyer's
moments.quote: I don't know if that aligns with your observation of what's going on with the sales.
moments.why: After a long diagnostic monologue he hands the verdict back to DJ instead of assuming agreement.

moments.title: Demo enthusiasm is not probability to close
moments.quote: Jeff would always misread — everybody loves the demo. Nobody looks at the demo and goes, no, this isn't what we were thinking, or this stinks. And he would always misread demo enthusiasm as probability to close. I couldn't get him to close the gap — that's great that they're enthusiastic, well, now be skeptical.
moments.why: A specific, recognizable forecasting failure described in the buyer's own world; worth stealing verbatim.

moments.title: Pushes twice on a dodged question
moments.quote: But you haven't experienced him enough to have your own opinion on if he'll work or not?
moments.why: DJ answered 'I think Michael is doing the appointment scheduling' — Rob rephrases rather than accepting a non-answer, then plants a flag: 'I'll be curious what you think.'

moments.title: Declines the invitation to blame the client
moments.quote: Clayton and I have always talked quite openly about everything that was going on. I don't disagree with any of his decisions through all that. I think he made all the right decisions, and I think you have to have some patience.
moments.why: DJ has just apologized for souring him on the prior engagement; Rob refuses to collect the grievance and gives the absent decision maker cover instead.

moments.title: Reopens the call after the buyer wrapped it
moments.quote: Hey, I'm sorry, one more question. Where did they land, or where did you land, with CRM?
moments.why: DJ had moved into sign-off; Rob adds eight minutes of useful discovery with one polite interruption.

moments.title: The CRM answer nobody expects
moments.quote: I always default to HubSpot, but to me it has more to do with — it's the same thing as what exercise system are you going to use. It's the thing that you will use, the thing that you will do repeatedly. The thing that sticks in an organization is the right choice. So whatever software sticks, where we can achieve the highest compliance.
moments.why: Refuses the tool-recommendation trap and converts it into a compliance question, which is the thing that actually determines whether the KPIs exist.

coaching_notes: This is not a first conversation. It is a re-engagement call with a new power sponsor on an account Rob previously worked, and it is filed in the FTC folder — treat it as a how-to-handle-a-regime-change call, not a first meeting.

Rob ran no up-front contract and asked roughly four questions in nineteen minutes. The buyer controlled the agenda from 5:32 to the end. It worked because DJ arrived pre-sold, but there is nothing here to study on structuring a call.

No next step was set. 'I'll let Clayton formalize it' and 'us touching base every month or so' is where it ends — no date, no scope conversation, no money. A coach should notice how easily a warm call ends without a calendar entry.

Best coachable material is the diagnostic language at 9:36 to 10:18 and the demo-enthusiasm observation at 12:42 — both are specific enough to reuse with any inbound, low-ticket, committee-buying client.

Transcript issues: speech begins at 5:14 after dead air; the prospect is addressed as 'DJ' at the open and 'Steve' at the close; at 18:30 a sentence beginning 'But anyway' is attributed to Speaker 2 but clearly belongs to Speaker 1 — speaker segmentation slips there.
company_note: Clayton's HOA / volunteer-organization software company (DJ is the incoming fractional COO; '1 to 100 Advisors' in the filename appears to be DJ's own advisory practice)

other_speakers.label: Speaker 1

headline: Logistics call on an already-sold association training program
summary: This is a delivery-planning call on a sold engagement, not a first conversation. Doug walks Shad through the two-part program OMA is rolling out: two breakout sessions at the annual meeting in the Phoenix area open to all salespeople, managers and owners, followed by monthly virtual sessions OMA will charge a small fee for, plus a tailored cohort of eight partners chosen because they each do between half a million and a million dollars of business with other OMA partners. Most of the call is schedule negotiation around Shad's flights, solved when Doug offers the Monday morning before the meeting starts. It ends with Doug telling Shad to invoice for the annual meeting work and Shad promising a written agreement for the select group.
outcome_note: Doug approved the pricing as sent and told Shad to invoice for the annual meeting; Shad committed to formalizing the select-group piece in writing for signature.

milestones.text: What do you want to make sure we cover here?

Doug describes the internal path for the cohort: only eight slots, four already spoken for by growth-committee members and board members, and every candidate still goes through a formal interview process.

Doug explains the selection logic for the eight partners — each does at least half a million up to a million dollars of business with other OMA partners, on the theory that if you can do half a million you can do a million.
And you guys are good with pricing everything I sent over?

We'll go ahead and do that, and then I'll just send over that for the select group. I'll just formalize it, send it over to you guys so we can get signed off, so we got it in writing and everybody's on the same page.

moments.title: One question, then he listens
moments.quote: What's been keeping you busy?
moments.why: Opens the knee-surgery conversation that occupies the first ninety seconds; Shad stays with it and relates it to his own family rather than steering to business.

moments.title: Hands the client the agenda
moments.quote: What do you want to make sure we cover here?
moments.why: On a delivery call the client usually has the list; asking for it gets the whole program laid out unprompted.

moments.title: The association builds the commitment in
moments.quote: So if you sign up for it, you signed up for it. All the way. That's your problem. You know, you paid for it.
moments.why: Doug designing attrition out of the program himself — useful language for any coach trying to get a client to enforce attendance.

moments.title: How the cohort was selected
moments.quote: How we chose those eight is we looked at partners that are doing at least half a million dollars of business with other OMA partners, up to a million. Our theory is if you can do half a million, you can do a million — you're doing something right, you just need to focus on it.
moments.why: A clean qualification rule for picking a pilot cohort inside a member organization.

moments.title: Pairing participants with mentors
moments.quote: What we would want to do is maybe grab 30 minutes of your time and just have a brief meeting with you and those eight individuals and the eight mentors.
moments.why: The mentor pairing is the detail that makes this cohort different from a breakout session; worth noting for anyone designing a program with an association.

moments.title: Removes his own constraint from the table
moments.quote: It should be. I mean, I don't care if I've got to do a red eye or something that night.
moments.why: Shad takes his travel problem off the client's plate, which is what prompts Doug to volunteer a better slot thirty seconds later.

moments.title: The client solves the scheduling problem
moments.quote: Our annual meeting doesn't start until noon on Monday. We could possibly take that Monday morning for three or four hours, meet with that group, and then meet with them again Wednesday for a few hours and then get out even earlier.
moments.why: Doug invents two touchpoints instead of one and gets Shad home earlier — the payoff for not pushing a solution of his own.

moments.title: Sweeps for objections before closing
moments.quote: What other things? Questions in regards to, like, the plan and what I sent over.
moments.why: Clears the plan before going anywhere near money, and gets a clean 'we're good with that.'

moments.title: Asks about money plainly, and late
moments.quote: And you guys are good with pricing everything I sent over?
moments.why: No hedging and no justification — one flat question that produces 'go ahead and invoice me.'

moments.title: Puts it in writing anyway
moments.quote: I'll just formalize it, send it over to you guys so we can get signed off, so we got it in writing and everybody's on the same page.
moments.why: Verbal yes from a friendly buyer still gets papered; the reason he gives is alignment, not protection.

coaching_notes: Mislabeled. The filename calls this a FirstTimeConversation, but it is an implementation and scheduling call on a sold engagement — pricing was already sent and the only commercial moment is Doug approving the invoice. File it as a delivery-planning example.

Nothing in the milestone taxonomy around pain appears, and it should not: there is no problem to surface because the problem was solved on an earlier call. Useful as a counterexample for coaches who expect every recording to show discovery.

The money question lands in the last ninety seconds and takes one sentence. Watch how little setup it needs with an existing client — and note that Shad still converts the verbal yes into a signed document.
Shad lets Doug run almost eight straight minutes on program design, interjecting only 'okay.' A coach can watch the restraint, but there is no qualifying or scoping work being done here.
Recording artifact: after the goodbye at 11:41 the transcript captures a stray profanity at 11:44, apparently a hot mic. Worth trimming before this is put in front of clients.

other_speakers.who: Keating — founder and owner of an HVAC company (Gold Eagle per the filename; the company is never named in the transcript), referred by Olga

headline: HVAC founder rates himself a one as a sales leader
summary: Keating started an HVAC company two years out of high school and now runs about $3M with three technicians, two install crews, an outside and an inside salesperson. Olga, a family friend, watched his team in her own home and told him his technicians are strong technically and weak in front of customers — which is why he took the call. Rob moved him off the people problem and onto numbers (memberships converting at 18% against a 50% target, reviews at 7%, average ticket below industry), then onto his own sales leadership, where Keating rated himself a one out of ten on coaching, accountability and motivation. Rob reframed the engagement from sales training to structure and leadership development, laid out the strategy-structure-staff-skills pyramid, and booked a follow-up with a pre-work survey.
outcome_note: Booked Wednesday at 10:00 Central for sixty minutes, with a six-minute survey sent the same day; Rob said they would pick up exactly where they left off.

milestones.text: We work with Olga, and she sent over that introduction email. So I didn't know if it would make sense if you just wanted to tell me what's going on and what made it make sense to you to talk to someone like me, and we can go from there. Is that okay?

Do you look at your top line and go, I'm at X and I should be at Y, or do you look at the KPIs as individual revenue streams? What I'm trying to understand is how far away you are from where you want to be, and then how big of a deal it is — how much money it actually is.
So you hit your number this year. Will you hit it next year if none of this changes? Are you saying we're talking now because that number next year is out of reach if I can't fill some of these gaps?

moments.title: Names the referrer and hands over the floor
moments.quote: We work with Olga, and she sent over that introduction email. So I didn't know if it would make sense if you just wanted to tell me what's going on and what made it make sense to you to talk to someone like me. Is that okay?
moments.why: Short, credits the referral source, and asks the two questions that matter — what's happening and why now.

moments.title: Turns a soft-skills complaint into outcomes
moments.quote: How does that impact, from an outcome standpoint? Do they miss opportunities they should win? Do you expect them to get some upsell things that they're not currently getting?
moments.why: Keating opened with 'intangibles' and 'how they're perceived.' This question forces the conversation onto things that can be counted.

moments.title: The gap in one question
moments.quote: And what did you hope or expect that to be?
moments.why: Five words that turn '18% on memberships' into a 32-point shortfall the owner himself declares.

moments.title: Refuses to accept a label
moments.quote: What is that? You walk me through that a little more — communication.
moments.why: 'Communication' is a non-answer until he makes Keating narrate the option-one-two-three conversation and the callback forty-five days later.

moments.title: Quotes him back, with an escape hatch
moments.quote: What did you say earlier? You said you have some work to do on your leadership skills. From a sales leadership standpoint, what do you think you could be better at or isn't happening that should — and I can make some suggestions if you don't know how to answer the question.
moments.why: The offer to supply suggestions makes it safe to admit he can't answer, which is exactly what happens.

moments.title: Three competencies, then a self-rating
moments.quote: The three things that I really need from my clients is that they can coach, they can hold people accountable, and they know how to motivate. So if you evaluated yourself against those three competencies, what would you come up with?
moments.why: Gives the owner a scoring rubric he didn't have, then asks him to use it on himself — a repeatable move in any owner conversation.

moments.title: The answer that makes the sale
moments.quote: Probably a one on all three.
moments.why: Twelve minutes in, the owner has disqualified himself as his own sales manager. Rob's only response is to add humility to the list, which keeps it from stinging.

moments.title: Puts a dollar sign on it
moments.quote: What I'm trying to understand is how far away you are from where you want to be, and then how big of a deal it is — how much money it actually is.
moments.why: Explains why he's asking before he asks, and gets $3M this year, $4M target, 10% profit in reply.

moments.title: Tests whether the pain is real
moments.quote: So you hit your number this year. Will you hit it next year if none of this changes? Are you saying we're talking now because that number next year is out of reach?
moments.why: Keating says no, he could hit the number — and then volunteers the true driver: 'I can't go through the same headaches I went through this year without catastrophe, whether that be mental health or the health of the company.' The best answer in the call came from a question designed to let him say no.

moments.title: Reframes from training the reps to building the owner
moments.quote: Instead of thinking about sales training for your salespeople — as the owner, let's talk about structure and leadership development. Your ability to have a major impact on their ability to move their own individual needles tends to be the most important needle to move.
moments.why: Converts a 'train my techs' request into a leadership engagement without dismissing the original ask.

moments.title: Gives his own words back as the framework
moments.quote: What did you say earlier? 'I struggle to differentiate — is it give a shit, or is it sales tactics and competencies?' That's an important question. There's will and there's skill, and you can develop skill all day long, but if the will's absent you tend to be spinning wheels.
moments.why: Takes the prospect's throwaway line from minute seven and makes it the organizing principle of the engagement.

moments.title: Sells the survey by what it saves
moments.quote: If I can get you to spend like six minutes on a Google form, I could avoid asking you 60 additional questions about what's going on in the business.
moments.why: Frames pre-work as a favor to the prospect rather than a hoop, and gets 'love it.'

coaching_notes: The hour's best sequence is 14:45 to 16:43: quote him back, give him a three-part rubric, let him rate himself, then soften the one-out-of-ten with humility. He sells the leadership engagement to himself.

The commitment test at 19:46 is worth studying because it fails on its face and succeeds in substance — Keating says he probably will hit the number, then names mental health and company culture as the real cost. Asking a question that permits a no produced the strongest motive in the call.

No money was discussed for the engagement itself, and Rob never asked who else is involved in the decision — defensible with a sole founder, but there is no confirmation that he can sign without a partner or spouse.

The next meeting is scheduled but has no stated purpose or decision attached to it: 'we'll pick up exactly where we left off.' Compare with the same coach's up-front contract for the next meeting on the Evan/Ovyl call, which names the agenda and includes scope and terms.
The prospect's company is never named in the recording — 'Gold Eagle' comes only from the filename. Confirm before publishing.
company_note: residential/commercial HVAC

other_speakers.label: Speaker 2
other_speakers.who: Ann — chair of a newly formed virtual peer-advisory circle at Quaid; former CEO of United Way of Central Indiana, former CEO of Indianapolis Power & Light, former head of AES's Northern and Central European division

headline: New circle chair vets Shad before booking a session
summary: Mark, who runs Quaid, introduced Shad to Ann and Jim as a possible outside resource for their peer circles. Ann's circle is one meeting old, fully virtual, with members scattered from Vegas to San Francisco who don't yet know each other — and her first outside speaker ran a DISC exercise that produced almost no conversation. She spent the first half of the call screening Shad on competitors, how he knows Mark, whether the content is sales-only or overlaps EOS, and whether it fits very small companies. Shad answered each, walked her through the four S's, and left with a date penciled in.
outcome_note: January 29 from 2:30 to 3:30 Eastern is penciled in and held, with a check-in after her October 15 meeting to confirm.

milestones.text: Ann names what went wrong with her first outside resource — a DISC exercise where the members did what was asked but barely talked — and says her goal is always take-home value and a two-way conversation rather than a presentation.
Ann screens him directly: who do you see as your biggest competitors?
Her second test: he said he works with companies of various sizes including very large ones, and Quaid members are mostly very small.
Ann sets the path herself — one more meeting with the new member on board to see what the group needs, then she will come back to Shad about putting a session on the calendar.
I'm going to pencil it out and put a hold in. Let's talk after October 15 — I'll reach out and we'll confirm everything from there. Does that sound good?

moments.title: One question opens a thirty-year career
moments.quote: What was work prior to helping market Quaid?
moments.why: An ordinary question that produces United Way, Indianapolis Power & Light and AES Europe in ninety seconds — context he would never have gotten from a bio.

moments.title: The payoff
moments.quote: I don't think I've ever actually told that story backwards before.
moments.why: Ann, a former utility CEO, noticing she just did something new. The reason to let a prospect talk about themselves before you talk about yourself.

moments.title: Disarming answer on competition
moments.quote: Literally, other Sandler franchises.
moments.why: No posturing, no slide of competitors. He then volunteers that the famous names rarely come up because there's so much business out there.

moments.title: Tells the referral story straight
moments.quote: One of my clients knew him and said you guys should get to know each other — probably could help each other out, think in kind of similar ways.
moments.why: Answers 'how do you know Mark' with the actual history, including the earlier sessions he's already run for Quaid circles.

moments.title: There is no deck, on purpose
moments.quote: Here's the reason why I raised my eyebrows — I think we did the majority of it off a whiteboard, and that's why there wouldn't be PowerPoint. Much more of an interactive workshop versus for an hour just listening.
moments.why: Turns a missing deliverable into the differentiator, aimed directly at the one-way-conversation problem she just described.

moments.title: He opens workshops with discovery
moments.quote: What was around was really first understanding from them and spending the first fifteen, twenty minutes on — what are the biggest challenges you're running into when it comes to scaling and growing your business?
moments.why: Tells the chair that the session itself starts with the members talking, which is the specific thing she wants.

moments.title: The four S's, named
moments.quote: That's what the four S's are. It's strategy, structure, staff and skills. And this is for a strong sales infrastructure.
moments.why: The same framework Rob Lime calls the pyramid in other calls in this batch; worth comparing how each coach delivers it.

moments.title: Forecasting by feel versus by milestone
moments.quote: It's not a hey, people look at stages of CRM and go, well, I feel it's 80%, I got a good feeling — versus no, it corresponds to the sales process. In this stage it's because these things have been done, and we can go back and validate that.
moments.why: Concrete contrast that makes an abstract process point land.

moments.title: Well, you felt good two months ago
moments.quote: Not just a gut feel and I feel good — and then, well, you felt good two months ago and it's still not closed. Why not? Because we're off of feeling versus actual milestones being achieved.
moments.why: The sharpest line in the call and the only moment Ann interrupts with a question of her own.

moments.title: Positions alongside EOS instead of against it
moments.quote: A lot of times we work hand in hand with EOS — I'd say 30% of my clients have EOS. If they're having L10s, we're talking about what do those look like from a sales side. They're setting rocks — how do we set good, effective sales goals that fit into the rocks of the company?
moments.why: Answers a competitive-overlap question by naming the client's own vocabulary and making the two systems complementary.

moments.title: Asks for the calendar before letting go
moments.quote: Just so I can keep time in my head — if I haven't heard from you, when's your next meeting and when would be good to touch base?
moments.why: Converts 'why don't I touch base with you' into her reading out four specific meeting dates, which is how a date ends up penciled in.

moments.title: Holds the date
moments.quote: I'm going to pencil it out and put a hold in. Let's talk after October 15, I'll reach out, and we'll confirm everything from there.
moments.why: Takes the follow-up obligation on himself and still puts a specific slot on both calendars.

coaching_notes: The buyer ran the qualification here, not the coach — competitors, how he knows Mark, sales-only versus EOS, company size. Shad answered all four well, but a coach should notice he never asked the reciprocal question: what would make this session a success for your members, or what do you need them to walk away able to do?
No up-front contract. The call opens into small talk and never gets a frame, which is part of why roughly six of nineteen minutes go to an uninterrupted walkthrough of the four S's.
Best steal is the 1:16 career question. Asking what came before, rather than what do you do, got a former utility CEO talking for ninety seconds and warmed the whole call.
He recovered the close well: 'when's your next meeting and when would be good to touch base' turned a vague I'll-call-you into a held January 29 slot and a defined check-in after October 15.

headline: Founder wants to hire a closer; coach sells infrastructure first
summary: Matt called about one thing: he needs a B2B salesperson and doesn't know where to look. His new staffing business serves two customers — veterans and spouses on the B2C side, which is working, and employers on the B2B side, where he gets first meetings and never gets the contract. Shad refused to answer the hiring question and instead asked whether the bird cage was ready for the bird: could he show a new rep a documented sales process that he knows works. Matt said no. Shad walked him through what's missing, absorbed the real objection — Matt doesn't have the time to build it — and countered by asking how he would ever know whether a hire was doing the right things. Matt conceded, and a working session was booked.
outcome_note: Booked Tuesday the 10th at 8:00 a.m. for 45 minutes with a ten-minute four-S survey sent ahead, and an explicit out at the end of that meeting if Matt wants to run with it himself.

milestones.text: What can I help you on this morning?
Right now I want to hear a little bit about what you're seeing from selling on your side. What are they saying if their deals aren't closing for you?

So meaning if I was to walk in as a new salesperson, Matt, and say, hey, what does your sales process look like — would you be able to show me that and go, here's documented, here's how we know it works and why it's effective?

Matt frames his own decision as a build-versus-buy of time: he isn't a sales professional, so creating a process and cadence himself feels like far more time and effort than hiring somebody who already knows how.
But how are you going to know, even if you bring somebody in — how are you going to know they're doing the right things and they have an effective process?

Here would be my suggestion: you and I set a time, 45 minutes coming up, where we can go a little deeper. I'll send you some homework ahead to help us figure out specifically where we're missing some things. And at the end of that conversation, if you go, hey, got some good stuff here, I'll run with it on my own — great. If you go, hey, I want your help, we'll talk through what that looks like.

I'll send you an invite. We'll meet for 45 minutes. And then I'm going to send you a separate email with a quick survey — about ten minutes. It's going to talk in four areas: strategy, structure, staff and skills. Rank them one to five. One, not a problem, we got it figured out. Five, gap area, here's a problem.

moments.title: Four words to start
moments.quote: What can I help you on this morning?
moments.why: No agenda-setting speech. The question produces the entire ask in the next ten seconds.

moments.title: Goes to the stall language first
moments.quote: Right now I want to hear a little bit about what you're seeing from selling on your side. What are they saying if their deals aren't closing for you?
moments.why: Before accepting that the problem is a missing salesperson, he asks what the buyers actually say — and gets a diagnosis.

moments.title: The answer that names the real problem
moments.quote: I have to go back and talk to my finance manager. I have to take it higher. I have to take it to somebody else. That's 100% the reply.
moments.why: Matt is selling to non-decision-makers every time and never gets a second meeting. One question surfaced it.

moments.title: What happens when you hire into a vacuum
moments.quote: They're either going to struggle — you're going to keep them around, or spend a lot of money paying them for lack of results — or they're going to quickly pick up on that and go elsewhere, and then you're back to square one anyway.
moments.why: Gives the cost of the hire-first path in terms the founder cares about: wasted payroll and a restart.

moments.title: The bird cage question
moments.quote: So I guess, do you guys have the bird cage ready for the bird?
moments.why: Set up thirty seconds earlier as an analogy, then asked as a direct question. It gets a confident 'I believe so' — which the next question demolishes.

moments.title: The test behind the analogy
moments.quote: If I was to walk in as a new salesperson and say, what does your sales process look like — would you be able to show me that and go, here's documented, here's how we know it works and why it's effective?
moments.why: Converts a rhetorical analogy into a falsifiable test, and Matt immediately concedes: 'why we know it works and why it's effective, no.'

moments.title: Stops talking and checks
moments.quote: What's going through your head?
moments.why: After a two-minute explanation that got only an 'okay,' he asks for the reaction instead of continuing — and gets Matt's real inventory of what he does and doesn't have.

moments.title: Nobody you hire will fix this for you
moments.quote: You can go out and hunt for those folks. I'm going to tell you from experience, they're not going to want to come in and finalize the process and figure out where the problems are and fix it. It's a very rare salesperson that comes in and wants to do that.
moments.why: Kills the premise of the request directly, from experience rather than theory, right after Matt restates it.

moments.title: The question that turns the call
moments.quote: But how are you going to know, even if you bring somebody in — how are you going to know they're doing the right things and they have an effective process?
moments.why: Meets the time objection without arguing about time. Matt's answer — 'I could set up some KPIs off of something I believe is right, but I don't know that they're right' — is the concession.

moments.title: Offers to shorten the time, then names the blind spot
moments.quote: That's where I could help — to help you evaluate and figure that out and help you shorten the time to set that up. But if you just go, I'm going to trust they're coming in and doing the right things — let's say they're struggling, we're getting meetings but things aren't closing. You're not going to know what to look for in order to help them.
moments.why: Answers the time objection with speed rather than virtue, then closes the loop. Matt: 'Yeah, you're right.'

moments.title: The proposal with a built-in exit
moments.quote: At the end of that conversation, if you go, hey, got some good stuff here, I'll run with it on my own — great. You go, hey, I want your help, we'll talk through what that looks like.
moments.why: Both outcomes named out loud before the meeting is booked, which makes the yes cheap.

coaching_notes: This is the clearest reframe in the batch: a founder asks for help hiring a closer and leaves with a working session on sales infrastructure, without ever being told his question was wrong. The pivot runs 6:54 to 8:27 and is worth listening to end to end.
The time objection at 15:04 is handled by changing what Matt is buying — speed and a way to evaluate a future hire — rather than by debating whether he has time. That's the move most coaches miss.

Money never comes up. There is no indication of what Matt could spend, what he has spent on recruiting, or what a salesperson would cost him, which would have strengthened the argument that building the structure first is cheaper than a bad hire.
Shad also never asks who else decides, though Matt says 'we' throughout and clearly has at least one partner. Worth flagging as the gap to close in the follow-up.

headline: Owner buying out his partner inherits the sales seat
summary: Evan is partway through buying out the partner who has been doing all of Ovyl's selling, financed by a personal loan at nearly 10% with roughly $16k monthly payments. He called because sales is the survival risk and the first question everyone will ask. Rob worked the numbers: 2024 is tracking to $3.2M against a $4.5M plan, two large projects short, with a loss last quarter; lead flow is a new marketing agency, a LinkedIn outreach vendor, chip-manufacturer partnerships and, by Evan's own account, dumb luck. Rob challenged the idea that long client timelines are untouchable, asked what ROI would make a $30,000 year worth it, and then sequenced the Sales X-Ray assessment ahead of the infrastructure work Evan wanted to start with.
outcome_note: Booked Wednesday at noon for 75 minutes to complete the assessment, begin on infrastructure, and talk scope and terms; the invite went out during the call and the assessment link was promised same day or next.

milestones.text: All right, so what's the bigger challenge for you — getting in front of new opportunities, or closing the opportunities you get in front of?
I assume you don't have an ability to spend money right now, right — until you get ahold of the profit and loss statement. Is that fair?
Scope out the underperformance in 2024 — how far away are you guys from where you were hoping to be, or where you needed to be?
How bad? Was it a bloodbath?
Is that — do we have to tolerate that? Or can we accept some responsibility for not impacting the timeline in all the ways that we could have?

Part of it too is — hey, if in 2025 you paid me $30,000 and you got a million bucks, you could point to a million bucks that you won that you wouldn't have won otherwise. What's that math have to look like for you to go, oh, that was worth it, this is really successful?

Evan won't put a number on it. He defines value as a second set of eyes so he isn't making all his own mistakes, and as peace of mind that he's doing the right things at the level they need to be done — because he is taking out a big loan and the downside risk is large.

I know that we just put a half an hour here to get it done, but if we can grab an hour next week, or maybe 75 minutes — we can get through the assessment, we can get started on infrastructure, we could talk about scope and terms, and we can get all that going all at once if that works for you.
Yeah, I sent you the invite, and then you'll get the link from me for the assessment here today or tomorrow.

moments.title: The prospect names the stakes himself
moments.quote: I think that our most urgent thing in terms of the survival odds of the company is sales, because that's what my partner's been doing for the most part. And I also know that that's going to be everybody's first question — what about sales?
moments.why: The whole engagement is justified in two sentences by the buyer. Rob's job for the rest of the call is to find out how big it is.

moments.title: Confirms the role before the problem
moments.quote: So are you inheriting the role of primary seller? Is that what this turns into?
moments.why: Establishes who will actually be coached before discussing anything else.

moments.title: The two-way fork
moments.quote: What's the bigger challenge for you — getting in front of new opportunities, or closing the opportunities you get in front of?
moments.why: A forced-choice question that splits the entire sales problem into the only two halves that matter, and works on any seller.

moments.title: Checks for money before spending the hour
moments.quote: I assume you don't have an ability to spend money right now — until you get ahold of the profit and loss statement. Is that fair?
moments.why: Assumes the constraint out loud, which makes it easy for Evan to correct him: 'I'm already an owner, so I can.' Authority cleared in fifteen seconds.

moments.title: Scope out the underperformance
moments.quote: Scope out the underperformance in 2024 — how far away are you guys from where you were hoping to be, or where you needed to be?
moments.why: Produces the entire financial picture: two missing $750k-$1M projects, $3.2M tracking against $4.5M, a loss last quarter.

moments.title: Refuses to accept a nine-month cycle as a fact of nature
moments.quote: Do we have to tolerate that? Or can we accept some responsibility for not impacting the timeline in all the ways that we could have?
moments.why: Evan's own answer — 'the only answer has to be yes, we can accept responsibility' — is the moment he becomes coachable.

moments.title: Applies the same standard to himself
moments.quote: Anytime that someone comes back to me and says let's talk again, I'm always grateful for the opportunity to talk again — but usually we're talking again because I missed it the first time. I could have done something to make them figure it out the first time, that now's the time.
moments.why: Takes the hard standard he just imposed and demonstrates it on his own selling, which is why it doesn't feel like a lecture.

moments.title: Puts a price in the air and asks for the return
moments.quote: If in 2025 you paid me $30,000 and you got a million bucks — you could point to a million bucks that you won that you wouldn't have won otherwise. What's that math have to look like for you to go, oh, that was worth it?
moments.why: Introduces the number himself, inside an ROI frame, before any proposal exists.

moments.title: The real buying motive
moments.quote: Part of the value of this coaching is having a second set of eyes and making sure I'm not making all of my own mistakes — that I can learn from your mistakes and mistakes you've seen other people make. Because I am going to be taking out a big loan, and so downside risk is big. For me, peace of mind of knowing that I'm at least doing the things I would be doing at a level that they need to be done is important.
moments.why: He never answers the ROI question. What he buys is risk reduction against a personal loan — a different sale than revenue growth, and the one Rob should price against.

moments.title: Sequences the assessment ahead of what the client asked for
moments.quote: I know that your curiosities and where you want to start has more to do with infrastructure. We're going to give you the sales X-ray first, though, just to give you a sense of where you're at from a skillset and competency standpoint, and what might be the most important things to focus on. Does that make sense?
moments.why: Overrides the client's preferred starting point, names that he's doing it, and asks for agreement.

moments.title: Asks about the feeling, not the plan
moments.quote: So are you excited, or are you still feeling the burn?
moments.why: Gets the most human line in the call: 'it is a bigger risk than I've ever taken. Starting the company, I only had zero to hit. But this is scary.'

moments.title: Trades his own debt story
moments.quote: We sold into our ESOP, which is overwhelmingly a great thing — but then you carry a ten-year note. It doesn't make us feel any better that if we didn't have that we would be wildly profitable. It's like when you're winning and you're still eking by. There's just something weird about how that feels.
moments.why: Matches the buyer's vulnerability with his own at the same scale, and it opens a succession-planning conversation Evan wants to continue.

The up-front contract for the next meeting at 23:51 is the model version from this batch — it names the assessment, the infrastructure start, and scope and terms, so the commercial conversation is pre-authorized rather than sprung.

headline: Role-play drill on inbound Facebook lead calls
summary: Despite the FTC label this is a standing coaching session with an existing client: Tyler brings two instructors, Wilson and Justin, who call Facebook and ticket leads to book free swing evaluations. Rob reframes how much pain, impact and commitment a lead call actually needs — only enough to get a parent in the door, not enough to close a $1,900 program — then runs both reps through live role plays with Tyler playing the dad. He hands them the opening question, the emotional question for dad, third-party close language, and a script for deflecting the early price question, and closes by telling Justin his conviction, not his technique, is the gap.
outcome_note: Not a sales call — a training session that ended with Rob noting both reps improved and the group agreeing to pick it up next time.

milestones.text: I would go with, hey, Tyler, what made you put the lead into Facebook in the first place? Because the question, what made you even want to inquire, is probably the sharpest, straightest path.
How do you feel about that, dad? Dad is emotionally involved in this conversation — go ahead and ask him an emotional question too.
You said that there's kids on the team out-hitting your kid. What do you see in them that you're not seeing in your kid? What are they doing differently?

Typically when dads tell me, hey, I can't get the kid to listen to me, outs, losing confidence, it sucks for me — typically that same guy would say, you know what, Wilson, I'll take you up on your offer to come in and do a free eval. Is that what you're saying?
Hey Tyler, it's a great question. We have a couple different programs. Would you mind if we figured out if we could help him first and then we could talk about what that looks like?

moments.title: Right-sizing the close
moments.quote: You still want pain and you want impact and you want commitment, but you only need enough pain, impact and commitment to get them to drag their asses in for the eval.
moments.why: The cleanest statement of a principle reps constantly get wrong — the discovery has to be proportional to what you are actually asking for.

moments.title: The straightest path to pain
moments.quote: I would go with, hey, Tyler, what made you put the lead into Facebook in the first place? What made you even want to opt into this conversation you're having with me?
moments.why: Shows how to replace a friendly warm-up question with the one that gets the compelling reason in the first ten seconds.

moments.title: Stops the role play right before the pitch
moments.quote: Let me stop you right there, Wilson. You're doing so good. And then let me stop right before we — let's get you guys in.
moments.why: Model of when to interrupt a role play: at the exact moment the rep stops asking and starts talking about themselves.

moments.title: Remember who writes the check
moments.quote: Dad's the one that's writing the check, so how dad feels about it is important too. Go ahead and ask him an emotional question too.
moments.why: The rep had taken the kid's pain but not the buyer's — a transferable miss in any call with a sponsor and an end user.

moments.title: Third-party close instead of an ask
moments.quote: Typically that same guy would say, you know what, Wilson, I'll take you up on your offer to come in and do a free eval. Is that what you're saying?
moments.why: The exact language for letting the prospect opt in rather than asking them for the appointment.

moments.title: Tie the appointment back to the pain
moments.quote: You're not coming in to check out the technology. You're coming in because your kid is hitting the ball on the ground, he's getting out, and he's losing his confidence. That's why you're coming in.
moments.why: A one-line fix for reps who close on their own capability instead of the prospect's reason.

moments.title: An upgrade from 'would it be worth it to you'
moments.quote: What is it worth it to you is better than here's what I want to do. But even one up from that might be, hey Tyler, people who tell me this and this and this tell me it would be worth it to come in and do the eval.
moments.why: Ranks three versions of the same close from weakest to strongest — easy to steal and teach.

moments.title: The gap question
moments.quote: What do you see in those guys you don't see in junior? It's a real simple way to get him talking directly. That's a nice layup that they give you.
moments.why: Turns an evasive 'just wanted to see what you have' into specific pain by using a comparison the prospect raised himself.

moments.title: Deflecting price without dodging it
moments.quote: Hey Tyler, great question. Price is important. We've got a couple of different ways that we do this, but would you mind if we get through the assessment to make sure there's even an opportunity to enroll you guys before we talked about the program?
moments.why: Permission-based sequencing language that works for any early price question.

moments.title: Conviction, not technique
moments.quote: You have to be more comfortable and speak with more conviction. They will make comparisons about your ability as an instructor based off of your conviction in this conversation.
moments.why: The real diagnosis of the second role play — the words were right and the delivery still cost the call.

moments.title: Con is short for confidence
moments.quote: I hate to say this because I know you guys aren't conning, but the word con is actually short for confidence, because people that are selling bullshit, as long as they're confident, people will buy it.
moments.why: A blunt, memorable way to make a rep take delivery seriously without making it about ego.

moments.title: If we get impact, they're coming in
moments.quote: People who haven't used a hitting coach yet, it's just about impact and commitment. If he says junior is struggling with confidence and it sucks to watch him do it, they're coming in.
moments.why: Closes the session by collapsing everything taught back to one predictive variable.

He coaches the second rep differently than the first: Wilson got technique corrections, Justin got a delivery correction. Worth noticing that he diagnosed the right problem rather than repeating the first lesson.

headline: Coaching a loyal customer's quiet price defection
summary: Stan brings Rob a scenario he raised in a group session: Arlen, a contractor Stan has a long personal history with and gives extraordinary service to, quietly bought an $18,000 order from a cheaper competitor — and when Stan drilled in, it turned out to be the third order in a month. Rob narrows it to a binary (Arlen has either lost awareness of what Ramco does for him or he doesn't care), teaches commitment and consistency as the tool for changing future behavior, and role plays the confrontation. The call lands on Stan's real insight — that Arlen doesn't know how often his own foremen lean on Ramco after hours — and Rob's correction that Stan told him instead of asking him.
outcome_note: Not a sales call — a coaching session that ended with Rob asking Stan to state his takeaway and how he would use it, which Stan did.

milestones.text: Give me the 30,000 foot view again. Long-time client, loyal client, bails on you this one time to get a lower price.
So is this a one-off? He placed an order somewhere else as a one-off?
Is that a lot of business, starting to turn into a lot?
He's either lost awareness of what you guys do so well, or he doesn't care.
Tell me what you took away from our conversation and then tell me how you'll use it.

moments.title: Four words that open the story
moments.quote: Taking advantage in what way?
moments.why: Stan had summarized; this one short question gets the whole service picture — before-hours deliveries, foremen calling at night — in his own words, which Rob reuses all call.

moments.title: Testing whether it's really a one-off
moments.quote: So is this a one-off? He placed an order somewhere else as a one-off?
moments.why: The question that uncovers it was three orders, not one — and it reframes the whole problem.

moments.title: The binary
moments.quote: He's either lost awareness of what you guys do so well, or he doesn't care.
moments.why: Collapses a messy relationship story into two options, both of which are actionable. The model move of the call.

moments.title: Confront, but conversationally
moments.quote: So why don't we confront him with that? And I use the word confront, but we'll do it conversationally, within the context of our relationship.
moments.why: Defuses the word that would otherwise stop a relationship-driven seller from acting.

moments.title: Giving the pain back in the client's own words
moments.quote: Handling your calls at six and seven at night, running around at night — these are your words, not his — but the out-of-this-world amazing service just must not be as important as price and proximity.
moments.why: Shows how to build the confrontation out of language the client already supplied, so it doesn't feel like a script.

moments.title: I don't believe him
moments.quote: I don't believe him. What you're thinking in your head is, convince me. I wouldn't say that out loud, but what you're thinking in your head is convince me.
moments.why: Stan accepted 'one and done' and stopped. This is the internal posture that would have kept him digging.

moments.title: Commitment and consistency
moments.quote: When people say things out loud, really clearly, especially when they repeat those things, they are incredibly likely to behave that into existence in the future.
moments.why: The principle behind the whole session, named explicitly and tied to a tactic.

moments.title: Making the commitment strong enough to hold
moments.quote: The next time you get a job in close proximity that's this particular type of material, you're calling me and only me. Yes, I promise. You promise? I promise. You promise? I promise.
moments.why: Demonstrates the difference between a weak commitment and one repeated until it binds.

moments.title: Permission to reopen a closed subject
moments.quote: I don't want to pick the scab again, but can we finish this conversation?
moments.why: A reusable opener for going back at a customer issue that was papered over the first time.

moments.title: Telling is not landing
moments.quote: All that's really good, Stan, but you've got to ask a question at some point in time to get that to sink in.
moments.why: The central correction — Stan defended Ramco's value persuasively and still didn't change Arlen's mind, because he never asked.

moments.title: A different person has to go to bed
moments.quote: The version of him that got up this morning going, my foremen don't call Ramco that often — a different person needs to go to bed in his body, and that person goes, man, we call Ramco a lot.
moments.why: The clearest statement of what a confrontation is actually for, and why only a question can produce it.

headline: Rob on the buying side of a sponsorship pitch
summary: The roles are reversed on this one: Matt, a newly seated board member of the EO Next chapter, is pitching Rob on an exclusive $20,000-a-year sales coaching sponsorship, and Rob is the prospect. Rob opens by handing Matt all the reasons Lushin wouldn't do it, then runs his own qualification — price, retreat costs, access versus true membership, chapter size, the one member who actually wants a sales coach — while narrating out loud how he would cash flow it against an ESOP note that has their net margin at one percent. It ends with Matt sending a brochure and offering a reference call, and no date on the calendar.
outcome_note: No commitment and no scheduled next meeting — Matt will send a brochure and possibly connect Rob with another sponsor, and Rob will 'let him know' his interest.

moments.title: The seller admits he's nervous

moments.title: Hands over the objections unprompted
moments.quote: You said you're nervous to talk to a sales coach. Let me make it easy on you by telling you all the reasons that we wouldn't do it. Does that make sense?
moments.why: Worth hearing as a buyer move — it disarms, controls the agenda and tells the seller exactly where to aim.

moments.title: The sponsorship history objection
moments.quote: We have historically not done a lot of sponsorships because there's usually not much of a net gain versus just what happens from referrals and goodwill.
