moments.title: No pain, and he says so
moments.quote: Our belief internally a little bit has been we don't necessarily struggle to get new business. And so it's like, what makes it worth it?
moments.why: This is the whole call in two sentences, and the seller never goes after it.

moments.title: Do you let the partner speak?
moments.quote: Do you let the partner speak?
moments.why: A five-word qualifying question that targets the only mechanism that would actually produce return for him.

moments.title: Asking price early and plainly
moments.quote: What kind of money range are we talking about?
moments.why: No throat-clearing, and he follows it immediately with the hidden cost — the retreats — that the quote didn't include.

moments.title: Thinking out loud about where the money comes from
moments.quote: We closed our ESOP like 18 months ago, and we write a huge check to the previous owners. We're killing it, but our net is so tight — like 1%. There's not much profit to pay for stuff.
moments.why: A buyer narrating his own affordability problem. A seller listening would hear exactly which objection to solve, and Matt mostly doesn't.

moments.title: How he'd sell it internally
moments.quote: If I was going to sell this to the leaders — there's four of us — it would be okay, we were ready to spend twelve five on joining, arguably a worse chapter.
moments.why: The decision process and the comparison anchor, volunteered. Rare to hear a buyer build the internal business case out loud.

moments.title: Qualifying the one live opportunity
moments.quote: Tell me about that business. Not that you need to introduce me to them, but what's a typical — who is this person? Just tell me the size of the business, what they do.
moments.why: Tests whether the seller's proof point is real. Matt's answer — hedged, 'I don't want to misspeak' — is the payoff.

moments.title: What am I actually buying
moments.quote: What's the difference in a sponsor, or whatever language you use there, someone like me — what's the difference in my access versus somebody who's a true member of the chapter?
moments.why: Cuts past the brochure to the one thing that determines value: real access or a seat at the kids' table.

moments.title: Rob sells his own capability to the seller
moments.quote: If you guys let us talk, it's not that hard to pull off. I could deliver a 60 or a 90 minute talk that makes them go, oh, no brainer, let's talk further. People don't have to stretch to want to talk to us.
moments.why: The moment the buyer becomes the seller — and the clearest version of how Rob sees his own go-to-market.

moments.title: Back to terms, not to yes
moments.quote: And you would let me cash flow it month at a time, right? Whatever the payment terms are, the simpler it is for us to cash flow it.
moments.why: Ends on structure rather than decision — a useful tell that a deal is interested but not close.

coaching_notes: Roles are reversed: Rob is the buyer and Matt is selling. The milestones here are Rob's buying behavior, which is why budget and decision-process are present and pain is conspicuously absent.
Matt never sets an up-front contract, never asks Rob a question about Lushin's goals, and never tests the ESOP cash flow objection Rob hands him twice. He answers questions well and runs no process.

The filename says 'CLA President' but nothing in the transcript identifies a CLA — Matt is a board member handling strategic partnerships for the EO Next chapter. Treat the filename label as unreliable.

Best use of this recording: play it as a buyer study. Rob states the objection, the affordability constraint, the internal decision path and the comparison anchor out loud, and a coach can mark every place a seller could have moved.
Lushin is rendered as 'Lucian' at 20:08 — the usual transcription quirk.

headline: Capability walkthrough with the partner who missed call one
summary: This is the follow-up to Rob's August 29 first conversation with Keating, with Keating's senior partner Dave brought in — Rob says so explicitly at 25:29 ('Dave, you weren't part of the first conversation that Keating and I had'). Dave wants to see the approach before discussing timing, so Rob walks the whole model: the five things he needs from leaders, the strategy-structure-staff-skills pyramid, the goal-KPI-accountability-behavior-skills-correction loop, the 21 core competencies and will versus DNA versus tactical. Dave is candid that they have no articulated strategy and that he and Keating have not discussed next steps since the last call. Rob gives him permission not to make it a priority and proposes a fail-safe meeting as the test.
outcome_note: No decision and no money discussed — they agreed to a fail-safe conversation in three to four weeks whose explicit purpose is to find out whether Keating and Dave ever had the internal conversation.

milestones.text: The point of this conversation mostly today is for me to share with you how I help the clients that I work with. We want to get to the point where it's easy for us to figure out — hey, this just doesn't make sense to keep talking, or here's a little step that we could take together when it does make sense. Would that be reasonable to figure out today, or how were you expecting or hoping this particular conversation to end?

Typically, Dave, my experience would be that the size of the problem and the urgency around the problem we're trying to fix is the thing that impacts timing. If it's a problem that's worth fixing now, then the timing is now.
Dave sets his own criteria: understand how Rob would approach fixing the problem, then test whether they have flushed out all the alternative approaches before picking a course.

One of the conversations that Keating and I had early was about average ticket size. You say we want to grow — that's a strategic imperative. We're going to increase our average ticket size. And then what's the strategy to do that? The guys just aren't asking for the opportunities.

Dave, you weren't part of the first conversation that Keating and I had. He was having the leader skill-will conflict in his head — is it a problem with will, is it a problem with skill, are they just not going to do it, or can they not do it?
The one thing that I say is, I doubt that everybody on your team is committed.
Dave describes the decision path: an organization of 13-14 people with a four-person leadership team including himself and Keating, and he and Keating will talk offline.

All my clients are pretty busy. The people who work with me, for whatever reason, it's just a priority. And if you guys go, hey, this isn't a priority — that's no harm, no foul. Don't take it personally.

Do you guys want to put a fail-safe conversation on the calendar — a week or two from now — and if you show up and you haven't had time to talk about this thing yet, then we could look at each other and go, man, if it hasn't happened in two weeks it's probably not going to happen. No big deal.
Dave agrees to the fail-safe call in three weeks and names the test for himself and Keating; Rob moves it to four weeks for fall break and will send the invite.

moments.title: Up-front contract with a no built in
moments.quote: We want to get to the point where it's easy for us to figure out — hey, this just doesn't make sense to keep talking, or here's a little step that we could take together when it does make sense.
moments.why: Sets a mutual exit as a legitimate outcome in the first three minutes, with a new decision maker in the room.

moments.title: Problem size drives timing, not capability
moments.quote: The size of the problem and the urgency around the problem that we're trying to fix is the thing that impacts timing. Usually if it's not a big enough problem, regardless of whether I'm any good, that would be the later choice.
moments.why: A direct challenge to the buyer's stated logic in the opening minutes — and the pushback that follows is the real value.

moments.title: The prospect disagrees out loud
moments.quote: Yeah, but I don't agree exactly.
moments.why: Dave refuses the frame and restates his own. Worth hearing how Rob takes the disagreement without defending.

moments.title: When this fails, here's why
moments.quote: When we fail, especially early, it's usually not you. It's not that the content is bad, it's that we couldn't create stickiness — either I wasn't clear about what it takes up front, or the people I'm working with just aren't doing what they need to do.
moments.why: Pre-frames failure and splits the responsibility before any commitment is made.

moments.title: We don't have a strategy
moments.quote: If we asked ourselves, do we have a strategy — I don't know what that word means as it pertains. We have a very high level, broad strategy to grow. Well, that's not really a strategy.
moments.why: The prospect's unguarded self-assessment, and the opening Rob chooses not to exploit but to reframe.

moments.title: Giving him credit for the strategy he has
moments.quote: You gave us a version of that where you say hard work, do the right thing, communicate. I would argue that that's a strategy, because that's a marketplace differentiator — as you know better than I know, most people don't do that.
moments.why: Takes the prospect's confession of weakness and reframes it as an asset without losing the gap. Hard to do well.

moments.title: Training without leverage
moments.quote: You teach committed people how to ask better questions, they're going to go out and ask better questions. You teach uncommitted people how to ask better questions, you might not get anything out of them.
moments.why: The cleanest argument for assessing before training, in two sentences a buyer can repeat internally.

moments.title: I doubt everybody on your team is committed
moments.quote: The one thing that I say is, I doubt that everybody on your team is committed.
moments.why: A flat, unhedged statement about the prospect's people — and Dave answers 'I think you're absolutely right.'

moments.title: The guarantee he actually offers
moments.quote: They don't get a guarantee that everybody will be committed, but we do get a guarantee that we'll have a plan. You've got a finish line where you've got perfectly clear evidence one way or another, and then you can make a decision.
moments.why: Solves the owner's real fear — firing someone he isn't sure he developed — rather than selling an outcome he can't promise.

moments.title: We don't make you fold into our program
moments.quote: We build a program that will succeed for the organization that you work with. You don't ask the organization you're trying to work with to fold into a thing that you've built because it's what's easiest for you.
moments.why: Positioning on delivery flexibility, which is exactly the concern Dave raises two minutes later about pulling four leaders offsite.

moments.title: Permission not to buy
moments.quote: The people who work with me, for whatever reason, it's just a priority. And if you guys go, hey, this isn't a priority — no harm, no foul. Don't take it personally. That's just the reality of it. So I'm okay with that.
moments.why: Dave has just admitted nothing happened since the last call. Rob doesn't chase — and the fail-safe meeting comes out of this.

moments.title: The fail-safe meeting
moments.quote: If you show up to that conversation and you haven't had time to talk about this thing yet, then we could probably look at each other and go, man, if it hasn't happened in two weeks, probably not going to happen. No big deal.
moments.why: Turns a vague 'we'll talk internally' into a dated behavioral test with a named result either way. The single most stealable move on the call.

coaching_notes: This is the second meeting in the Gold Eagle sequence. The first is 2024_08_29_RL_FirstTimeConversations_Prospect_Keating_Gold_Eagle_FTC_NA — Rob's referral-based first conversation with Keating alone (referred by Olga), which ended with Rob sending an assessment survey and booking a follow-up. On this call Keating's senior partner Dave is added and says almost nothing has happened in between; Rob confirms the link himself at 25:29.

Money is never mentioned in 54 minutes. There is no budget milestone because there is no budget conversation — a defensible choice with a new decision maker who wanted to see the approach first, but it means nothing was qualified financially.

Watch the handling of disagreement at 5:46. Dave rejects Rob's timing logic outright and Rob says 'okay' and moves, then gets the same point back from Dave at 52:54 in Dave's own words ('if we go down this path, we have to be committed, period'). Letting the prospect arrive there himself worked better than winning the argument.

Speaker diarization is poor. Keating is on the call from about 2:12 but his few lines (2:19, 11:42, 11:47) are merged into Speaker 1 along with Dave's, so the transcript reads as though one person said both.

Dave does most of the talking for a prospect company, which is good, but Rob presents for long uninterrupted stretches between 7:00 and 40:00 with only 'does that make sense' as a check. A coach could study where tighter questions would have surfaced pain earlier.

headline: Employer of record wants OMG, and Rob prices it live
summary: Debra runs an employer-of-record and recruiting firm placing Caribbean workers with US companies, and met the OMG assessment while filling a sales role for Rob's client Bright Star. She wants to know what it is and whether to adopt it. Rob leads with the contrarian version — recruiters usually dislike OMG because it screens most applicants out — explains sales-specific versus sales-adaptive assessment, walks a live Bright Star registration and candidate report on screen, and then phones his colleague Brian mid-call to work out how a multi-client recruiter license would be priced. He declines her follow-on ask for customer service and leadership assessments.
outcome_note: Debra asked for a quote and Rob owes her pricing for a recruiter-style license once Brian works it out — but no follow-up meeting was scheduled.

milestones.text: Debra reframes her business: as the employer of record, turnover hurts them directly, they have multiple open sales roles, and they struggle with sales specifically.
The Bright Star sales role took two months to fill — long by their standards — and that is the role that exposed them to the assessment.
Debra names her criteria: they believe in data and technology, they only use what works, and they trust vendors to have the science behind the tool.
Bright Star, I think, wanted to hire for eight or nine sales roles, and it was probably like $12,000 for the year. That's kind of what that price range looks like.

If you were going to hire for four roles in your organization in the next four months, that's $7,400 — and essentially you get unlimited assessments and you make four hires. You could assess 700 candidates if you wanted to.
Rob will get the recruiter-license pricing from Brian and email it to Debra; she will wait for it. No meeting set.

moments.title: Opening on her agenda, not his
moments.quote: You had some experience with the Objective Management Group assessment, and you had some questions about if the assessment was a fit. I don't know if you want to tell me the story, or how I could be the most...
moments.why: Names what he already knows and hands her the floor — a clean referral-call opener.

moments.title: Leads with why her industry hates it
moments.quote: Most folks in that sort of industry don't like the Objective Management Group assessment because it screens out such a significant portion of applicants that sometimes they find that to be burdensome or hindering.
moments.why: Puts the objection on the table before she can, then flips it — a negative-sell opening on a product she is already predisposed to.

moments.title: Reframing the screen-out as the point
moments.quote: The reason Jonathan insists on it is because he wants all of those candidates screened out. OMG actually empowers my clients to do way less interviews, because we're only going to interview folks who have survived the assessment.
moments.why: The same fact as the objection, reframed as the benefit, using a client she already knows.

moments.title: The prospect pushes back twice
moments.quote: Yeah, it does. Doesn't tell me about your company, though.
moments.why: Debra refuses to be led and makes him answer her actual question. Worth hearing how little Rob resists — he just asks 'what do you want to know?'

moments.title: Clarifying what he actually sells
moments.quote: I'm actually a distributor for Objective Management Group. They only sell through distributors. My company — I'm a partner in a company called Lushin and Associates, where we do sales force development.
moments.why: The structural answer that resets the conversation; up to this point she thought he was OMG.

moments.title: Sales-specific versus sales-adaptive
moments.quote: Most assessment tools are sales adaptive. DISC is a legitimate science that can predict behavioral traits, but it's not sales specific — it doesn't tell you about the 21 core sales competencies like desire and commitment and need for approval.
moments.why: The category distinction that does the real differentiation work, delivered without disparaging a tool she already uses.

moments.title: Hunting skills are useless without will
moments.quote: Everybody knows salespeople should hunt and ask great questions and sell value. But if they can hunt, if they can ask great questions, if they can sell value — it's pretty useless if they're not committed, if they don't have a high degree of desire.
moments.why: The core argument, stated as the light bulb he turns on for every client.

moments.title: The iceberg
moments.quote: The technical and tactical competencies tend to be above the waterline. The will to sell and the sales DNA competencies tend to be below. Those are the things where clients go, I didn't have that information and I don't know how to interview for it.
moments.why: A one-image explanation of the product's value that a recruiter can repeat to her own clients.

moments.title: Refusing to let her do the per-unit math
moments.quote: Well, how many do you know? Like, what would it look like? Do you have three roles, three different companies? Can you get me in range at all?
moments.why: She converts his number to '$1,500 a pop'; he turns it back into a scoping question instead of defending the price.

moments.title: Commitment is universal
moments.quote: Commitment is universal. It doesn't matter what the role specificity is. Low commitment gets you kicked out, high commitment gets you invited in.
moments.why: The non-negotiable, stated as a rule rather than a feature.

moments.title: Calling a colleague live on the call
moments.quote: I'm on a Zoom right now, live with somebody, and I think the recruiter hiring license for OMG is what she would want. Do you know how to price it?
moments.why: Rob doesn't know how to price her use case, so he says so and solves it in front of her. Unusual and effective transparency.

moments.title: Declining the adjacent work
moments.quote: That's the only thing that I would have any expertise in, because our entire business is helping owners get better at sales.
moments.why: She offers customer service and leadership assessment work and he turns most of it down rather than stretching to fit.

coaching_notes: The prospect ran more of this call than the coach did — Debra set the agenda twice ('doesn't tell me about your company, though'), asked for price, and asked for the next step. Worth studying as a call where the product demand was already there and process discipline slipped.

No decision-process work: Debra is the CEO, but her HR manager Rushane sat on the whole call unaddressed except for one 'any questions?' at 22:06, and Rob never asked how a tool like this gets adopted internally or what would need to be true to say yes.

The live call to Brian at 22:32 is the standout. Rather than promising to get back to her, he solved his own pricing gap on screen. It cost nothing in credibility and bought her patience for a quote he still owes.
The call ends with no scheduled follow-up — just 'I'll email you.' A single question ('when should we get back together once you have it?') would have made this a clean advance.

Diarization problems: Rushane's one line at 22:12 is labeled Speaker 1 (Rob), and both sides of the phone call to Brian from 22:32 to 23:47 are run together under Speaker 1. headline: Reading a manager assessment to its subject and his boss
summary: Not a first conversation — this is an OMG sales managerial assessment debrief with an existing client. Alex is the interim sales manager and a candidate to take the VP of Sales job permanently; Bree is still running an external search. Rob gives the verdict up front (he should expect to succeed if he wants the role), teaches how to read an assessment, explains why will outranks DNA outranks tactical, and walks the coaching, motivating and buy cycle findings. Alex asks the honest question — is hiring me a risk? — and gets an honest answer. Bree stays on afterward for a private debrief where she says her instinct is still no, and the conversation turns to whether Polygon needs both a VP and a manager, and to 2025 commission structure.
outcome_note: Not a sales call — an assessment review for an existing client; Rob owes Alex the PDF and a takeaway survey, and Bree opened new work on the 2025 commission plan.

milestones.text: Bree states the decision context: she is continuing the external VP of Sales search and wants to know whether Alex leaning in further, or taking it full time, is a reasonable alternative.
Alex names the criterion himself — am I right that anybody reading this assessment would conclude it would be taking a risk on Alex to put him in this role and believing he could be successful?

In the private debrief Bree says JA asked whether she would hire Alex as VP and her initial answer is no — he struggles to think outside the box on compensation and strategy and wants to move slower than she will accept.

It either feels like a kid right out of MBA college, or this corporate safety. There's a culture in corporate America where you only risk so much, because fixing the problem only gets you so far — you also can't make mistakes.
Because you've had a hell of a time with this search.
I'll send you over the assessment and then I'll send you over a little takeaway survey — basically, what were your takeaways, and what are you going to do about it?

moments.title: The verdict before the data
moments.quote: From the assessment's perspective, you should expect to succeed in that role if you wanted to. That's the verdict from the assessment.
moments.why: Leads with the answer so the subject can hear the rest of the findings without waiting for a judgment. A model opening for any debrief.

moments.title: Three buckets for reading your own results
moments.quote: There'll be findings you agree with, findings you understand but might not agree with, and findings you might not agree with because you don't get the context yet. A difference in definition oftentimes accounts for the gap.
moments.why: Pre-handles defensiveness by giving the subject a framework for disagreeing productively.

moments.title: Why will can't be taught
moments.quote: It's really challenging to teach somebody that's not committed to become committed, because that comes from places within and requires a certain openness. If you didn't bring it to the dance, I don't know that I could help you find it.
moments.why: The whole hierarchy argument in one image, and the reason a tactical-weak candidate can still be the right bet.

moments.title: How good are you at tennis in week one
moments.quote: You just haven't done it. It's like, how good are you at tennis the first time, the first week you try to play?
moments.why: Disarms a page full of red tactical scores without softening them.

moments.title: The buy cycle we actually want
moments.quote: The buy cycle that we want is one that is lacking research, that moves pretty quickly, that prioritizes value over price. It's not a judgment that the way you buy is stupid — it's that it's not supportive of navigating prospects with the least resistance.
moments.why: The cleanest explanation of the most misunderstood OMG finding, and how to deliver it without insulting the person.

moments.title: A slow buyer slows his prospects
moments.quote: You'll encounter a prospect with a faster buy cycle than you, and you'll slow them down because it's uncomfortable for you how quickly they're moving.
moments.why: Makes an abstract attitudinal finding concrete and commercially expensive.

moments.title: Both ways to lose the moment
moments.quote: Lonnie comes in really excited about three opportunities and we go, this is so great — and nobody understands what's really happening. Or Ted throws a curveball and instead of staying in our adult ego state we get frustrated.
moments.why: Answers Bree's question with two named examples from her own team instead of a definition.

moments.title: Would I hire this assessment?
moments.quote: If we opened up this assessment from somebody with ten years of management experience, I would still consider the candidate hireable — as long as the contract is there that you are not tactically proficient and we need to work on it.
moments.why: Answers Alex's risk question honestly and attaches the condition that makes the answer yes.

moments.title: The part of the job you can't plan your way through
moments.quote: Challenging the shit out of people on the team that really need to be challenged, dealing with their nonsense and excuse making — that's not planning, we're not accomplishing that on a spreadsheet. It's standing in there, a little verbal boxing.
moments.why: The most useful thing said to Alex all call, and it is about temperament rather than a competency score.

moments.title: Corporate safety versus entrepreneurs
moments.quote: There's a culture in corporate America where you only risk so much, because fixing the problem only gets you so far — you also can't make mistakes. Versus entrepreneurs: we'll make whatever mistake we need to fix a problem.
moments.why: Diagnoses Bree's unease about Alex in one sentence, and then names the condition under which it's fixable.

moments.title: What do you want to make, and why

moments.why: Redirects a comp-plan design question into a motivation question — the actual problem Bree described.

moments.title: What a soft number tells you

coaching_notes: Treated on its own terms: this is an OMG sales managerial assessment review for an existing client, not a first conversation. The milestones present are decision process and criteria around an internal promotion, not a sale.

The structure is the lesson — verdict first, then how to read the report, then the hierarchy, then two or three findings in depth, then one place to start. Reverse that order and the subject stops listening after page one.

Reviewing an assessment with the subject and his boss in the same room is risky, and Rob manages it by keeping the findings developmental and letting Alex ask the risk question himself at 22:51. The honest part of the conversation then happens with Bree after Alex drops off — worth noting that the setup produced two different conversations.

Bree asks for commission plan guidance at 36:01 and Rob redirects to 'what problem are you trying to fix — is it motivation?' before answering. That is the right instinct, and it opens a piece of 2025 work that nobody scheduled.
Lushin renders as 'Lucian' at 28:21 and 28:36 — the usual transcription quirk. Alex's connection drops around 23:40 and a few seconds of his question are lost; Rob asks him to repeat it.

moments.title: Restating the deal

coaching_notes: Mislabeled as a prospect conversation — this is an existing-client working session with no selling in it, which is why it carries only next-step and ufc-next milestones.

The whole call is a case study in what a thirty-second up-front contract prevents. Two separate expectation gaps surface — who builds the content, and whether today is the training — and both were created by not confirming the agenda at the start of this call or the end of the last one.
Rob's recovery at 11:57 is the thing to copy: he stops arguing about what was agreed, parks it, and spends the remaining time specifying the next meeting instead.

Yeimira's real requirement — train the trainers, because turnover means the same session gets repeated forever — only emerges at 17:46. A question about why she wants it that way, asked at minute nine, would have saved the call.

Transcript quality is fine but English is a second language for both client speakers and several lines are fragmentary; the training platform is referred to once as 'this handler platform' (Sandler) and once as 'the insandler.'

moments.why: Disqualifying parts of his own product is the cheapest credibility in the call.

moments.title: A compliment that is also a standard
moments.quote: I'm glad to hear you say you do role play interviews, because none of my clients are smart enough to do that.

coaching_notes: There is no up-front contract anywhere in this call. Damion joined late and Rob went straight to explaining; no time frame, no agenda, no exit ramp. It worked only because Damion asked for the story himself.
The single best move is 'What was Deborah's outlook?' — one question that did the work of an entire decision-process block and saved Rob from pitching the wrong person.
Rob disqualified parts of OMG out loud ('here's where it actually doesn't help'), which bought more trust than any feature list would have.
The opportunity is still completely unsized going into the three-way: no hire volume, no cost of a bad hire, no money of any kind was discussed.

coaching_notes: Call one of three with Public Media Apps. Colin is the champion with no authority over the rep and no budget, so Aaron spends the hour qualifying and champion-building, not pitching — there is no money discussion anywhere in 53 minutes, by design.
'Let's start with outcomes and work backwards' saved roughly twenty minutes of product explanation and produced a usable problem list in one answer.
Three questions do almost all the diagnostic work: who leads Kate, does Pete think the way you do, and who does the convincing. Each one moves the problem away from the rep and toward leadership.

Aaron sized the opportunity out loud and let the prospect hear him nearly disqualify it. Steal the mechanic: name the math, then name what would have to be true for it to be worth doing. The ufc-next is likewise explicit that the three-way may end in a handshake goodbye, which keeps the next meeting from being read as a proposal meeting.

moments.why: The whole first-conversation philosophy in four sentences, given as an answer to a referral-partner question.

moments.title: Free advice as the product demo
moments.quote: We'll just give free advice for that, so that they know this is what it's like to work with you guys.
moments.why: Positions the first conversation as the sample, which is why no proposal is ever needed at that stage.

coaching_notes: This is a re-entry, not a cold first conversation. Lushin already trained Charles and Brian personally assessed two of the four reps. His best move is refusing to treat the meeting as a fresh start — 'I want to go back in time a little bit' resets the whole frame.
'Who is going to reinforce this? Is that you?' is the load-bearing question. Brian establishes a sponsor with firing authority before he will spend an hour on their sales meeting.

Nothing was priced and nothing was asked about budget, even though Robert opened the money door twice ('I know what Neody's paying you,' 'what it would look like to do what we're thinking about'). The clinic is free work with no agreed decision attached to it — the ufc-next says 'we'll decide after that' but never says who decides what.

The strategic-partner idea is the bigger opportunity in the call — Robert has 30,000 LinkedIn connections and says 95% of the CEOs he works with name sales as the problem — and it got a good philosophical answer but no next step of its own.

Transcript quirk: Fireflies merged at least two Lushin voices into Speaker 2 and misassigns several exchanges (for example 6:17-7:20, where a Lushin answer sits inside Robert's block). Robert greets both an 'Albert' and a 'Brian' at 0:23 and is himself called 'jb' at 26:22.

other_speakers.who: Jitender, owner and CEO of Induspad and its warehousing/3PL arm referred to as EXO; referred to Rob by a mutual contact named Lauren

headline: Owner wants ten million without owning the accountability
summary: Jitender is trying to take EXO from roughly $3.5M to $10M across two new warehouse locations and needs to add salespeople to do it. Rob made him score his existing team one to ten, landed on an average of 1.5 out of 10, then spent ten minutes on pallet economics before accepting the $10M target as real. The heart of the call is Rob telling him plainly that he can supply system and structure but cannot supply the commitment and accountability, which has to come from an equity holder — and Jitender conceding he is not yet in a position to remove himself from sales. Jitender then declined the $3,000 Chicago strategy session and counter-proposed hiring help first; Rob took the pivot and put a Thursday 4pm invite out on the call.
outcome_note: Jitender redirected the engagement from a paid strategy session to 'first help me hire the sales people'; Rob agreed, deferred the cost question to the next conversation, and sent the Thursday 4pm invite before hanging up.

milestones.text: The two folks that are in the role, their average score is one and a half out of 10. Do you worry when you go to market to hire that you wouldn't attract more of the same?
Jitender says the current team only works the small leads marketing generates and has no idea how to get in front of the thousand-to-three-thousand pallet clients the $10M target depends on.
What else, in addition to handling objections? Pricing strategy.
Have you supported them with system and structure to help with this, or is that part of what's missing?
So we're closing a gap of six and a half million. Does that fill the whole gap?
And then how much profit do you make when you get to 10 million?

Given that challenge — I could help you with system and structure, but I just will not be present enough for the support of the system. We could give it to you, but in terms of how to implement and follow system and structure, which requires coaching and accountability and a little bit of motivating work — how would you pull that off?

The commitment and the accountability to the structure has to come within and from a stakeholder, from an equity holder. That's where the commitment comes from. If you'd want an engagement with someone like me to succeed, to some degree you would have to drive that.

If you tag me in to help train and develop this team, I promise you there will be moments where I have to come back to you and say this is something that's outside of their comfort zone, they're resisting just a little bit, I need you to reinforce this.

The cost of $3,000, you said, was a lot of money or a challenging amount of money. So we just need to talk through that, because you're hoping that I could help you add millions of dollars of revenue and hundreds of thousands of dollars of profit. And it's just — I can't do it for free.
Jitender asks directly: 'What is the cost of involving you per hire?' Rob answers that it depends on how much of his involvement they want and defers a real number to the next conversation.
Okay, here comes the invite.
So next time that we get together — and we'll schedule that before we leave here — we're going to talk about the largest fire to address, which is hiring, and we'll start there.

moments.title: Opens on capability, not plans
moments.quote: How comfortable do you feel being able to do that? How comfortable do you feel in your ability to staff up with the right people?
moments.why: Jitender tries to answer about finances and Rob says 'all of it', which forces the first honest admission of the call.

moments.title: Makes the owner grade his own team
moments.quote: Let me ask you this way — the team that you've hired, how well are they performing? One to ten, ten being best, one being terrible.
moments.why: Four minutes of scoring produces harder data than an hour of description, and the prospect can't dispute his own numbers.

moments.title: The number, and the trap in it
moments.quote: The two folks in the role, their average score is one and a half out of ten. Do you worry when you go to market to hire that you wouldn't attract more of the same?
moments.why: Turns the score into a forward-looking risk rather than a criticism of people already employed.

moments.title: Won't accept a goal he can't see the math behind
moments.quote: Where did the $10 million number come from? Have you done the math backwards to get profitable? Is there a 'that gets me X gross and Y net profit'?
moments.why: A coach refusing to work on a target until he knows what it's made of.

moments.title: Does the prospect's arithmetic in front of him
moments.quote: It's a lot more than 10 clients then. Because 10 clients is 2 million.
moments.why: Jitender had just said six to ten clients would get him to $10M; Rob checks it against the per-client number Jitender gave two minutes earlier.

moments.title: Isolates the one fix that would move the goal
moments.quote: If we fix nothing else and they found a systematic way to get in front of more of these opportunities, that goal starts to come into focus.
moments.why: Narrows a sprawling problem list to the single highest-leverage change and gets agreement on it.

moments.title: Says plainly what he cannot do
moments.quote: I could help you with system and structure, but I just will not be present enough for the support of the system. How would you pull that off?
moments.why: Pre-empts the most common reason engagements fail by naming the gap before anyone has bought anything.

moments.title: Why sales is different from every other function
moments.quote: Finance, operations, marketing — they could do those successfully. Sales is a little different because sales is where the weaknesses of being a human get exposed. We have to leave our comfort zone, we have to expose ourselves to social risk, unlike other areas of the business.
moments.why: The clearest available answer to an owner who thinks sales should run itself like operations does.

moments.title: Uses himself as the example
moments.quote: As strong as I am at this point in my career, I have accountability structure to help me with all the challenging parts of the 10x transformation that I'm trying to pull off.
moments.why: Makes the accountability requirement a universal condition rather than a judgement about the prospect.

moments.title: Grants the goal and withholds the timing
moments.quote: One of your goals could be 'I would like to remove myself from any day to day of sales.' You have the right to set that goal and you have the right to do that once you've achieved it. It's just, from my observation and our conversations, it doesn't feel like you're there just yet.
moments.why: Disagrees without arguing — concedes the destination and only contests the current position.

moments.title: Names the value gap behind the price objection
moments.quote: You're hoping that I could help you add millions of dollars of revenue and hundreds of thousands of dollars of profit. And it's just — I can't do it for free.
moments.why: Handles a $3,000 objection by putting it next to the number the prospect gave for the upside.

moments.title: Reframes an admission as a strength
moments.quote: I don't think you made that mistake. It's that you could admit to it and say it out loud. That matters.
moments.why: Jitender had just said he brought in hundreds of wrong people; Rob converts the confession into coachability.

coaching_notes: Despite 'FTC' in the filename this is not a first conversation. Rob references a prior Chicago proposal at $3,000 and Jitender says 'as I told you last time.' The recording also starts mid-sentence, so whatever up-front contract existed is not captured.
The one-to-ten rep scoring is the cheapest diagnostic in the batch — it produced a 1.5 average in four minutes and set up the best question in the call ('would you attract more of the same?').
Rob spent ten minutes on pallets, in-and-out fees and rotation rates before talking about people. He would not let a revenue target stand until he could reconstruct it from unit economics.

The block from 30:02 to 39:40 is the model for an owner-accountability conversation: say what you cannot do, name where commitment has to come from, use yourself as the example, grant the long-term goal, then pre-frame the exact future moment you will need them to reinforce you.

Rob lost the Chicago session and let Jitender rewrite the scope to hiring. He booked the meeting, but the $3,000 objection was never resolved, just deferred — 'we could answer that pretty quickly the next time that we talk' — and the per-hire price is now an open question going into Thursday.

other_speakers.label: Speaker 2
other_speakers.who: Matt, founder of Iconic Insurance, an independent individual-health-insurance brokerage licensed in 25 states; Indianapolis-based, dialing in from a five-week stay in Austin

headline: Solo founder hits a ceiling and goes shopping for a mentor
summary: Matt was referred by Brad, a client he signed and then asked to coffee, and came in wanting a coach who would tell him what to do rather than ask him what he thinks. He has been stuck at a revenue ceiling for two years, is the only client-facing person in the business, and has hired seven people in two years and let six go. Brian handed him the agenda — 'how would you like to vet me?' — then worked three problems live: the scarcity either/or, the hiring process that has no objectivity in it, and the free-education platform Matt was talked out of two years ago. He priced at $1,500 a month with no contract and an explicit stopping rule, and Matt asked whether he was worthy and told him to have Susie schedule it.
outcome_note: Matt asked 'am I worthy?', Brian said yes, and Matt told him to have Susie reach out to schedule — a verbal yes at $1,500/month with no contract, with the in-person kickoff waiting on his return from Austin and a questionnaire going out first.

The Brad referral and the search for a real mentor
Use this time to vet me

milestones.text: Well, what do you want to get out of this call? What are we working towards? I'll give you kind of a guide here — what do you want to take away?

The key is I want you to use this time to vet me, so that when I say 'where do you want to go from here?' it's easier for you to say 'I think I need to continue my search,' or 'what's this look like, how do we do this?' And if you say I want to do this, there will be a path. It's not a 'I don't know if I could do this, I don't know if I could afford you.' We'll always come up with a path. So is that fair?

Matt names the ceiling: flat revenue for two years, trying to be everything to everyone, his lowest-revenue clients absorbing the most time, and himself as the only client-facing person doing the customer service.
Over the last two years I've hired seven different people and let six of them go.
So why did the other six not work out?

There is a way to fix that. It's to remove subjectivity. Whenever that occurs it means you're hiring by subjective criteria, not objective. In your head you're going to argue it's objective, but it's not. Objectivity is score sheets, proof, assessments.
Why haven't you done it?

Matt frames the cost of the current model as himself: the education platform is 'so much more scalable than Matt working 50 hours a week instead of 40.' No revenue figure is ever attached to the ceiling.
Matt pre-commits on money before he hears a price: 'If we end up working together, that's not a problem for me. We need the money, I'll find the money. It'll work itself out.'
Matt asks how Brian typically works with a client and benchmarks it against his previous coach, who only ever flipped questions back at him.
How much did you pay?

I work on a monthly amount, and it's an amount that you say this is what works for my business. Typically it's $1,500 a month. But what people will do is say, well, my business doesn't support that, but here's what I can pay — and that's fine. That's just where we start.
We just want to get her working on scheduling beforehand so that by the time you're there, it's locked in.

I will send you a questionnaire — not to fill out, but to probe. Here's all the areas. It's sort of a 'what do I want to get your mind thinking about' on the Matt stuff, and it combines personally, professionally, spiritually. You don't have to sit there and answer it, but it'll help with how do I prioritize what I want to work on.

moments.title: Opens by handing over the agenda
moments.quote: Well, what do you want to get out of this call? What are we working towards?
moments.why: Second line of the call. Matt talks for three and a half minutes and gives Brian the entire backstory unprompted.

moments.title: Offers to be test-driven
moments.quote: You can actually ask me stuff you'd ask a coach. Like, I've got this problem, blah blah blah. I'll give you real answers, so you can go, okay, am I going to outrun Brian, or is Brian going to outrun me?
moments.why: Names the prospect's real fear — he outgrew his last coach — and converts the meeting into a working session.

moments.title: The question that runs the rest of the hour
moments.quote: Well, how would you like to vet me?
moments.why: Four words. Matt rejects his own stock questions and asks a better one, and from here the prospect drives.

moments.title: Who he chooses to work with
moments.quote: I basically wrote it down as a prayer. And the prayer was: Lord, bring me people who need help, and help me decide who deserves it.
moments.why: An answer to 'who do you like working with' that sets up a qualification standard the prospect then tries to meet.

moments.title: Scarcity as either/or instead of and
moments.quote: The scarcity mindset is the mindset that says there's an either/or, not an and. The game you're playing in your head is 'I have to either sell more or lose these bad clients.' Once you open your mind to and, you start to think, well, maybe I should hire somebody to do that part.
moments.why: A reusable reframe, delivered live on the prospect's own stated block.

moments.title: Names the hiring pattern and prescribes the fix
moments.quote: It's to remove subjectivity. In your head you're going to argue it's objective, but it's not. Objectivity is score sheets, proof, assessments. When you hire somebody they should have already proved their capability in the role. Anything short of that, it's not going to work out.
moments.why: Separates the one departure outside Matt's control from the five that weren't, then gives a mechanism rather than sympathy.

moments.title: Write the ad to repel, not attract
moments.quote: Most ads have a lot of 'here's what we're offering' versus 'here's what's required.' It needs to be 99% here's what's required — and by the way, this is a great job. Higher criteria, lower applicants.
moments.why: Immediately actionable: Matt is writing a customer-service job ad that same day.

moments.title: Corrects the prospect's favourite book
moments.quote: That is a marketing strategy. It is a marketing strategy. Where Marcus is not correct is — it is not a sales strategy. It's funny, because River Pools is not my client. Marcus still works for him, but he's not allowed to train the sales team anymore.
moments.why: Disagrees with a guru the prospect quotes, backs it with a first-hand story, and still endorses the underlying idea.

moments.title: Deletes the first hire from the plan
moments.quote: Your first hire, which is content and database for future customer service training — you can now do that with no hire. You just have transcripts. You can even say: now create a training program for my next hire based on these conversations.
moments.why: Gives away real, usable advice inside the first conversation, which is what Matt said he wanted a coach for.

moments.title: The line Matt came for
moments.quote: Your life is not defined by your yeses. It is defined by your nos. So the switch you need to make is: what do I need to say no to that gets me to my yeses?
moments.why: Matt had asked for 'Matt strategy, not business strategy'; this is the answer and it reframes everything before it.

moments.title: Ends a meeting to prove a point
moments.quote: He said, you can't get rich in catering. And I said, then we don't need to meet. We can end the meeting right now. He goes, whoa, you're kicking me out? I go, well, if you've already decided you can't get rich in catering, we're done.
moments.why: The willingness-to-walk story, told as a client example, that also happens to demonstrate the standard Matt is being measured against.

moments.title: De-risks the sale without discounting it
moments.quote: I don't do six months, I don't do one year, I don't do one month. There's zero commitment, there's no paperwork. We stop when we run out of stuff. If you ever get to the point where you're showing up for meetings going 'I don't really know what to talk about,' we stop.
moments.why: Removes every exit objection at once and makes the stopping condition the coach's own standard rather than the client's.

coaching_notes: Brian spends the first six minutes handing the controls over — what do you want out of this, how would you like to vet me — and never pitches. The prospect sets the agenda and talks himself into the engagement.
The hiring diagnosis is a repeatable sequence: count the failures, separate the one outside his control, name the pattern (subjectivity), prescribe the mechanism (proof before hire), then fix the ad.
He contradicted the prospect twice — 'you should have done this two years ago' and the Marcus Sheridan correction — and both landed because each came with a better mechanism attached, not just a no.

Price arrives at minute 46, after Brian first asks what Matt paid his last coach. The framing ('typically $1,500, but tell me what works and that's where we start') plus zero commitment and an explicit stopping rule is the whole close.

There is no quantified pain anywhere in 53 minutes — no revenue number, no cost of the ceiling, no value on the time he wants back. Brian closed on fit and chemistry, which worked here but leaves nothing to re-anchor on when the invoices start.

headline: OMG debrief that ends with a price and a yes/no date
summary: Call two of three: Aaron and Taylor walk Pete and Colin through the OMG results on Pete as a sales leader and Kate as the lone seller. The findings line up with everything Colin described in call one — Pete's commitment score is split across nineteen hats, Kate has a high need for approval, asks good questions but stops short, and the hidden questions show she is quoting the digital manager instead of the GM. Aaron spends the back half running a clean commitment sequence: do you believe we can help, do you want us to help, when is too late, are you committed to being alongside Kate, how much time would you actually give — and only then names $1,950 a month with no agreement. The call closed with a 30-minute Friday 2pm slot framed explicitly as go or no-go.
outcome_note: Pete got the price and the structure but did not say yes on the call; he and Colin wanted to confer first, and Aaron booked a 30-minute Friday 2pm call framed as bail or lock arms.

milestones.text: Peter, Colin — once we bring clarity to the data, I'll just look at you guys and ask if we can help and if you want help. But if the answer is no, no harm, no foul. I'll bring a crap ton of clarity to you. If it's yes, let's lock arms and go. We'll walk through exactly what that looks like, we'll set goals, objectives, time and touches, and go.
Pete states the problem in his own words: nineteen hats, not a salesperson, and he needs Kate motivated enough that he isn't monitoring every single conversation.

Aaron shows the hidden-question result: Kate says she is talking to the person who can say yes or no, and the assessment says she isn't — she is quoting the digital manager rather than getting the GM into the next conversation.
Where does the fuzzy perception come from?

I believe we're also talking about the wrong end of the problem. My challenge would be, ensure we're coaching and motivating, because it may not be a compensation issue of why she's not doing things. Let's put the challenge on us to properly coach and motivate and see if that unlocks it before you just change compensation.
When's too late?
Did you believe we can help you guys with that?
So I'll be happy to answer that. Do you want us to help you?
Are you committed to being alongside Kate through this process?
If I told you it was 30 hours a month and you'd get 250 more stations, would you do it?
Pete names what would disqualify it: 'it sounds like this process is more of a canned type of presentation as opposed to something which is personalized for us.'
And Pete, sounds like you and Colin want to get on the same page with a couple things from your side, correct?
If you want an average number on that, you're going to look at four to eight hours a month.
We will start first from a leadership perspective. You will get a whopping 1950 invoice a month. $1,950. And you'll see a little 5% line item — I'll explain that in a minute.
When do we want to put a quick 30 minutes on the calendar next, then?

You guys just tell Taylor and I what works and we'll match up calendars, and you can either say 'wow, something crazy happened, a meteorite crashed on us, we're bailing' — or 'nope, we still believe you can help, and we want help.' We're on the same page now; we need the logistics piece to take step one and get moving.

moments.title: No harm, no foul — stated before the data
moments.quote: Once we bring clarity to the data, I'll just look at you guys and ask if we can help and if you want help. But if the answer is no, no harm, no foul. I'll bring a crap ton of clarity to you. If it's yes, let's lock arms and go.
moments.why: The whole decision frame is set in fifteen seconds, before a single finding is shown, which is why the ask at the end doesn't feel like a pitch.

moments.title: The number one goal of leadership
moments.quote: What do you think the number one goal of leadership is as a whole? And it's not driving revenue. It's all about self-sufficiency.
moments.why: Asks the question, rejects the obvious answer, and gives Colin credit for getting close — then anchors the entire debrief on one word.

moments.title: Consistently coaches, not consistently talks
moments.quote: I'll have leaders say 'Aaron, Taylor, I talk with my folks all the time.' It doesn't say consistently talks with your people. It's consistently coaches. That's the difference between trainer and coach — trainer tells, coach helps discover.
moments.why: Takes a scoring label off a report and turns it into a behavioural distinction a leader can act on tomorrow.

moments.title: Permission to be himself
moments.quote: Can I give you permission to be yourself? The minute Pete is not Pete and we are inauthentic is the minute our people will see right through us. If you came in Monday slapping people on the back and rah-rahing, they'd be like, Pete must be on drugs. The good news is we don't need that Pete.
moments.why: Pete had just disqualified himself as 'an engineer, not a fuzzy salesy type.' Aaron removes the objection by making the engineering style the asset.

moments.title: The combine story on unpaid consulting
moments.quote: Doug calls me a couple months ago, says Aaron, I'm pissed. He got a call from a potential customer whose combine was down, drove it all the way to his farm — and the guy had bought a brand new combine from somebody else the day before. And I looked at his altruistic score. He was in the 20s.
moments.why: Turns an abstract motivation score into a story Pete recognises himself in, right after Pete defended his own over-demoing.

moments.title: Refuses the compensation question
moments.quote: I believe we're also talking about the wrong end of the problem. Blame process first, then people. I'd be careful of changing comp first until process, motivation, all that other stuff holds true — and then you can look at comp.
moments.why: Pete asked him to design a comp plan. Aaron declines the easy consulting answer and redirects to the thing he can actually fix.

moments.title: Drown or ignite
moments.quote: Typically, after four to six months with us, people either drown or ignite. You start to separate cream, because now they're armed with a process where they can be themselves, they're actually getting the effective coaching, we know what motivates them. It's your choice.
moments.why: Sets expectations for what happens to an underperforming rep without promising to save her — and without threatening her either.

moments.title: Teaches the GM problem using his own sales process
moments.quote: Pete, do you know why you were in Colin and I's second conversation? Because he did the legwork on the first one. And if Colin said 'Aaron, why don't you put a proposal together' — I'd go, no, you silly goose. If you want to keep talking, get Pete in the next conversation.
moments.why: The single best teaching move in the batch: the prospect is standing inside the example he is being taught.

moments.title: Nobody needs us
moments.quote: This company has done very well for 20-some years. Nobody needs us. People are going to get up the mountain regardless of us. All we do is take weight off people's shoulders so they can get up the mountain faster, with less effort and energy.
moments.why: Removes pressure at the exact moment he has just told them their sales process is wrong.

moments.title: Answers 'how much' with 'do you want this'
moments.quote: So I'll be happy to answer that. Do you want us to help you?
moments.why: Pete asked how it proceeds and how much it costs. Aaron acknowledges the question and spends the next seven minutes on commitment before giving a number.

moments.title: Overshoots deliberately to find the real line
moments.quote: If I told you it was 30 hours a month and you'd get 250 more stations, would you do it? ... I wanted to see if you push back. You tell me 30 hours a month, you're crazy. You tell me four to eight, I'm in.
moments.why: A negotiation move stated out loud afterwards — exaggerate, let them set the boundary, then land under it.

moments.title: No agreement, fire us any time
moments.quote: We don't do agreements, Pete, so you can fire us at any time. Just so you know, we send invoices until you say stop. Just be warned, people get addicted — our average client is with us 4.8 years.
moments.why: Removes the commitment objection and substitutes a retention statistic for a contract term.

coaching_notes: Call two of three. The filename says 'First Time Conversation' but this is the OMG debrief with the decision maker, run with Pete and Colin after assessments on Pete and Kate. The recording starts mid up-front contract.

The sequence from 59:53 to 1:07:25 is the spine: believe, want, urgency ('when's too late?'), commitment, time, then price. Pete asked 'how much does it cost' at 59:59 and did not get a number for seven and a half minutes.

'When's too late?' got an honest, unhelpful answer — there is no deadline, the recurring revenue carries them — and Aaron did not try to manufacture urgency out of it. That restraint is worth noticing. Pete raised the canned-programme objection at 1:08:56, after the structure was described. The answer ('I'm not finished yet — here's the back half') worked, but the public content / private context split would have landed better framed before the structure, not in response to it.

Two-coach mechanics: Taylor carried consultative selling and the need-for-approval example, and Aaron handed Kate's coaching to her on the spot ('Taylor is much more nurturing than I am, which is why she'd help Kate better than me'). A clean model for dividing a debrief.

Transcript quirks: the Fireflies header dates this April 12, 2025, which is the upload date, not the call date. 'Lushin' renders as 'Lucian' throughout. Speaker attribution blurs around 1:07:02-1:07:20, where Pete's 'Aaron, let's not be unrealistic, I'm committed' and Aaron's 'I wanted to see if you push back' are merged into one Speaker 1 block.

coach_confidence: medium — Speaker 1 carries all of Aaron's content and addresses Taylor, Colin and Peter by name, but diarization on this short call is loose and at least one of Peter's lines (the 'no, it's just crazy' answer at 2:27) is filed under Speaker 1.

headline: The yes arrives in sixty seconds, then logistics
summary: The third and final call in the Public Media Apps arc, one week after the OMG debrief and the $1,950 number. Aaron opens with banter, turns the floor over at 1:01, and Peter leads with 'we'd like to move forward' plus a request to push the start to mid-February. Aaron accepts the delay, extends it further rather than defending the date, and converts the rest of the nine minutes into sequencing: a February 20 three-to-five block found live on screen, HubSpot dashboard and pipeline-definition homework, and a plan to give Kate a month's written notice before she is pulled in. No re-selling, no celebration.
outcome_note: Peter opened with 'we'd like to move forward,' pushed the start to the week of February 17, and the call became pure logistics — February 20 structure session booked, pre-work requested, Kate joining in March.

milestones.text: Peter delivers the yes himself, unprompted: 'I don't know we have a whole lot to talk about besides — I mean, we'd like to move forward. I'm going to have to delay it a little bit in terms of start dates because there's a lot of stuff happening these next couple weeks.'

Peter sets the condition on his own: he wants Colin buddied up with him through the training, both because Colin will be modifying all the dashboard reports and because Colin is taking over the company at some point.
Okay, so step one, we'll get the time block to work through structure pieces.

When we meet on the 20th, first thing we'll do is work through getting process templated. We'll match it back to pipeline, we'll have your metric pieces and see if there's anything that needs tweaked or changed. So we'll keep that three-to-five block on the 20th — I'll send that invite out.

We'll have an email to you Monday on initial pieces. We'll outlay actual clear steps with dates and times for the Public Media side of things, so those can start to get blocked out in the calendar, and we'll make it through the chaos for the next couple weeks and then hit the ground running on the 20th.

moments.title: Asks for nothing and says nothing
moments.quote: Colin, I'll turn it over to you guys and we'll take the conversation from there.
moments.why: This is the entire close. Aaron does not recap, does not justify the price, does not ask for the decision — he hands them the floor and lets the yes come out of their mouths.

moments.title: The yes, with a condition attached
moments.quote: We'd like to move forward. I'm going to have to delay it a little bit in terms of start dates. If maybe we could start the week of the 17th or so of February.
moments.why: The payoff of the three-call arc. Note that it arrives as a logistics statement, not a declaration — which is what a well-run process produces.

moments.title: Extends the delay instead of defending the date
moments.quote: Yeah, it might even be like the week of March.
moments.why: The most counterintuitive move on the call. Agreeing with the postponement — and offering more of it — keeps the yes from being re-litigated.

moments.title: Converts the yes into step one immediately
moments.quote: Okay, so step one, we'll get the time block to work through structure pieces. Where are you guys physically located?
moments.why: Under ninety seconds from decision to first scheduled working session. No celebration, no re-selling.

moments.title: Removes friction before it's raised
moments.quote: So we'll keep that aspect virtual, then — save on travel time.
moments.why: Pete is in West Lafayette and Colin in Carmel; Aaron solves the logistics objection the moment he learns it exists.

moments.title: The pre-work ask, kept small
moments.quote: Here's the short answer: can you send me anything that you currently track now, like a snapshot of dashboards? What CRM do you guys use?
moments.why: Frames the homework as low effort — screenshots, snapshots — rather than a document request that stalls.

moments.title: Why the labels don't matter
moments.quote: If you guys have certain labels — and we don't care what the labels are — we're just going to make sure it attaches to sales process. That way Peter can have a two-minute conversation with Kate versus a twenty-minute conversation, so we can all start speaking the same language.
moments.why: Ties the pipeline work directly back to the leadership time problem from the debrief. The benefit is Pete's calendar, not a tidy CRM.

moments.title: Unprompted credit for the champion
moments.quote: Wow. You guys actually have definitions of what the pipeline stages mean. With billion-dollar companies, pipeline stages — we just use whatever was in the CRM, and they all don't mean the same thing.
moments.why: Colin built those definitions. Aaron praises them in front of Colin's father and benchmarks the company above much larger clients.

moments.title: Protects the paid session from discovery questions
moments.quote: Get that to us ahead of time. That'll allow us to not have to spend thirty minutes asking the question — we'll have the background and then we can hit the ground running and make the most of our time.
moments.why: Justifies the homework by the value of the session rather than by his own convenience.

moments.title: How the rep finds out
moments.quote: Kate will start to get involved in March. We'll send a clean email so she can start to block her calendar. That way it's not 'hey, starting tomorrow' — she's got a month in advance.
moments.why: The rep being assessed and coached is given a month's written notice rather than being ambushed. Small, and it protects the engagement.

moments.title: Paces the rollout down
moments.quote: We'll take one thing at a time. We'll just take one piece at a time. It'll be good.
moments.why: Said twice to a founder who had just explained he is drowning. Reassurance delivered as a scope limit.

coaching_notes: Call three of three, one week after the OMG debrief and the $1,950. Aaron runs a yes/no by not running one: he turns the floor over at 1:01, stays silent, and lets Peter announce the decision. Worth studying as the alternative to asking 'so, what did you decide?'

When the yes came with a delay, Aaron extended the delay further instead of defending the start date. Agreeing with a postponement you can afford is cheaper than arguing with a buyer who just said yes.
Within ninety seconds the call is pure sequencing — a date found live on screen, a short homework list, and who gets looped in when. Nothing is re-sold and the price is never mentioned again.
The Kate handling is the most transferable thing here: a month's notice by email so the rep being coached is never ambushed into a training schedule.

Transcript quirks: the Fireflies header dates the call April 12, 2025 (the upload date) and the filename says January 31; the body references starting 'the week of the 17th of February' and a February 20 session, which is consistent with a late-January call. Diarization is loose — at least one of Peter's answers sits under Speaker 1 — and 'Friday Book Club' is the running joke, not a real meeting.

coach_confidence: high — Speaker 2 runs the entire session and is addressed as "Brian" twice (0:54, 23:48). Caveat: Fireflies also dropped a few client lines into Speaker 2, including the 1:13 account update and the 39:32 question that begins "Brian, how do you feel about going around said person."

other_speakers.label: Speaker 1
other_speakers.who: A single merged bucket for the whole Precimac sales team — Jason, Nick, George, David and Hans are all named in the call but Fireflies gave them one shared label

headline: Negotiating-gambit training for an aerospace machining team
summary: Precimac sells precision machined parts to aerospace and defense OEMs — Triumph, SpaceX, Intermountain Turbine, Ozark Air Works, Vericore Power Systems — and its reps keep getting worked over by trained purchasing agents on government and OEM programs. Brian Kavicky spends the hour naming eleven gambits (flinch, competition-is-cheaper, lower authority, good cop/bad cop, hot potato, fait accompli, best and final, stonewalling, nibbling, changing the rules, splitting the difference, "you have to do better") and giving a preventive and an in-the-moment counter for each, all built on one rule: pre-decide your walk-away point and be willing to use it. The last eight minutes turn into a working session where the team names what they actually hit, and David lands on using deal-killing language to purge stalled quotes out of the pipeline.
outcome_note: Not a sales call — a recurring training session with an existing client that ends on "all right, let's have a great week" with no next step and no commitment asked for.

arc.label: Round-robin: anything positive happening
David surfaces the SpaceX problem
Brian frames the session: negotiating gambits
Selling vs negotiating, pain as the trump card
Rule one — know your walk-away point
The flinch and the parent-child response
Lower authority, bad cop, hot potato
Best and final, stonewalling, nibbling
Splitting the difference and "do better"
What the team actually runs into, live

milestones.text: What we're going to do today is I'm going to walk you through some negotiating gambits. These are all tactics that are used by purchasing people and professionally trained negotiators in order to have leverage on you during the process. So we're going to go through what their names are, we're going to go through why they work, and we're going to go through the counters of what you can do — sometimes to prevent, but sometimes how you respond.
Is there any negotiating tactics that you guys go, hey, we have this happen all the time? Is there any that we need to make sure we talk about that you guys are aware of happening?

moments.title: It is a game, and the game means they need you
moments.quote: A lot of this today, the emphasis is going to be recognizing that a game is being played with you, and respecting that that game is being played for a reason, which is leverage.
moments.why: Reframes manipulation from personal insult into information — the whole hour depends on reps hearing a gambit and feeling curious rather than scolded.

moments.title: Selling versus negotiating, defined
moments.quote: Selling is I get what I want on my terms. Negotiation is both parties entering with a perceived posture of win-win, but both parties are trying to actually create a win-lose.
moments.why: The cleanest two-sentence distinction in the file, and the premise for everything that follows.

moments.title: No pain, no negotiation
moments.quote: The rule we teach is no pain, no sale. You guys have been getting sales all the time with no pain. It's more: no pain, no negotiation — or less negotiation, or more leverage in the conversation if you have pain.
moments.why: He adapts the Sandler maxim on the fly to a quoting business that genuinely does close without pain, instead of insisting the rule applies as written.

moments.title: Decide the walk-away before you need it
moments.quote: First rule is, when negotiating, know your walk away point and be okay with going there if needed. Pre-decide what you're going to walk away from and when, so that when that point comes it's easy for you. If you don't decide, or it's wishy washy, or it's a moving target, that will cause you to be emotional.
moments.why: Every counter he teaches later is unusable without this; worth hearing why the decision has to be made in advance.

moments.title: Why a flinch actually hurts
moments.quote: The whole point of that reaction is it unlocks what's called the parent child response.
moments.why: He explains the mechanism — disproportionate reaction after a long cooperative stretch — which is what makes reps stop taking price objections personally.

moments.title: Princess and the pea: build up to the number
moments.quote: You ever ride a roller coaster? You get on the roller coaster, you put your seatbelt on, then they pull the lap bar down. I want you to pull your lap bar down. And this roller coaster also goes upside down, so you know the big shoulder harness thing — I want you to put that on, because I'm about to tell you it's expensive.
moments.why: A reusable script for taking the air out of a price flinch before the price is ever said.

moments.title: Answer "the competition is cheaper" by killing the deal
moments.quote: The biggest fix in the moment to this is to react by saying: so does that mean you're going to buy it from them?
moments.why: The single most repeated move in the hour — go straight to the deal-kill to find out whether the threat is real.

moments.title: Never negotiate with someone who cannot concede
moments.quote: The fix to this is: don't negotiate at all with anybody who can't offer a concession. You'd say, so if we lower our price to this level, does that mean you're committing to buy? And they'll say, well, I can't do that. You say, that's fine — I would like to present that price to the person who can actually commit, so we'll reserve it for that meeting.
moments.why: Converts a lower-authority gambit into a path to the decision maker, which is the outcome the rep wanted anyway.

moments.title: Turn a nibbler into a non-nibbler
moments.quote: You turn a nibbler into a non-nibbler by saying: ooh, that's an important thing. By the way, I'm sure there's other stuff. What's all the other stuff we should also be talking about right now?
moments.why: Short, polite, and immediately usable; he then adds that naming the tactic out loud is always fair game.

moments.title: Whoever names a number first loses
moments.quote: The rule of negotiation is the person who goes first is always the loser. So get them to go first and say, you know, I'd love to come down on it, I'd love to work with you, but I don't even know what's going to get it done. Can you tell me what gets it done?
moments.why: Comes with the reason it matters — salespeople discount themselves further than the buyer would have asked for.

moments.title: The team converts it into a decision
moments.quote: An easier way to get feedback and really just kill the deal and move on, rather than tie up our pipeline with stuff that we're not going to win anyway.
moments.why: The one place in the hour where training becomes an action — David applies deal-killing language to his own stalled quote log. Prospect-side payoff.

coaching_notes: Filed under FirstTimeConversations but it is not one — no prospecting, no qualifying, no next step. This is a recurring training session with an existing client. Useful for teaching negotiation, not for studying a first conversation.

Fireflies collapsed five named client voices (Jason, Nick, George, David, Hans) into a single "Speaker 1" and misattributed several of their lines to Speaker 2. Read speaker labels loosely; attribute by content.

The structure is the steal: name the tactic, explain the psychology that makes it work, then give both a preventive and an in-the-moment counter. Every counter is the same underlying move — mirror it and go straight to the deal-kill to test whether the threat is real.

The hour only becomes a working session in the last eight minutes, once he stops presenting and asks which gambits they actually see. The live exchange from 51:12 on is worth more than the first forty minutes.
He teaches at 52:30 that "the fix to a stonewall is always to get a next step" and then closes his own session without one. Worth flagging when this clip gets used in training.

coach_confidence: high — Tony greets him "Good morning, Rob" at 2:17, asks "Who's responsible, Rob?" at 13:18, and thanks "Rob" at 51:34. The filename's "Rob_Tony" is coach-then-prospect.

other_speakers.who: Tony — owner of Artisan Buildconstruct and currently its only salesperson

headline: Owner-only rainmaker buys a year of sales infrastructure
summary: Tony owns a design-build remodeling and construction firm, personally sells every job, and wants out of being the only rainmaker — a salesperson hired, a system built, and eventually a manager running it. Rob Lime opens by putting scope and money on the table before any detail: $42,000 for twelve months, immediately reframed as $3,500 a month and handed back as an ROI test. He then spends the rest of the call answering Tony's real objections — the time commitment, whether Rob understands a complex sales cycle, and whether the infrastructure Tony already has gets thrown away. Tony commits verbally at 13:26, pushes hard on hiring philosophy and contract terms, and the call ends with an MOU to send and a working session booked for Monday the 17th at 9:00 Central.
outcome_note: Tony committed verbally to $3,500 a month, asked for the MOU and payment terms, and booked Monday the 17th at 9:00 Central for the first working session.
