milestones.text: Let me kind of throw you a little bit of an idea of plan, scope, and then if this is close at all, before we talk about details, we could talk about money and time and stuff like that.

Tony restates what he is actually buying: salespeople in place, a system to train and onboard them, and himself out of day-to-day management. He has never led a sales organization and has been the only salesperson in the company.
Tony prices the dependency out loud — deals move when he is in front of the customer, and when he hands them to Zev or Leah they stall, nobody pulls the client to the next step, and the work drifts.
So the number that I wanted to try to ROI is 42,000. And that's for a year. That's a number for a year.
So if those were some of the results, does that money make sense?

The cool thing about my business is you could either visualize ROI-ing that number over 12 months, or you can't. If you can't, we have a problem. If you can, typically people don't mind writing a $3,500-a-month check.

Tony closes himself — "I'm game... I don't want to skirt around this. I'm going to tell you we're going to commit to the $3,500 a month" — and then immediately names the real objection, which is time, not money.

Tony names the basis he is actually deciding on: he cannot evaluate the expertise himself, so he is leaning on Kyle, a peer from his CEO forum and an existing Rob client, who told him to "just bite the bullet."
Monday the 17th at 9 Central.

I'm going to start with: tell me about what's going on in your personal sales. What are your instincts? Where can you get better? What would the measurable improvement look like — a higher margin, or deals close sooner, or I lose less to this one? I've got some basic two-way expectations that we'll clear, and then if we have time left over I would start with infrastructure, which is normally sales process.

moments.title: Scope first, money second, detail last
moments.quote: Let me kind of throw you a little bit of an idea of plan, scope, and then if this is close at all, before we talk about details, we could talk about money and time and stuff like that.
moments.why: He sequences the meeting so the fee lands before the feature list, which means the rest of the hour is spent justifying value to a man who has already heard the number.

moments.title: The number, said flat
moments.quote: So the number that I wanted to try to ROI is 42,000. And that's for a year.
moments.why: Six minutes into a 51-minute call. No softening, no range, no build-up — listen to how much time this frees up later.

moments.title: He lets "that is a big sum of money" sit
moments.quote: Yeah.
moments.why: One syllable in response to a price objection. Tony then does his own arithmetic out loud, gets it wrong by a factor of two, and Rob corrects the math instead of defending the fee.

moments.title: Hands the ROI test to the buyer
moments.quote: The cool thing about my business is you could either visualize ROI-ing that number over 12 months, or you can't. If you can't, we have a problem.
moments.why: Converts "is it worth it" from something Rob has to prove into something Tony has to answer, and gives him a clean exit if the answer is no.

moments.title: Three investments, not one
moments.quote: It's a great question, because you're making three investments — money, time, and then change capital. And most leaders aren't scared off by the number. The thing that we really have to figure out is the time, and I'm glad that you brought it up, so let's do it now, especially if it's going to be a problem.
moments.why: Names the objection category out loud and insists on handling it before signing rather than discovering it in month two.

moments.title: "Why does that give you pause?"
moments.quote: Why does that give you pause?
moments.why: The best question in the call. Tony had buried his real worry — that Rob thinks their sale is transactional — inside a ninety-second monologue, and one question pulled it out so it could be killed.

moments.title: Complex, not long
moments.quote: I don't ever want to say long sales cycle, because then we're kind of making an excuse of: it needs to be longer, it couldn't be shorter. I would say complex.
moments.why: A vocabulary swap that removes the owner's favorite reason nothing can be sped up, without arguing with him.

moments.title: "I'll never noodle with what's working"
moments.quote: I'll never noodle with what's working. I don't even care if what you're doing is the opposite of how I would do it. If it's working, why? No, I'm leaving it alone.
moments.why: Directly answers the fear every owner has about a consultant — that the consultant will rip out the systems the business actually runs on.

moments.title: You are already doing things you cannot explain
moments.quote: It's very likely that you are unconsciously, subconsciously, mindlessly doing repeatable things that aren't articulated. We need to take the things that you do and make them repeatable for other people.
moments.why: Reframes "build us a sales process" as documenting Tony's own winning behavior, which is both flattering and true, and sets up the first working session.

moments.title: Capabilities over experience, and the Mike Tyson test
moments.quote: I'm never going to shut up about prioritizing capabilities over experience. That's the problem when you pull somebody out of retail — they have no idea what it feels like to get your ass kicked in the way that you have to get your ass kicked to be successful at business development. So even if you know some things about dimensional lumber, it's like, I haven't seen you get punched in the face yet.
moments.why: He disagrees flatly with the client's hiring instinct, in a call where the client has already committed money. Watch how he frames it as a standing bias rather than a correction.

moments.title: No binding contract, by design
moments.quote: I don't do binding contracts, because number one, if someone else wants out, I also want out. And the four times in the last eight years where someone owed me money, the contract didn't help.
moments.why: Removes the last friction point by making the exit mutual, and justifies it with evidence rather than generosity.

coaching_notes: Not a first conversation — Rob and Tony have met before ("last we spoke") and this is the scope-and-price meeting. Watch it for how to put a number on the table early, not for discovery.

The fee is stated in minute six, before the program is explained, and re-anchored per month the moment Tony's arithmetic goes wrong. Rob never defends the number; he hands Tony the ROI test and lets him decide.
Best single move: "Why does that give you pause?" at 19:30. Tony had buried the real objection inside a long story about long sales cycles, and the question surfaced it in one beat.

He pre-sells the pushback — "most people do the opposite, and I go, why didn't you tell me this two months ago" — and tells Tony to keep doing it. Inviting objections in month zero is cheaper than discovering them in month three.

Transcript starts at 2:17 with dead air before it, and Fireflies garbles "sales cycles" as "bicycles" throughout and "go to market" as "go to mart." The filename date (March 4) disagrees with both the header date (March 14) and the in-call references to Friday the 14th and Monday the 17th.

coach_confidence: high — Annette addresses him as "Brian" at 6:23 and 28:00, and he speaks for Lushin throughout ("we tell people," "Sandler gives us 80% off," "our newest guy here").

other_speakers.label: Speaker 1
other_speakers.who: Annette — owner of Effectivity, a solo consulting and coaching practice prospecting into executive search firms; 25 years in recruiting

headline: Solo founder with no pipeline asks whether to quit
summary: Annette runs a one-person consultancy cold-calling executive search firms. She has just come off four weeks of flu, has nobody in her pipeline, and has exhausted her original 60-name list. Brian spends the first half as a tooling consult — stop researching prospects before calls, get to 14 touches before you give up on a name, buy Apollo rather than a CRM — and the second half on what she actually called about, which is whether to shut the business. He refuses the "tell me I don't have it" framing, reframes entrepreneurship as a bet on time rather than talent, and tells her to solve the income problem separately so the business gets more runway. She leaves committed to buying Apollo and building a 300-name call list.
outcome_note: A coaching call with an existing client, not a sale. It ends with Annette promising to pursue Apollo and have a 300-name list by the next conversation; no date is set.

Something flipped: she looks forward to calls now
She is out of names; the tooling question opens
Data tool vs CRM vs automation — do I need all three
Apollo's tiers, intent data, and what $59 buys

milestones.text: Annette names the actual problem: "I am going to networking, I'm making the calls, I'm not getting results, I have nobody in pipeline," and asks whether it even makes sense to spend money on tools when there is nothing to track.
Optimal is 6 per 45. Six for 45. You're a third of the way there to optimal.

And you've got to make the decision whether you're going to hang with it or not. If you can't hang with it, make a different decision. Because what I see is people leave it right before it gets good — they invest all this time, they just haven't seen the fruits of what they've invested. But if you can't do it, don't do it.
Annette sets her own price band for a data tool — the options she is vetting run $20 to $150 a month and she is trying to work out which one is worth a monthly commitment.

If you go to the basic, which is 50 bucks per month — 59 per month if you pay monthly — that is where it gives you a scheduling link and it gives you intent. Their hundred-dollar-a-month is where it adds in a dialer. For 99 bucks a month to do all that stuff, that's pretty good. And they'll do it monthly, which is what you should always start with.
Annette names her own next step — pursue Apollo and have a 300-name call list by the next conversation. No date is agreed and Brian does not ask for one.

moments.title: "Don't do any research"
moments.quote: We tell people, don't know that much. Don't do any research. Because any research you do starts to have you form assumptions.
moments.why: Counterintuitive enough to be worth stealing, and he qualifies it thirty seconds later: research is fine for qualification — is this even a real target — and should stop there.

moments.title: What "do you even know what we do" really means
moments.quote: They're telling you that what you're saying to them isn't relevant. And so the response is: is what I'm saying not relevant? What they're trying to do is trap you into a reason to get rid of you — that you don't know Jack about me. But what it really is about is that what you said was probably relevant, and they're just double checking it. You're hearing it as an interrogation.
moments.why: Reinterprets the most common cold-call stop sign as a relevance check, with a one-line response that sends the call back to pain.

moments.title: Whatever you rehearse, you summon
moments.quote: You're actually subconsciously preparing the conditions so that they will ask you. It's very strange — whatever you're worried about, you will find a way to make that happen.
moments.why: The payoff is Annette's own next line: "Well, then what I should worry about is how much money to charge them." She redirects her own rehearsal in one beat.

moments.title: Fourteen touches, not eight
moments.quote: When you hit about 14, you should be like, I'm done. Next. Because they're not going to call you back after that. There's a diminishing return after eight, but you've got to get to 14 to get to the average.
moments.why: Gives her a hard stopping rule and a hard minimum, which is what she was actually asking for when she said she was about to give up on a list.

moments.title: "Just please make it rain"
moments.quote: As you go through this next stage, you say: I'm going to do this stuff because I'm going to do this stuff, but just please make it rain. That's it. Give up control.
moments.why: He matches her stated frame of reference — she had just quoted Second Corinthians — rather than pushing a technique fix onto a motivation problem.

moments.title: Correcting the self-report before the activity
moments.quote: Hold on. You said I can't, but you found another path to get around gatekeepers. You have more traction than you had before, so be careful about that language.
moments.why: She says "I can't get anybody on the phone," he makes her restate it as "I haven't yet gotten many people," and the accurate version turns out to be a third of the way to optimal.

moments.title: The real math on her dial rate
moments.quote: That's why 45 attempts is typically a daily average for people, because you have to hit that to get enough. Optimal is 6 per 45.
moments.why: Two conversations out of 45 attempts sounded like failure until it was benchmarked. Worth hearing how fast a number dissolves a mood.

moments.title: The Rotary story, and its last line
moments.quote: But it started with her telling me she didn't need me.
moments.why: A four-minute war story about a prospect who was 45 minutes late, gave him 15 minutes, and said she didn't need sales — ending with the one line that makes the whole thing instructive.

moments.title: How to pick a networking group
moments.quote: Judge it by the strength in the room and who the people are, not what the structure is.
moments.why: Simple test, and he backs it with how he actually worked a Rotary chapter: prospect the strong people, and leave when you run out of them.

moments.title: Entrepreneurship is a bet on time
moments.quote: The entrepreneurship journey is about the risk of time and how it affects money. You're going to want the money, and the time is going to burn away, and you're going to go, wow, I'm out of money. But if you really believe in what you're doing, you solve the money problem differently. I've told people, why don't you wait tables on the weekends? If you really believe in this, solve the money problem.
moments.why: He separates "is the business viable" from "can I pay rent," which is the reframe that keeps her in. He also notes he has told other clients their idea was terrible — so this is not blanket encouragement.

moments.title: It gets worse before it gets better, on purpose

headline: VP tests her team's OMG data, then asks pricing
summary: Aaron ran OMG assessments across Fischer Homes' sales counselors — tops, middles, bottoms, plus two people already let go — and this hour is Emily, their VP of Sales, testing the data against people she knows cold. She arrives half-skeptical and uses her hardest cases to try to break the instrument: Brenda scored a 95 sales percentile and was fired, Katie is an elite coach with low commitment. Aaron answers each by narrowing what OMG claims to measure rather than defending it, then shows her the three kick-out triggers and benchmarks the whole team against 112,000 assessments. By the end she is asking whether she can run the current team through it for coaching, whether there is a management version for succession planning, and for pricing.
outcome_note: Emily asked for pricing in writing, a sample management assessment, and explicit permission to be chased; Aaron committed to send it the same day with his calendar link embedded so the next meeting books itself.

moments.title: Why you cannot interview for commitment

moments.title: The one desire question

moments.title: The close, as an either/or
moments.quote: You share either A, I have some more questions I want answered, or B, I got it, makes sense, here's how many hires we want, let's go.

coaching_notes: The prospect here is named Emily and is Fischer Homes' VP of Sales — not Emily Shaw. The coach is AP. Ben Kniffen sits in for the first half and his lines are merged into the coach's speaker label.

Aaron never defends OMG. Every objection is answered by making the tool's claim smaller — it does not measure likability, aptitude, culture fit, or anything outside sales — and he volunteers that he would score low on commitment himself. The restraint is what makes the rest land.

He gives away the good news for free at 24:49 and had done unpaid prep to do it, adding a 112,000-assessment average line to her sheet. Fear-selling a weak team would have been the easier play and a worse one.

The close is soft. He lets Emily ask what the next step is, answers with an either/or, and settles for sending pricing with a calendar link. Nothing is on the calendar when the call ends — on a VP who just told him she is standing up two new markets, a date in the room was available and not taken.

moments.title: Four questions that collapse the plan
moments.quote: Who's going to go through it with them? Who's going to help put it into everyday real life with them? Who's going to reinforce the pieces coming at them? Are you just going to rely on them to go, oh, I'll take this, and then go into our system to find the things?

moments.quote: It has nothing to do with personality, nothing to do with behavioral traits. It's literally: can and will somebody sell. moments.title: "Just don't do it"

moments.title: "What should I be asking you?" / "Literally nothing"
moments.quote: Literally nothing. The only other questions to ask after this point are more of the tactical implementation pieces, once there is somebody in play that can be the expert. Otherwise they're just premature questions, and now we're trying to solve problems that don't exist yet.
moments.why: The strongest line in the file. He refuses the invitation to keep selling and names exactly what has to be true before the conversation resumes.

moments.title: Why they will not just take the money
moments.quote: It sounds bad, but Todd, we're not going to let anyone just buy and go, because it loses its potency and then this thing backfires. It's not worth it.
moments.why: Turns a disqualification into a standard. The refusal becomes evidence of quality rather than a brush-off.

moments.title: The close on a no
moments.quote: Bottom line, Todd, we're here. You have my direct email. If you want to cut out the middleman, just come straight to me when the time comes. And if we can help, great. And if not, we'll help you figure out that we can't help.
moments.why: How to leave a deferred deal — no pressure, a direct channel, and the same honesty posture that got him this far.

coaching_notes: The whole call is one disqualification done well. Todd arrives ready to buy and Aaron refuses to sell, because the delivery mechanism — property managers interpreting findings in front of a rep — does not exist. That is the reason to listen to this file.
He asks permission before delivering bad news, and Todd actively invites it. Framing the objection as a favor bought him a hearing that a flat warning would not have gotten.

He names a real price unprompted — $550 a head — in the middle of explaining why it would be wasted. Todd notices and says so. A specific number attached to a warning reads as honesty, not as a quote.

"What should I be asking you?" / "Literally nothing" is the moment worth clipping. He declines to answer implementation questions before implementation is possible, on the grounds that they are premature and would have them solving problems that don't exist yet.

He leaves without a next step and without a follow-up date, which is defensible but means re-engagement depends entirely on Todd remembering; a soft calendar hold against the 2026 trainer hire would have cost nothing. Note also that the file header date (February 20) disagrees with the filename date (February 13).

milestones.text: From this conversation — and I don't see this taking an hour — we'll bring whatever clarity you absolutely want to make sure you get before we walk out of here. The reason why it's called initial draft: we are not going to be Morgan and James experts in one conversation. This is not Rob and Aaron go through something for 20 minutes and stop and say, so you got any questions. Just either say, wow, this was so far off, what are you guys even thinking — and then we can shake hands and part friends — or, I can see the path we're going down, this makes sense. And if that's the case, then we'll figure out when do we talk next, what do we talk next about, what are we figuring out then.

Morgan names the gap the program has to close: high dealer salesperson and technician turnover starting in the pandemic and still running, which means a large share of the field has no established customer relationships to lean on.
What do you think drove that turnover? And that may sound like a silly question.
And if you were to lick your finger and take a wild stab, what percent of all the sellers in the field do you think are two years or less?

Morgan names what he is judging on — the other vendors he spoke to "made it seem like they'd be able to connect the dots, but they were just going to pull something off their shelf," and he will not spend money on something that is not right for the 8,000 salespeople CNH has in North America.
So now what?
How many potential partners was that? Hey, we're going to litmus test down to the final two — or we're just going to bring in the one we think's best and then see what happens?

Morgan volunteers the deciding factor unprompted: "you guys were the only one who actually wanted to tailor to our specific business need. And at the end of the day, selling is selling — but those little details make a huge difference."
Let's just find a 15 minute block of time like the week after next or whatever works.
Morgan and Rob lock Tuesday, February 17th at 4:00 Eastern, with Aaron sending the invite plus the deck and recording that night.
Either the update is there is no update, or we took a drastic change and we're changing this to accounting training, or nope, we're on track, we need to get some dates.

moments.title: "The reason why it's called initial draft"
moments.quote: We are not going to be Morgan and James experts in one conversation. You'll see where we took the items that were the most relevant and key and impactful from your guys' perspective and wrapped the outcomes around it.
moments.why: Lowers the bar on his own deliverable before showing it, which converts every gap from a miss into an invitation.

moments.title: Rules out the presentation format out loud
moments.quote: This is not Rob and Aaron go through something for 20 minutes and stop and say, so you got any questions? No, we can just have a conversation. You guys aren't boring, so we won't do this in a boring way.
moments.why: Tells the buyer what kind of meeting this is going to be, which is why Morgan interrupts freely for the next forty minutes.

moments.title: Asks the question he thinks is silly
moments.quote: What do you think drove that turnover? And that may sound like a silly question.
moments.why: Morgan's honest answer — "to be honest, I don't know" — is more useful than a confident one, and it sets up the next question.

moments.title: "Lick your finger and take a wild stab"
moments.quote: And if you were to lick your finger and take a wild stab, what percent of all the sellers in the field do you think are two years or less?
moments.why: Thirty seconds after Morgan said he doesn't have the data, this gets a 30% estimate out of him — a number that justifies the entire program and came from the buyer's own mouth.

moments.title: Pays the buyer back for a correction
moments.quote: It may seem minor, but to your exact comments, when we walk through the next three pieces, that shifts how we have a conversation around certain things because of that nuance.
moments.why: Morgan apologises for adding "minor" points about Kubota and dealer contracts; Aaron tells him exactly which downstream sections his input changes. The buyer keeps contributing for the rest of the call.

moments.title: Checks comprehension, then offers proof on demand
moments.quote: Is this digestible for you guys? ... Is there anything here you'd like a real life example of?
moments.why: He doesn't illustrate by default — he waits to be asked. Morgan picks one, and gets a tight, specific answer about conquest accounts instead of four examples nobody wanted.

moments.title: "No you don't, because you're over 14"
moments.quote: It's more on the ones where we're doing quote reviews for the 15th time and we're over 14, and they go, but I've got a good relationship with them. No you don't — because you're over 14.
moments.why: The single sharpest line in the file, and it lands because Morgan immediately extends it: "they might like the lunch you buy them."

moments.title: Minimize objections, don't handle them
moments.quote: Let's not pride ourselves on being good at handling objections. Let's be phenomenal at minimizing them in the first place. Let's be real — some of us are on our B or C or D games from time to time, and you do have to handle them. That's just how life goes.
moments.why: States the philosophy and then undercuts the purism in the same breath, which is why it does not read as a slogan.

moments.title: Competitor or no decision?
moments.quote: Do you believe that when the sellers are in the field, is their biggest competition somebody using a competitor, or somebody doing nothing?
moments.why: When Morgan doesn't follow, Aaron explains it using CNH's own decision about Lushin as the example — the buyer is made to see his own buying process in the diagnostic.

moments.title: Rob's one line
moments.quote: The easiest way to get someone to do nothing is to confuse them.
moments.why: Lands on the back of Morgan's own admission that a few CNH product lines are "just cluttered" — seven tractors with the same PTO horsepower. Pure co-authoring.

moments.title: Gets the absent decision maker vouched for
moments.quote: And when you guys have piloted things internally before, do you ever have too many voices? ... Boom. That's all I needed to hear.
moments.why: James isn't on the call, so instead of rescheduling, Aaron has Morgan confirm that James keeps pilot groups the right size — and says exactly why that answer was what he needed.

moments.title: "Which basket you talking about?"
moments.quote: You say this basket — which basket you talking about?
moments.why: Morgan says he isn't putting all his eggs in this basket. Rather than let the ambiguity sit, Aaron makes him say it, and gets the clearest buying signal on the call plus the reason behind it.

coaching_notes: Chronology is inverted by the filenames. This 51-minute call is the first of the two CNH files — it ends by booking Tuesday, February 17th at 4:00 Eastern, which is the call stored under the 2026_02_17 "First Time Conversation" filename. The header date (February 28) is almost certainly wrong.

The curriculum walkthrough is a model of co-authoring rather than presenting. Every section ends with "anything here you think we're drastically off on?", and when Morgan adds a nuance Aaron names the downstream sections it changes. By the end the buyer is defending a program he helped build.

The best question is the one that was refused first. Morgan said he didn't have enough data on turnover; thirty seconds later "lick your finger and take a wild stab" produced the 30% figure that justifies the whole engagement.

He asks for the competition directly at 40:33 instead of hoping. Morgan names the competing vendor pilot and then volunteers, unprompted, the reason Lushin is winning — tailoring. That answer only exists because the question got asked.

The absent decision maker is handled well — no rescheduling, no re-presenting; he gets Morgan to vouch for James's judgment, then asks for the deck and recording so Morgan can catch James up himself. Transcription note: "Lushin" renders as "Lucian" at 43:20 and Rob Lime appears as "Bobby" in several places.
